# Tangen

The complete Tangen developer documentation, one page after another in the
order the documentation itself presents them. Every page below is part of the
public developer corpus; internal engineering notes are not included.

Each page begins with a `# <title>` heading and a `Source:` line giving its
canonical URL, so a passage can always be traced back to the page it came from.

These docs describe the current Tangen release line.

---

# Learn

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn
Section: Getting Started / Learn
Verification: executable

> Sequential tutorials that build something real, from an empty directory to a running site.

# Learn

Sequential tutorials that build something real, from an empty directory to a running site.

- **[Quick Start](/learn/quick-start)** - about 15 minutes. Create a project,
  define one content type, publish an article, query it with the SDK, and render
  it. The smallest complete loop, and the fastest way to know whether Tangen
  fits.

- **[Build the Enterprise Website](/learn/enterprise-website)** - the long
  form, in fourteen chapters. A realistic multilingual B2B site: eight content
  types, a page builder an editor can use, media, three languages, two forms, an
  automation that routes demo requests, and three deployments ending in a
  production boot.

Take the Quick Start first if you have never used Tangen. The Enterprise Website
assumes you have seen the loop once, and then stops assuming anything.

[Build with Tangen](/build) covers the same ground as individual tasks when you
want one answer rather than a sequence.

---

# Quick Start

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/quick-start
Section: Getting Started / Learn
Verification: executable

> From nothing to a running Tangen with one content type, published content, and a typed query rendering on your own page.

# Quick Start

About 15 minutes. At the end you will have Tangen running, one content type you
defined, a published article, and your own code rendering it.

## Before you start

| you need | why |
|---|---|
| **Bun** | Tangen runs on Bun |
| **PostgreSQL**, reachable, and an empty database | Tangen stores content in Postgres. There is no file-backed mode |

Create the database first:

```bash
createdb my_blog
```

Ports: the API uses **3000** and the Admin **3001** by default. Both are set in
the `.env` the scaffold writes, so change them there if something else has them.

## 1. Create the project

```bash
bunx @tangen/cli create my-blog \
  --name "My Blog" \
  --db "postgres://localhost:5432/my_blog"
```

```text
✓  Workspace "My Blog" created

Next steps:
  1.  cd my-blog
  2.  Create the database tables
      npx tangen bootstrap development
```

`--db` is checked before anything is written, so a wrong connection string fails
here rather than three steps later.

```bash
cd my-blog
bun install
```

<Warning>
Check the install output. If any `@tangen/*` package failed to resolve, stop and
fix that first - the scaffold reports success even when its install step could
not fetch a package, and every later step will fail confusingly.
</Warning>

## 2. The files that matter

Four, out of everything the scaffold wrote:

```text
app/
├── tangen.config.ts                     the CLI anchor
├── config/                              feature config (mail, storage, ai, ...)
├── content-objects/index.ts             the barrel of your content types
└── workspaces/my-blog/workspace.config.ts
.env                                     DATABASE_URL, PORT, JWT_SECRET
```

`app/config/` is **how the server runs**. `app/content-objects/` is **what your
content looks like**. Everything else can wait -
[Project structure](/build/getting-started/project-structure) has the rest.

## 3. Create the tables

```bash
bun run tangen bootstrap
```

```text
~  Content tables
✓  Bootstrap complete.
```

This creates Tangen's own tables in your database. You run it once per
deployment, before the first push.

**Why this is not part of `create`.** `tangen create` writes files and installs
dependencies; it touches no database. Bootstrap is the first thing that does, so
it is the step that fails loudly if your connection string is wrong - which is
much easier to read here than three steps later. `tangen dev` also migrates on
boot, so a project you start before you push will already have these tables; you
still need this command for **staging and production**, where you never run
`tangen dev`.

## 4. Define a content type

```bash
bun run tangen add object article
```

That writes `app/content-objects/article/schema.ts` and adds it to the barrel.
Open it and give it two fields:

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
import { defineObjectType, field } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineObjectType({
  name: 'article',
  label: 'Article',
  fields: {
    summary: field.textarea({ label: 'Summary' }),
    body: field.richtext({ label: 'Body' }),
  },
})
```

The field's **name is the key**, and each builder takes one object.

<Note>
You do not declare `title`, `slug`, `status` or the timestamps. Every content
type already has them, and declaring one is an error that names the field.
</Note>

Check it before you touch the database:

```bash
bun run tangen check
```

```text
○  Type-checking schema files...  ✓  Schema types OK
```

## 5. Push the schema

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

```text
~  Content tables
     + article: create table
~  Indexes
     + article: scope index
     + article: slug uniqueness

✓  content tables → generated/content-tables.ts
✓  types → generated/tangen-types.d.ts (1 content types)
✓  Schema applied to "development"
```

**Push prints its plan before it applies anything.** Read it - it is the last
point at which a mistake is cheap. Removing a field later needs an explicit
approval, and production refuses destructive changes outright.

It also wrote `app/generated/tangen-types.d.ts`. That file is why your query in
step 8 is typed without a generic. Commit it, never edit it, and re-run
`tangen types` if your editor falls behind.
[More on generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types).

## 6. Start Tangen

```bash
bun run dev
```

```text
[api]    workers   scheduler · webhooks · forms
[admin]  ready
```

The API is on `http://localhost:3000` and the Admin on `http://localhost:3001`.

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/health
# {"status":"ok","version":"…"}
```

## 7. Add content

Open **`http://localhost:3001`**. The first visit asks you to create the owner
account - email, password, done.

Then: **Content → Article → New**.

- **Title**: `Hello Tangen`
- **Slug**: `hello-tangen`
- **Summary**: `My first article.`

Save, then **Publish**.

<Check>
Article appears in the sidebar, and your item shows as **published** rather than
draft.
</Check>

The distinction matters for the next step: a read returns **published** content
only. A draft is invisible to your site until somebody publishes it.

## 8. Query it

Create a key the frontend can use. In the Admin: **Settings → API keys → New**,
label it `Quick Start`, grant **objects: read**, and copy the key - it is shown
once.

```bash
bun add @tangen/sdk
```

```ts app/read.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
})

const { data } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .props(['id', 'title', 'slug', 'summary'])
  .limit(10)
  .get()

for (const article of data) {
  console.log(`<article><h1>${article.title}</h1><p>${article.summary ?? ''}</p></article>`)
}
```

`objects('article')` is typed from the file push generated: the name is a
literal union, so `objects('articel')` is a compile error, and `data` is
`Article[]`.

<Note>
Put it under `app/`. The scaffolded `tsconfig.json` includes `app` and nothing
else, so a file at the project root gets none of the generated typing - it
still runs, it just stops catching your typos.
</Note>

## 9. Render it

```bash
TANGEN_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
TANGEN_API_KEY=tgn_your_key_here \
bun app/read.ts
```

```html
<article><h1>Hello Tangen</h1><p>My first article.</p></article>
```

<Check>
Your published article is there, and any draft is not. That is the whole loop:
schema you wrote, content someone published, typed data, your own output.
</Check>

Put that same query in a page component and you have a website. Tangen serves
the content; the routes, markup and styling are yours.

## If you code with an AI agent

`tangen create` already wrote the agent files into your project - you saw them
scroll past. The one that matters is the **Tangen Agent Skill**:

```text
skills/tangen-developer/SKILL.md      the skill itself
.claude/skills/…                      a discovery stub for tools that look there
AGENTS.md · CLAUDE.md · GEMINI.md     the guardrails
```

The skill is a procedure, not a copy of these pages: it tells an agent to look
before it touches, find the page that owns a contract at
[docs.tangen.app](https://docs.tangen.app), and prove the result against a
running server.

Two commands keep it current:

```bash
tangen ai init          # write the agent files into a project that has none
tangen skills update    # refresh them after upgrading @tangen/cli
```

`ai init` is for an **existing** project, or one scaffolded with `--no-ai`. A
fresh `tangen create` has already done it. `skills update` overwrites the
`tangen-*` skills and leaves any skill of your own alone.

More in [AI Agents](/ai).

## What you just used

| | where to go deeper |
|---|---|
| a content type in TypeScript | [Content modeling](/build/content-modeling) |
| `tangen push` and its plan | [The schema workflow](/build/getting-started/schema-workflow) |
| generated types | [Generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types) |
| draft and published | [Drafts and publishing](/build/content/publishing) |
| the query | [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) · [Using the SDK](/build/querying/sdk) |
| the API key | [Permissions](/reference/permissions) |

Then: [Globals](/build/globals) for site settings and navigation ·
[Localization](/build/localization) · [Forms](/extensions/forms) ·
[Search](/build/search) · [Extend Tangen](/extend) ·
[Deploying](/operate/deployment).

## If something went wrong

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| `could not connect to --db` | Postgres is not running, or the database does not exist. `createdb my_blog` |
| `A database that was never migrated has no registry` | you skipped step 3. Run `tangen bootstrap` |
| `field "slug" is built in` | you declared `title`, `slug` or `status`. Remove it |
| the query returns `[]` | the article is still a draft, or the key was issued on another deployment |
| your editor does not know `Article` | run `bun run tangen types` |
| a `@tangen/*` package failed to resolve | re-run `bun install` and read the output |

More: [Query troubleshooting](/build/querying/troubleshooting) ·
[Errors](/reference/errors).

# Build the Enterprise Website

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> A fourteen-chapter tutorial that builds a realistic multilingual B2B site on Tangen, composing every capability a real project uses.

# Build the Enterprise Website

You will build **Northwind Systems**, a fictional B2B infrastructure company:
eight content types, a page builder an editor can use, three languages, two
forms, an automation that routes demo requests, and three deployments ending
in a production boot.

It is not a blog with a title and a body. It is the shape of site people
actually get paid to build, and every chapter is executed against a running
server before it is published.

## What you end up with

| | |
|---|---|
| Content types | page, product, solution, person, category, article, caseStudy, download |
| Page blocks | hero, rich text, feature grid, stats band, CTA banner, FAQ |
| Globals | site settings, navigation, footer, SEO defaults |
| Locales | English, French, German, with per-field fallback |
| Forms | Contact Us and Request a Demo, submitted without a credential |
| Automation | a demo request branching on company size |
| Deployments | development, staging, production |
| SEO | a sitemap with hreflang alternates and a robots policy that differs by deployment role |

## The chapters

1. [Create the project](/learn/enterprise-website/create-the-project)
2. [Model the site](/learn/enterprise-website/model-the-site)
3. [Build reusable page blocks](/learn/enterprise-website/page-blocks)
4. [Add Globals and navigation](/learn/enterprise-website/globals-and-navigation)
5. [Add media and relationships](/learn/enterprise-website/media-and-relations)
6. [Seed and publish content](/learn/enterprise-website/seed-and-publish)
7. [Query with TangenQL and the SDK](/learn/enterprise-website/querying)
8. [Build dynamic frontend routes](/learn/enterprise-website/frontend-routes)
9. [Add localization](/learn/enterprise-website/localization)
10. [Add contact and demo forms](/learn/enterprise-website/forms)
11. [Automate demo requests with Flow](/learn/enterprise-website/flow)
12. [Deployments and permissions](/learn/enterprise-website/deployments)
13. [Cache and production](/learn/enterprise-website/production)
14. [SEO](/learn/enterprise-website/seo)

## How to read it

This tutorial **composes**; it does not re-explain. Each chapter says why the
site needs a capability, shows the exact integrated code, tells you what you
should see, and then links to the canonical page that owns the full contract.
When you want the complete rules for fields, TangenQL or Flow, follow the link:
that page is the authority, and this one only shows one project using it.

Every chapter is independently resumable. If you already have a Tangen project,
you can start at chapter 2 with your own workspace name.

## Prerequisites

- Bun, and a PostgreSQL you can create databases in
- [Quick start](/learn/quick-start) finished, or a willingness to meet the same
  material here at a slower pace

## The finished project

The complete implementation is `examples/enterprise-website` in the Tangen
repository. Every snippet in these chapters comes from that project, and a
guard fails the documentation build if the two disagree.

## Related

- [Quick start](/learn/quick-start) · [Build with Tangen](/build) ·
  [Resources](/resources)

# Create the project

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/create-the-project
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Scaffold Northwind Systems, create its database, and get the API, admin and a health check answering.

# 1. Create the project

**Goal** a running Tangen project called Northwind Systems, with an admin
account and a health endpoint that answers.

**Prerequisites** Bun, and a PostgreSQL you can create databases in.

## What we are building

Nothing yet. This chapter gets the platform running so the next thirteen have
somewhere to put the site.

If you have already finished [Quick start](/learn/quick-start), this is the same
setup with a different workspace name, and you can move faster.

## Steps

Create the database first. Tangen will not create it for you, and the error if
it is missing is the first one people hit:

```bash
createdb northwind_dev
```

Scaffold the project. The `--name` and `--db` flags skip every prompt, which is
also the form to use in CI:

```bash
bunx @tangen/cli create northwind \
  --name "Northwind Systems" \
  --db postgres://localhost:5432/northwind_dev
cd northwind
```

Create the tables. **Bootstrap comes before push**: bootstrap creates the system
tables that everything else needs, and `tangen push` on a database without them
stops and names this command.

```bash
bun x tangen bootstrap development
```

Start the API and the admin panel together:

```bash
bun run dev
```

Then open `http://localhost:3001` and create your admin account. You need it in
chapter 6.

## Expected result

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/health
{"status":"ok","version":"0.1.x"}
```

`?deep=1` adds a real database check, which is the one to use as a readiness
probe:

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/health?deep=1'
{"status":"ok","version":"0.1.x","checks":{"postgres":{"ok":true}}}
```

## Verification

- `http://localhost:3000/api/health` answers `ok`
- `http://localhost:3001` shows the admin panel and accepts your new account
- `app/` exists, with `config/`, `content-objects/`, `components/` and
  `workspaces/northwind-systems/`

## Why this matters

Two ports, two things. `3000` is the API your site reads; `3001` is the admin
your editors use. They are separate processes started by one command, and
`bun run dev` runs both.

## Common mistake

**Running `tangen push` first.** Push applies your schema; bootstrap creates the
database structure push writes into. The order is bootstrap, then push, and the
error message says so.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Quick start](/learn/quick-start) - the same ground, explained at length
- [CLI reference](/reference/cli) - every command and flag
- [Project structure](/build/getting-started) - what each directory is for
- [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables)

---

# Model the site

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/model-the-site
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Eight content types that follow the information architecture, and why each one exists.

# 2. Model the site

**Goal** eight content types in the database, generated types on disk.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 1](/learn/enterprise-website/create-the-project).

## What we are building

Northwind's information architecture:

```text
/
├── Products        Gridlock, Ledgerline
├── Solutions       Enterprise, Developers
├── Resources       Articles, Case studies, Downloads
├── Company         About, Careers, Contact
└── Legal
```

Three of those are marketing pages that an editor composes from blocks. The
rest are things with fields of their own, and that is the line the model draws:
**a page is a stack of blocks; everything that is not a page is a type.**

| type | exists because |
|---|---|
| `page` | marketing pages, composed not coded |
| `product` | a product has a tagline, a logo and a sort order a page does not |
| `solution` | the same products sold to a different audience, so it relates to products |
| `person` | an author is a record, so a name changes in one place |
| `category` | article taxonomy |
| `article` | prose with an author and categories |
| `caseStudy` | a client story with named metrics |
| `download` | a gated file |

## Steps

Write `app/content-objects/index.ts`. Two things to know before you do.

**Some fields already exist.** `title`, `slug`, `status`, `publishedAt`,
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy`, `updatedBy` and `id` are built in.
Declaring one is refused, with a message naming it. That is why no type below
has a title, and why `article` has no `publishedAt` even though it sorts by one.

**Top-level fields are a keyed map.** The key is the field name. Containers
(repeater, component) take the array form instead, which chapter 3 uses.

```ts app/content-objects/index.ts
import { defineSchema, defineObjectType, field } from '@tangen/cms'
import { PAGE_BLOCKS } from '../components'

/**
 * `path` is the routable URL and is authored, not derived: the IA nests
 * (/solutions/enterprise) and a slug alone cannot express that. Home is '/'.
 */
export const Page = defineObjectType({
  name: 'page',
  label: 'Page',
  plural: 'Pages',
  fields: {
    path: field.text({
      label: 'URL path',
      validation: { required: true, unique: true },
      admin: { helpText: 'Leading slash. The home page is "/".' },
    }),
    summary: field.textarea({ label: 'Summary', localized: true, admin: { helpText: 'Used as the meta description fallback.' } }),
    body: field.component({ label: 'Body', config: { components: PAGE_BLOCKS } }),
  },
})

export const Product = defineObjectType({
  name: 'product',
  label: 'Product',
  plural: 'Products',
  fields: {
    tagline: field.text({ label: 'Tagline', validation: { required: true }, localized: true }),
    summary: field.textarea({ label: 'Summary', validation: { required: true }, localized: true }),
    logo: field.media({ label: 'Logo', config: { accept: ['image'] } }),
    order: field.number({ label: 'Sort order', config: { default: 0 } }),
    body: field.component({ label: 'Body', config: { components: PAGE_BLOCKS } }),
  },
})
```

The remaining six follow the same shape. Take them from
`examples/enterprise-website/app/content-objects/index.ts`, which is the
complete file this tutorial is built from.

Note `localized: true` on `tagline` and `summary` and **not** on `order` or
`logo`. Localization is per field, and chapter 9 uses exactly these.

## Apply it

```bash
bun x tangen push
```

## Expected result

```text
✓  content tables → generated/content-tables.ts
✓  custom tables → generated/custom-tables.ts
✓  types → generated/tangen-types.d.ts (8 content types)
✓  Schema applied to "development"
```

Run it twice. The second run says `No schema changes`, because push compares
rather than replays.

## Verification

- push reports **8 content types**
- `app/generated/tangen-types.d.ts` exists and names your types
- the admin shows all eight in its sidebar

## Why this matters

`tangen push` writes three things: the database, the generated table map, and
your TypeScript types. They cannot disagree, which is what makes a typo in a
field name a compile error later rather than an empty page.

## Common mistake

**Declaring `title` or `slug`.** They exist already. The refusal names the
field, so read it rather than renaming around it.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Content modeling](/build/content-modeling) - the full modelling guide
- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) - every field type and its config
- [Type safety](/build/getting-started) - what the generated types give you
- [CLI: push](/reference/cli)

---

# Build reusable page blocks

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/page-blocks
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Six components an editor stacks into a page, and the difference between a component and a block.

# 3. Build reusable page blocks

**Goal** six reusable sections a marketer can stack into any page without a
developer.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 2](/learn/enterprise-website/model-the-site).

## What we are building

Northwind's marketing pages are all the same three or four shapes in different
orders. If each were a frontend template, every new landing page would be a
deploy. So the shapes become content.

| block | what it is |
|---|---|
| `hero` | headline, supporting line, image, up to two calls to action |
| `richText` | a prose section |
| `featureGrid` | a heading and a repeater of features |
| `statsBand` | a row of numbers |
| `ctaBanner` | a heading and one call to action |
| `faq` | question and answer pairs |

## Component and block are not synonyms

A **component** is the reusable definition you write with `defineComponent`. A
**block** is one instance of a component sitting in a content field. You define
components; an editor arranges blocks. The distinction matters the moment you
render, because a block carries a `_type` naming the component that produced it.

## Steps

Sub-fields of a component use the **array form**, not the keyed `field.*` map
that top-level type fields use. This is the single most common shape error.

```ts app/components/index.ts
import { defineComponent } from '@tangen/cms'

export const Hero = defineComponent({
  name: 'hero',
  label: 'Hero',
  description: 'Headline, supporting line, one or two calls to action.',
  fields: [
    { name: 'heading', label: 'Heading', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
    { name: 'subheading', label: 'Subheading', fieldType: 'textarea' },
    { name: 'image', label: 'Image', fieldType: 'media', config: { accept: ['image'] } },
    { name: 'primaryCta', label: 'Primary call to action', fieldType: 'link' },
    { name: 'secondaryCta', label: 'Secondary call to action', fieldType: 'link' },
  ],
})

export const FeatureGrid = defineComponent({
  name: 'featureGrid',
  label: 'Feature grid',
  fields: [
    { name: 'heading', label: 'Heading', fieldType: 'text' },
    {
      name: 'features', label: 'Features', fieldType: 'repeater',
      config: { fields: [
        { name: 'title', label: 'Title', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
        { name: 'body', label: 'Body', fieldType: 'textarea' },
      ] },
    },
  ],
})
```

The other four are in `examples/enterprise-website/app/components/index.ts`.

Then export the list the page field references. Chapter 2's `page` and `product`
both used `PAGE_BLOCKS`:

```ts app/components/index.ts
export const PAGE_BLOCKS = ['hero', 'richText', 'featureGrid', 'statsBand', 'ctaBanner', 'faq']

export default [Hero, RichText, FeatureGrid, StatsBand, CtaBanner, Faq]
```

Apply it:

```bash
bun x tangen push
```

## Expected result

Push reports no new tables. Blocks are stored inside the object's own column,
not in tables of their own, so adding a component changes what an editor can
put in a page without changing the database shape.

In the admin, opening a Page now offers an **Add block** control listing all
six.

## Verification

- the admin's Page editor offers six block types
- `bun x tangen push` reports `No schema changes` on a
  second run

## Why this matters

The `_type` on each stored block is the contract between the editor and your
frontend. Chapter 8 renders these with a function that switches on it, and an
unknown `_type` renders nothing rather than crashing, so adding a component
never takes the site down before the frontend knows about it.

## Common mistake

**Using the keyed `field.*` map inside a component.** Component sub-fields are
`{ name, label, fieldType, config }` objects in an array. The keyed builder is
for a content type's top-level fields.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Structuring content](/build/content-modeling/structuring-content) - the full contract
- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) - `fieldType` values for sub-fields
- [Repeaters](/build/content-modeling)

---

# Add Globals and navigation

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/globals-and-navigation
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Four Globals for site-wide content, including a menu an editor owns, and how to wire them into the workspace.

# 4. Add Globals and navigation

**Goal** four Globals, and a primary menu that lives in the CMS rather than in
frontend code.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 3](/learn/enterprise-website/page-blocks).

## What we are building

| global | holds |
|---|---|
| `site-settings` | name, tagline, logo, support and sales email |
| `navigation` | the primary menu, two levels |
| `footer` | a blurb, link columns, a legal line |
| `seo-defaults` | title suffix and default description |

None of this belongs in the frontend. An editor changes the sales address or
reorders the menu without a deploy, and that is the whole point.

## Steps

Globals are **not scaffolded**, so this chapter creates the directory and wires
it in by hand. Two steps, both required.

Global fields use the **array form**, like component sub-fields:

```ts app/globals/index.ts
import { defineGlobals } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineGlobals([
  {
    name: 'site-settings',
    label: 'Site settings',
    description: 'Identity and contact details used across the site.',
    fields: [
      { name: 'siteName', label: 'Site name', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
      { name: 'tagline', label: 'Tagline', fieldType: 'text' },
      { name: 'logo', label: 'Logo', fieldType: 'media', config: { accept: ['image'] } },
      { name: 'supportEmail', label: 'Support email', fieldType: 'email' },
      { name: 'salesEmail', label: 'Sales email', fieldType: 'email' },
    ],
  },
  {
    name: 'navigation',
    label: 'Navigation',
    description: 'The primary menu. Two levels, which is all this IA needs.',
    fields: [
      {
        name: 'primary', label: 'Primary menu', fieldType: 'repeater',
        config: { fields: [
          { name: 'label', label: 'Label', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
          { name: 'href', label: 'Link', fieldType: 'link', required: true },
          { name: 'children', label: 'Sub-items', fieldType: 'repeater', config: { fields: [
            { name: 'label', label: 'Label', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
            { name: 'href', label: 'Link', fieldType: 'link', required: true },
          ] } },
        ] },
      },
    ],
  },
])
```

Then wire it into the workspace config. Nothing does this for you:

```ts app/workspaces/northwind-systems/workspace.config.ts
import globals from '../../globals'

export default defineWorkspace({
  // …
  components,
  globals,
})
```

```bash
bun x tangen push
```

## A menu item is a link, not a string

`href` is `fieldType: 'link'`, not text. A link stores what it points at rather
than where that thing currently lives, so renaming a page's path does not leave
the menu pointing at a 404. Chapter 8 resolves them.

## Expected result

Push applies cleanly, and the admin sidebar gains a **Globals** section with
your four entries, each editable as a single record.

## Verification

- the admin shows Globals: Site settings, Navigation, Footer, SEO defaults
- editing Site settings and saving succeeds

## Common mistake

**Forgetting to wire `globals` into the workspace config.** The file compiles,
push succeeds, and nothing appears in the admin. There is no error, because
from the platform's side you simply declared no Globals.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Globals](/build/globals) - defining, reading, and the response shape
- [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links) - what a link stores
- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration) - the workspace config

---

# Add media and relationships

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/media-and-relations
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Upload real assets, reference them from content, and relate types to each other.

# 5. Add media and relationships

**Goal** files uploaded through the API and referenced from content, and types
that point at each other.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 4](/learn/enterprise-website/globals-and-navigation).

## What we are building

Northwind's relations are all editorial facts, not demonstrations:

```text
solution  → products      a solution is sold THROUGH products
article   → person        an author, so a name changes in one place
article   → category      taxonomy
caseStudy → product       which product the story is about
```

And its media: a logo in Site settings, a hero image on the home page and on an
article, two author photos, one PDF.

## Relations, in the model

You already wrote these in chapter 2. This is what they mean:

```ts
// A solution is sold through products, so the relation is the point of the type.
products: field.relation({ label: 'Products', config: { targetType: 'product', many: true } }),

// Authorship is a relation, not a string.
author: field.relation({ label: 'Author', config: { targetType: 'person' } }),
```

A relation stores an id. It becomes the full record when you ask for it with
`.depth(1)`, which chapter 7 does.

## Uploading

Media is **multipart**, so it is one of the few things that does not go through
the SDK. Note the response envelope: `{ asset }`, not the `{ data }` every
content route returns.

```ts scripts/seed.ts
async function upload(file: string): Promise<string> {
  const body = new FormData()
  body.append('file', new File([await Bun.file(`${import.meta.dir}/../assets/${file}`).arrayBuffer()], file))
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/media/upload`, {
    method: 'POST', headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${TOKEN}` }, body,
  })
  const json: any = await res.json().catch(() => null)
  const id = json.asset.id as string
  return id
}
```

Then reference the returned id from any media field:

```ts
await create('person', { role: 'Principal Engineer', avatar: await upload('ava-owen.png') },
  'Ava Owen', 'ava-owen')
```

## Two shapes, one field

This is worth knowing before chapter 8 renders anything:

- a media field on a **content object** expands to the full asset under
  `.depth(1)`
- the same field on a **Global** comes back as the **bare id string**, because
  Globals have no depth

Both are enough to build an image URL, since a transform only needs the id.

## Expected result

```bash
curl -s "$API/media?limit=1" -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

returns assets with `id`, `originalName`, `mimeType`, `width`, `height` and
`altText`. The Admin's Media section shows them.

## Verification

- five assets exist: three PNGs, one PDF, one logo
- a `download` object has a `file` that expands under `.depth(1)`
- the Admin's Media library lists them

## Common mistake

**Expecting `tangen.media.upload()`.** Uploading is REST and multipart. Reading
and URL building are on the SDK's `media` accessor.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Media](/build/media) - upload, transforms, variants, rendering
- [Relations](/build/content-modeling/relations) - many, depth, and back-references
- [Fields reference](/reference/fields)

---

# Seed and publish content

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/seed-and-publish
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Enough content to render the whole site, and the draft-to-published rule that explains an empty frontend.

# 6. Seed and publish content

**Goal** the site's content in the database, published, and the publishing rule
understood before it confuses you.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 5](/learn/enterprise-website/media-and-relations),
and an admin account from chapter 1.

## The rule that explains everything later

**A read returns published content only.** A draft is invisible to the Delivery
API. When chapter 8's frontend returns nothing, this is almost always why.

So the seed script creates *and* publishes:

```ts scripts/seed.ts
async function create(type: string, values: Record<string, unknown>, title: string, slug: string) {
  const found = await call('POST', `/objects/${type}/query`, { query: { slug: { eq: slug } }, limit: 1 })
  // Update, do not skip. A seed that only creates looks idempotent and is not:
  // edit a value here, re-run, and the old record silently survives.
  const id: string = found?.data?.length
    ? ((await call('PATCH', `/objects/${type}/${found.data[0].id}`, { title, ...values })).data.id as string)
    : ((await call('POST', `/objects/${type}`, { title, slug, ...values })).data.id as string)
  // Publishing is what makes it visible to the Delivery API, and a republish
  // is also what makes an edited translation visible.
  await call('POST', `/objects/${type}/${id}/publish`, {})
  return id
}
```

## Getting a token

The seed writes as a member, so it needs an admin token:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workspaceId":"wsp_northwind_systems","email":"you@example.com","password":"…"}' \
  | jq -r .accessToken)
```

Two things about that URL. The admin login is `/api/auth/login`, **not** under
`/api/v1` like everything else. And the response key is `accessToken`.
`/api/v1/ext/auth/login` is site-user authentication (the Site users
extension), a different system, and it fails with a message about a missing
API key that reads like a bug when you are looking for the admin login.

## Run it

```bash
API=http://localhost:3000/api/v1 TOKEN=$TOKEN bun scripts/seed.ts
```

Take `scripts/seed.ts` from `examples/enterprise-website`. It creates two
products, two solutions, two people, two categories, two articles, one case
study, one download, six pages and all four Globals.

## Expected result

```text
seeded
```

and, counted through the API:

```text
page 6 · product 2 · solution 2 · article 2 · caseStudy 1 · download 1 · person 2 · category 2
```

## Verification

- the admin lists content under every type
- a published page is readable with a delivery key (chapter 7 makes one)
- re-running the seed changes nothing and fails nothing

## Why this matters

The seed is the deterministic equivalent of an editor's afternoon. You would not
ship one, but you want the site's data reproducible while you are building it,
and you want it to survive being run twice.

## Common mistake

**Creating without publishing.** The object exists, the admin shows it, and the
site cannot see it. Nothing warns you, because a draft is a legitimate state.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Publishing and visibility](/build/content/publishing) - the full contract
- [Content API](/reference/delivery-api) - create, update, publish, delete
- [Authentication](/reference/authentication) - which login is which

---

# Query with TangenQL and the SDK

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/querying
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> A delivery key, and the six queries this site actually needs.

# 7. Query with TangenQL and the SDK

**Goal** a scoped API key, and every query the frontend needs, executing.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 6](/learn/enterprise-website/seed-and-publish).

## Make a delivery key

In the Admin: **Settings → API keys → New**. Label it `Northwind website`, and
grant read on **objects**, **globals**, **media** and **forms**. The key is
shown once.

Scope it to what the site reads and nothing more. A website never writes, and a
key that can write is a key that can be made to write.

Creating one through the API instead, the permission shape is a map of scopes to
actions, not a list:

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/api-keys' \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"label":"Northwind website",
       "permissions":{"objects":{"actions":["read"]},"globals":{"actions":["read"]},
                      "media":{"actions":["read"]},"forms":{"actions":["read"]}}}'
```

`{"objects":["read"]}` is refused with a 422 naming every scope that got it
wrong. The key comes back once, on `data.key`.

Your server process then needs two variables:

```bash
TANGEN_API_URL=http://localhost:3000     # the Tangen API, not the admin
TANGEN_API_KEY=tgn_…                     # the key above
```

**This key is a server credential.** It goes in the environment of your server
process. A key in a browser bundle is a public key.

```bash
bun add @tangen/sdk
bun add -d @types/bun
```

`@types/bun` is what makes `Bun.file` and `import.meta.dir` typecheck in the
scripts and the server. Add `"bun"` to `types` in `tsconfig.json`, and add
`web` and `scripts` to `include` - the scaffold covers `app` only, so without
this the site's own code is never typechecked.

```ts web/server.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
})
```

## The six queries

**A page by its path.** The commonest query a website makes:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('page')
  .where({ path: { eq: '/company/about' } })
  .limit(1)
  .get()
```

**A list, sorted, with only the fields the card needs:**

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('product')
  .props(['id', 'title', 'slug', 'tagline'])
  .sort('order', 'asc')
  .get()
```

`props` is worth using on list pages. It is the difference between shipping a
card and shipping every block body on the page.

**A relation, expanded:**

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('article')
  .depth(1)                       // author and categories become records
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .limit(10)
  .get()

data[0].author.title              // 'Ava Owen'
```

**One thing by slug:**

```ts
const [item] = (await tangen.objects('product')
  .where({ slug: { eq: 'gridlock' } })
  .limit(1)
  .get()).data
```

**A Global.** Note the extra unwrap: values sit at `data.values`, unlike
objects, which return rows at `data`:

```ts
const settings = (await tangen.globals('site-settings').get()).data.values
settings.siteName          // 'Northwind Systems'
```

Wrap it once and stop thinking about it:

```ts
const global = async (name: string) => (await tangen.globals(name).get()).data.values
```

**A miss.** An unmatched query is an empty array and a `200`, not an error. Your
route decides what a miss means, which for a website is a 404.

## Expected result

Every query above returns data. The article query's `author` is an object with
a `title`, not an id string.

## Verification

- a page query by `path` returns exactly one row
- `depth(1)` expands `author` into a record
- `tangen.globals('site-settings')` returns your seeded values
- an unknown slug returns `{ data: [] }` with status `200`

## Common mistake

**Writing the wire body by hand and putting the filter at the top level.** The
filter goes under `query`. A stray top-level key used to be dropped silently;
it is refused now, and the message names `query`.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) - every operator, boolean groups,
  pagination, depth, and what it refuses
- [SDK reference](/reference/sdk) - the client, cancellation, retries
- [Globals](/build/globals) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions) - key scopes

---

# Build dynamic frontend routes

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/frontend-routes
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Thirteen routes driven by CMS slugs, a block renderer, and media on the page.

# 8. Build dynamic frontend routes

**Goal** the site rendering: every route from CMS data, blocks rendered,
images and files served.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 7](/learn/enterprise-website/querying).

## What we are building

```text
/                                     the home page, from blocks
/products  /products/<slug>
/solutions /solutions/<slug>
/resources /resources/articles /resources/articles/<slug>
           /resources/case-studies /resources/case-studies/<slug>
           /resources/downloads
/company/<slug>  /legal/<slug>        pages, matched by their authored path
```

## Framework

This tutorial uses a plain `Bun.serve` HTTP server. That is deliberate: it keeps
the Tangen part visible instead of buried in a framework's conventions.
Everything here is ordinary `fetch` and string templates, and the data layer
moves to Next, Astro or anything else unchanged.

The one line worth copying exactly:

```ts web/server.ts
const server = Bun.serve({
  // WEB_PORT, not PORT: Bun auto-loads the project's .env, where PORT is the
  // TANGEN API's port. A frontend reading PORT here binds 3000 and collides
  // with the API it is trying to read from.
  port: Number(process.env.WEB_PORT ?? 4321),
  async fetch(req) { /* … */ },
})
```

## Rendering blocks

One function, switching on `_type`. An unknown block renders nothing rather
than crashing, so adding a component in the admin never takes the site down
before the frontend knows about it:

```ts web/server.ts
function block(b: any): string {
  switch (b?._type) {
    case 'hero':
      return `<section class="hero"><h1>${esc(b.heading)}</h1>${b.subheading ? `<p class="lede">${esc(b.subheading)}</p>` : ''}
        ${img(b.image, 1200, 'hero-image')}
    case 'richText':
      return `<section class="prose">${b.body ?? ''}</section>`
    // …
    default:
      return ''
  }
}
```

## Rendering media

`transformUrl` is a method on the client's `media` accessor. It only builds a
URL, and transforms serve **without a key**, which is why a browser can load one
directly:

```ts web/server.ts
function img(asset: any, w: number, cls = ''): string {
  // A media field on a CONTENT OBJECT expands to the asset under depth(1). The
  // same field on a GLOBAL comes back as the bare id string. Accept both.
  const id = typeof asset === 'string' ? asset : asset?.id
  if (!id) return ''
  const meta = typeof asset === 'string' ? {} : asset
  const src = tangen.media.transformUrl(id, { width: w, format: 'webp' })
  return `<img${cls ? ` class="${cls}"` : ''} src="${esc(src)}" alt="${esc(meta.altText ?? '')}"${
    meta.width ? ` width="${meta.width}" height="${meta.height}"` : ''} loading="lazy">`
}
```

The alt text is `altText`, not `alt`. For a PDF use `tangen.media.fileUrl(id)`:
a transform of a PDF is a mistake.

## Rendering navigation

The menu is a Global, so the header is data:

```ts
const nav = await global('navigation')
const menu = (nav.primary ?? []).map((i: any) =>
  `<li><a href="${href(i.href)}">${esc(i.label)}</a>${
    i.children?.length
      ? `<ul>${i.children.map((c: any) => `<li><a href="${href(c.href)}">${esc(c.label)}</a></li>`).join('')}</ul>`
      : ''}</li>`).join('')
```

`href()` turns a stored link into a URL. Because a link stores identity rather
than a path, this is where routing lives, in one function.

## Run it

```bash
TANGEN_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 TANGEN_API_KEY=$TANGEN_API_KEY \
  bun web/server.ts
```

## Expected result

```text
northwind web on http://localhost:4321
```

`http://localhost:4321/` shows the hero with its image, the stats band, the CTA,
a two-level menu from the Global, and the footer. `/nope` returns 404.

## Verification

- thirteen routes answer `200`, and an unknown path answers `404`
- the home page carries two images: the logo from Site settings and the hero
- `/resources/downloads` links to a PDF that downloads

## Common mistake

**Reading `PORT` in the frontend.** The project's `.env` sets it for the API.
Your site will try to bind the port the API is already on.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Frontend integration](/build/frontend) - the patterns, framework by framework
- [Media](/build/media) - transforms, variants, rendering
- [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links)
- [Structuring content](/build/content-modeling/structuring-content)

# Add localization

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/localization
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> English, French and German, per-field, with the republish rule that catches everyone.

# 9. Add localization

**Goal** the site in three languages, with translations visible on the frontend
and untranslated fields falling back.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 8](/learn/enterprise-website/frontend-routes).

## Not every field is translated

Northwind marks `localized: true` on the fields a translator actually owns: a
product's `tagline` and `summary`, a page's `summary`, an article's `excerpt`
and `body`. Not on `order`, not on `logo`, not on relations. Localization is
per field, and marking everything creates work nobody does.

## Steps

**Enable it.** This rewrites your workspace config and reports every change it
makes:

```bash
bun x tangen enable localization
```

**Add the locales** in the file it created:

```ts app/config/localization.ts
import { defineLocalizationConfig } from '@tangen/cms'

export const localizationConfig = defineLocalizationConfig({
  enabled: true,
  defaultLocale: 'en',
  locales: [
    { code: 'en', label: 'English' },
    { code: 'fr', label: 'Français' },
    { code: 'de', label: 'Deutsch' },
  ],
})
```

**Apply it.** Push creates a `<type>_i18n` side table per localized type. The
default locale stays in the main table; translations live beside it:

```bash
bun x tangen push
```

```text
+ page_i18n: create side table
+ page_i18n.summary: add localized column TEXT
+ product_i18n: create side table
+ product_i18n.tagline: add localized column TEXT
```

## Writing a translation

A locale-scoped `PATCH`, then a **republish**:

```ts scripts/translate.ts
async function translate(type: string, id: string, locale: string, values: Record<string, unknown>) {
  await call('PATCH', `/objects/${type}/${id}?locale=${locale}`, values)
  await call('POST', `/objects/${type}/${id}/publish`, {})
}

await translate('product', gridlock, 'fr', {
  tagline: "Une ingestion qui ne perd aucun événement",
})
```

**The republish is the whole trick.** A locale-scoped write returns `200` and
writes the side row, but the Delivery API keeps serving the published snapshot.
Without that second line every translation is invisible to the site while every
write looks successful. This costs people an afternoon; it is the single most
important sentence on this page.

## Reading a locale

On the SDK, `.locale()` is a builder method:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('product')
  .locale('fr')
  .where({ slug: { eq: 'gridlock' } })
  .limit(1).get()

data[0].tagline    // 'Une ingestion qui ne perd aucun événement'
```

If you call the query route directly, `locale` is a **top-level key of the
request body**. A `?locale=fr` on that route is ignored rather than refused, so
you get a `200` carrying English and it looks like a missing translation.

## Locale-prefixed routes

The site serves `/fr/...` and `/de/...` by taking the prefix off the path and
passing the rest through the same routes:

```ts
const seg = url.pathname.split('/')[1]
const locale = ['fr', 'de'].includes(seg) ? seg : 'en'
const path = locale === 'en' ? url.pathname : url.pathname.slice(locale.length + 1) || '/'
```

Links stored in the CMS are default-locale form, so the site adds the prefix:

```ts
const L = (p: string) => (locale === 'en' || !p.startsWith('/') ? p : `/${locale}${p === '/' ? '' : p}`)
```

## Expected result

| route | shows |
|---|---|
| `/products/gridlock` | Streaming ingestion that does not drop events |
| `/fr/products/gridlock` | Une ingestion qui ne perd aucun événement |
| `/de/products/gridlock` | Streaming-Ingestion, die keine Ereignisse verliert |

And `<title>` on `/fr/company/about` is `À propos`.

## Fallback

`/fr/company/careers` has no French translation and still renders, in English.
Fallback is **per field**, to the default locale, so a half-translated record
shows French where it has French and English where it does not.

## Verification

- the three product routes above show three different taglines
- `/fr/company/careers` returns `200` with English content
- a translation written without a republish is not visible, and is after one

## Common mistake

**Translating and not republishing.** See above. It is not a warning you will
get; it is one you have to remember.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Localization](/build/localization) - the full model, side tables, fallback
- [TangenQL: locale](/reference/tangenql) - the wire form
- [SDK reference](/reference/sdk) - `.locale()`

---

# Add contact and demo forms

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/forms
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Two forms, rendered from a public schema and submitted without a credential.

# 10. Add contact and demo forms

**Goal** Contact Us and Request a Demo on the site, validated and storing
submissions.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 9](/learn/enterprise-website/localization).

## What we are building

**Contact Us**: name, email, company, message.

**Request a Demo**: name, business email, company, role, **company size**,
country, message. That company size field is not decoration. Chapter 11 branches
on it, and this is where the two capabilities meet.

## Enable Forms

Forms is a built-in capability, not an installed extension, so it is `enable`
and not `extension install`:

```bash
bun x tangen extension install forms
```

## Define them

A form is data, created through the API:

```ts scripts/forms.ts
const forms = [
  {
    name: 'Request a Demo', slug: 'request-a-demo',
    fields: [
      f('n', 'text', 'name', 'Your name', { required: true }),
      f('e', 'email', 'businessEmail', 'Business email', { required: true }),
      f('c', 'text', 'company', 'Company', { required: true }),
      f('r', 'text', 'role', 'Role'),
      f('s', 'select', 'companySize', 'Company size', { required: true, options: [
        { label: '1-50', value: '1-50' }, { label: '51-500', value: '51-500' }, { label: '500+', value: '500+' },
      ] }),
      f('m', 'textarea', 'message', 'What would you like to see?'),
    ],
    settings: { notifications: [], uniqueBy: 'none', successTitle: 'Request received', successMessage: 'An architect will contact you.', submitButtonText: 'Request a demo' },
  },
]

const body = { ...form, isLive: true }
await call('POST', '/forms', body)
```

`isLive` is what makes the public schema route answer. A form that is not live
exists and still 404s to your frontend.

## Rendering one

The schema route is **public**: no credential, and it takes the slug. This is
what a frontend uses, and a delivery key correctly cannot list forms:

```ts web/server.ts
  const schema = await fetch(`${base}/api/v1/forms/${encodeURIComponent(slug)}/schema`)
    .then((r) => (r.ok ? r.json() : null)).catch(() => null) as any
  const f = schema?.data ?? schema
  if (!f?.fields) return '<p>Form unavailable.</p>'
```

The response carries a `submitUrl`. **Use it** rather than composing one:

```ts
`<form method="post" action="${form.submitUrl}">…</form>`
```

## Submitting

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/embed/forms/<id>/submit \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Dana Reyes","businessEmail":"dana@harbourline.test",
       "company":"Harbourline Freight","companySize":"500+","country":"GB"}'
```

Public, no credential, a flat body. A missing required field comes back keyed by
field name, using your labels:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "status": 400, "fieldErrors": {
  "businessEmail": "Business email is required",
  "companySize": "Company size is required" } } }
```

## Who can read submissions

| caller | result |
|---|---|
| anonymous | `401` |
| a delivery key | `403` |
| a member | `200` |

The public half of Forms is deliberately narrow: render the schema, accept a
submission. Everything else is behind an admin session.

## Expected result

`/company/contact` renders both forms with eleven inputs between them. A valid
demo submission returns your success message.

## Verification

- `GET /api/v1/forms/request-a-demo/schema` answers with **no** credential
- a submission missing required fields returns `400` naming each one
- a valid submission returns `submitted: true`
- the submissions list is `401` anonymous, `403` with a delivery key, `200` as a
  member

## Common mistake

**Composing the submit URL.** It is on the schema response. The embed path
differs from the API path, and guessing it produces a 404 that looks like a
disabled form.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Forms](/extensions/forms) - fields, validation, notifications, settings
- [Forms: submissions](/extensions/forms/submissions) - reading and exporting
- [Permissions](/reference/permissions)

---

# Automate demo requests with Flow

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/flow
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> Route a demo request by company size, branching on what the visitor actually submitted.

# 11. Automate demo requests with Flow

**Goal** an enterprise-sized demo request routed differently from everyone
else, triggered by a real public submission.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 10](/learn/enterprise-website/forms).

## What we are building

```text
Request a Demo submitted
        │
   companySize = '500+' ?
        ├── yes → the field team
        └── no  → the standard queue
```

This is the chapter where the site stops being a set of separate features. The
form from chapter 10 feeds an automation, with no glue code in between.

## Install Flow

Flow ships with the platform and is already declared in
`app/config/extensions.ts`. Installing and enabling is per deployment:

```bash
bun x tangen extension install flows
bun x tangen extension list
```

## The submission arrives whole

The trigger payload carries the submission **hydrated**, not just its id:

```ts
trigger.submission = { id, formId, formSlug, values, createdAt }
```

So the condition reads the answer directly. No lookup step, no code step:

```ts scripts/flow.ts
const flow = {
  version: 2,
  name: 'Route demo requests',
  enabled: true,
  nodes: [
    { id: 'start', kind: 'trigger', position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
      data: { type: 'form.submitted', formSlug: 'request-a-demo' } },
    // The submission arrives HYDRATED: trigger.submission carries id, formId,
    // formSlug, createdAt and the submitted `values`. So the branch reads the
    // answer directly - no code step needed to fetch or reshape anything.
    { id: 'gate', kind: 'condition', position: { x: 0, y: 100 },
      data: { conditions: [{ path: 'trigger.submission.values.companySize', op: 'eq', value: '500+' }] } },
    { id: 'hot', kind: 'action', position: { x: -160, y: 220 },
      data: { action: 'log', config: {
        message: 'ENTERPRISE demo request from {{trigger.submission.values.company}} ({{trigger.submission.values.businessEmail}}) - route to the field team',
      } } },
    { id: 'standard', kind: 'action', position: { x: 160, y: 220 },
      data: { action: 'log', config: {
        message: 'demo request from {{trigger.submission.values.company}} (size {{trigger.submission.values.companySize}}) - standard queue',
      } } },
  ],
  edges: [
    { id: 'e1', from: 'start', to: 'gate' },
    { id: 'e2', from: 'gate', to: 'hot', outlet: 'yes' },
    { id: 'e3', from: 'gate', to: 'standard', outlet: 'no' },
  ],
}
```

Two shapes to note. A condition's `path` is a plain expression path with no
braces. A message uses `{{…}}` because it interpolates into text. They address
the same data.

`log` is the honest placeholder here. Swap it for `email` or `http` when you
have somewhere to send this, and nothing else in the flow changes.

## Create it

```bash
API=http://localhost:3000/api/v1 TOKEN=$TOKEN bun scripts/flow.ts
```

Flow's admin routes are under `/api/v1/admin/ext/flows/` and are
member-authenticated. `/api/v1/ext/*` mounts only public and key routes, which
is why these are not there.

## Run it for real

Submit the form twice, from the site or with curl: once with `companySize:
"500+"`, once with `"1-50"`.

## Expected result

```text
completed | path: start->gate->hot
    gate     : {"result": "yes"}
    hot      : {"message": "ENTERPRISE demo request from Harbourline Freight (dana@harbourline.test) - route to the field team"}

completed | path: start->gate->standard
    gate     : {"result": "no"}
    standard : {"message": "demo request from Tidecraft (size 1-50) - standard queue"}
```

`path` is the route the run actually took, which is the fastest way to see which
branch ran.

## Verification

- two runs exist, one per branch
- each run's `path` ends at a different node
- the message contains the company the visitor typed

## Common mistake

**Ignoring the message on a refused graph.** A graph Flow cannot enable comes
back as a `422` whose message is the whole diagnosis: "Loop node l needs its
'body' outlet connected", "The action 'x' on node a is not available in this
environment". It names the node, so read it before changing anything else.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Flow](/extensions/flow) - concepts, logic, actions, triggers, runs
- [Flow: Forms integration](/extensions/flow/forms-integration) - the trigger contract
- [Flow reference](/reference/flow) - node kinds, operators, limits
- [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions) - adding your own actions

# Deployments and permissions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/deployments
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> A staging deployment with the same schema and none of the data, and which credential each actor uses.

# 12. Deployments and permissions

**Goal** a staging deployment with the same schema and none of the data, and a
clear answer to who holds which credential.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 11](/learn/enterprise-website/flow).

## Four words that are not synonyms

| word | is |
|---|---|
| **project** | the directory on disk |
| **workspace** | one site's content and configuration (`wsp_northwind_systems`) |
| **deployment** | one process with one database and one role: development, staging, production |
| **process environment** | the variables the server process reads (`.env`) |

The confusion that costs time is the last two. `DATABASE_URL` is a process
variable that tells one deployment where **its** database lives; the staging
deployment has its own `.env` with its own `DATABASE_URL`.

## Three roles, not arbitrary names

Tangen has exactly three deployment roles, set by `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE`.
They are roles of the process, not labels on a database, and things behave
differently by role: chapter 14's robots policy is the clearest example.

## Add staging

```bash
createdb northwind_staging
```

The scaffold's `.env` is the development deployment. Staging is a second
`.env`, used by the commands that act on it:

```bash .env.staging
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/northwind_staging
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=staging
JWT_SECRET=<a different secret>
PORT=3100
```

Then the same two commands, in the same order, against that file:

```bash
bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen bootstrap
bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen push
```

## Expected result

Same schema, no content:

```text
northwind_dev       tables=72   pages=6
northwind_staging   tables=72   pages=0
```

That is the entire point. Staging is a real deployment, not a copy, and
content gets there by being moved with Porter rather than by being shared.

Extensions are per deployment too, so staging needs its own:

```bash
bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen extension install seo
bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen extension install flows
```

## Who holds what

| actor | credential | can |
|---|---|---|
| your server process | an API key, `Authorization: Bearer tgn_…` | read published content it is scoped to |
| an editor | an admin session from `/api/auth/login` | everything their role allows |
| a visitor | none | read a public form schema, submit a form, load a media transform |

Northwind's key is read-only on objects, globals, media and forms. A website
never writes.

**The key never reaches a browser.** It is read by your server, and data goes
down to the page. A key in a bundle is a public key, and it is scoped to the
whole workspace on that deployment. A key issued on staging does not exist on
production: each deployment issues its own.

## Verification

- both databases report the same table count
- staging returns no content
- `bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen extension list` shows both
  extensions installed

## Common mistake

**Assuming one `.env` covers every deployment.** Each deployment has its own
`DATABASE_URL` and its own role; a command run with the wrong file acts on
the wrong database, and a production role refuses destructive work whatever
you approve.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Deployments](/build/deployments) - the model, Porter and Releases
- [Deployments reference](/reference/deployments) · [Environment
  variables](/reference/environment-variables)
- [Permissions](/reference/permissions) - key scopes and roles
- [Authentication](/reference/authentication)

---

# Cache and production

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/production
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> What caching does to a read, and running the site in production mode with no build step.

# 13. Cache and production

**Goal** understand the cache lifecycle, and boot the site in production.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 12](/learn/enterprise-website/deployments).

## The cache, in four reads

You configured nothing. Reads are cached, and a publish invalidates:

```text
cold read            620 ms   'About'
warm read             13 ms   'About'
edit, then publish
next read              5 ms   'About Northwind'      ← the NEW value
warm again             3 ms   'About Northwind'
```

Those numbers are one laptop with no Redis, on the Postgres fallback. **The
numbers are not the contract; the lifecycle is.** What you can rely on is that a
publish makes the next read return the new value, without you clearing anything.

That is the whole story for a site developer. Redis makes it faster and shared
across processes; it does not change the behaviour above.

## Production

Create the database, then provision it exactly like staging - with its own
`.env`:

```bash .env.production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/northwind_prod
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
JWT_SECRET=<32+ random characters>
SERVER_URL=https://cms.northwind.example
FRONTEND_URL=https://northwind.example
ADMIN_URL=https://admin.northwind.example
```

```bash
createdb northwind_prod
bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen bootstrap
bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen push
bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen extension install seo
bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen extension install flows
```

## There is no build step

`tangen start` runs the server from your TypeScript under Bun. There is no
bundle, no `dist/`, no compile stage to get wrong in CI.

```bash
bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen start
```

`TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production` makes this a **production deployment**:
secure cookies, a required `JWT_SECRET`, redacted errors, and no destructive
push, purge or seed. The process holds the one database in its
`DATABASE_URL` and nothing else, so serving the wrong data is impossible
rather than unlikely.

## Expected result

```text
deployment role: production
```

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/health?deep=1'
{"status":"ok","version":"0.1.x","checks":{"postgres":{"ok":true}}}
```

Use `/api/health` as a liveness probe and `?deep=1` as readiness: the deep
variant actually queries the database, so it fails when Postgres is unreachable
rather than reporting a healthy process in front of a dead one.

## What production needs

- `DATABASE_URL`, production's own
- `JWT_SECRET`, at least 32 characters
- `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production`
- `SERVER_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL` and `ADMIN_URL`, the real domains
- an API key created **on the production deployment**; keys do not cross

## Where this tutorial stops

At a production-ready, host-neutral runtime. Which container platform or VM you
put it on is your decision and does not change anything above.

## Verification

- the boot log says `deployment role: production`
- `?deep=1` reports `postgres: ok`
- a read against production returns no content until you move some there with Porter

## Common mistake

**Reusing the development API key in production.** A key belongs to one
deployment's database. It does not exist on the other one, and the failure is
an auth error.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [Deployment](/operate/deployment) - hosts, probes, secrets
- [Running Tangen](/operate) · [Caching](/build/performance)
- [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables)

---

# SEO

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/learn/enterprise-website/seo
Section: Getting Started / Build the Enterprise Website
Verification: executable

> One resolveUrl function drives canonical URLs, OpenGraph, a sitemap with hreflang, and a robots policy that differs by deployment role.

# 14. SEO

**Goal** a sitemap with language alternates, canonical URLs in the page head,
and a robots policy that cannot get staging indexed.

**Prerequisites** [chapter 13](/learn/enterprise-website/production).

## The boundary

**SEO owns the metadata. Your application owns routing.** Tangen knows a
product's identity; only your site knows that a product lives at
`/products/<slug>`. So you supply exactly one function, and everything else is
derived from it: canonical URLs, OpenGraph, the sitemap, hreflang alternates.

Never store a canonical URL on the object. It goes stale the moment a slug
changes.

## Install and configure

```bash
bun x tangen extension install seo
```

Configuration is the extension's **options**, in
`app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
export default defineExtensions([
  {
    resolve: '@tangen/ext-seo',
    options: {
      siteUrl: process.env.SITE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:4321',
      locales: ['en', 'fr', 'de'],
      sitemapTypes: ['product', 'solution', 'article', 'caseStudy'],
      resolveUrl: ({ type, slug, locale }: { type: string; slug?: string | null; locale?: string | null }) => {
        if (!slug) return null
        const base = process.env.SITE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:4321'
        const prefix = locale && locale !== 'en' ? `/${locale}` : ''
        const path = {
          product: `/products/${slug}`,
          solution: `/solutions/${slug}`,
          article: `/resources/articles/${slug}`,
          caseStudy: `/resources/case-studies/${slug}`,
        }[type]
        return path ? `${base}${prefix}${path}` : null
      },
      // `userAgents` is a LIST. A group written with singular `userAgent` is
      // dropped silently, and you get a robots.txt with no rules in it.
      robotsTxt: {
        groups: [{ userAgents: ['*'], allow: ['/'], disallow: ['/api/'] }],
        sitemaps: [`${process.env.SITE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:4321'}/sitemap.xml`],
      },
    },
  },
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows' },
])
```

### Why `page` is not in `sitemapTypes`

`resolveUrl` receives `{ type, id, slug, locale }`. It does not receive the
object's fields. Northwind's `page` type routes by an authored `path`, not by
its slug, so this function cannot resolve one. The four slug-routed types go in
the sitemap here, and pages are served by the site's own sitemap route.

Worth knowing when you design your model: a type whose routing is derivable from
its slug is a type SEO can resolve on its own.

## The page head

The metadata route is public and gives you resolved values:

```ts web/server.ts
async function seoMeta(type: string, id: string, locale: string) {
  const base = process.env.TANGEN_API_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000'
  try {
    const r = await fetch(`${base}/api/v1/ext/seo/meta?type=${type}&id=${id}&locale=${locale}`)
    if (!r.ok) return null
    return ((await r.json()) as any).data ?? null
  } catch { return null }
}
```

Render what it returns rather than composing tags yourself, so one routing
change moves the canonical URL, the OpenGraph URL and the sitemap together:

```html
<link rel="canonical" href="http://localhost:4321/fr/products/gridlock">
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
<meta property="og:title" content="Gridlock">
<meta property="og:url" content="http://localhost:4321/fr/products/gridlock">
```

## The sitemap

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/ext/seo/sitemap.xml'
```

```xml
<url>
  <loc>http://localhost:4321/products/gridlock</loc>
  <lastmod>2026-09-02T06:15:36.337Z</lastmod>
  <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="http://localhost:4321/products/gridlock"/>
  <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="http://localhost:4321/fr/products/gridlock"/>
  <xhtml:link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="http://localhost:4321/de/products/gridlock"/>
</url>
```

The alternates come from the same `resolveUrl`, called once per locale. You did
not write hreflang logic.

Tangen supplies the contents; **your framework serves `/sitemap.xml`**. Proxy the
route above from your site.

## robots.txt differs by deployment role

This is the safety feature, and it works because deployments have roles:

```text
development                     production
User-agent: *                   User-agent: *
Disallow: /                     Allow: /
                                Disallow: /api/
                                Sitemap: …/sitemap.xml
```

Non-production disallows everything by default, so a staging site is never
indexed by accident. You do not opt in to that protection; you opt out by
giving production a real policy.

## Verification

- the sitemap lists your slug-routed content with three hreflang alternates each
- a product page carries a canonical matching its locale
- `robots.txt` is `Disallow: /` in development and your policy in production

## Common mistake

**Writing `userAgent` instead of `userAgents`.** The group is dropped without an
error and you ship a robots.txt with no rules.

## Relevant canonical docs

- [SEO](/extensions/seo) - the full extension, redirects, structured data
- [Deployments](/build/deployments) - what a role changes
- [Localization](/build/localization) - where the alternates come from

# Project structure

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/getting-started/project-structure
Section: Build with Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> What each directory in a Tangen project is for, and which files you edit.

# Project structure

```text
app/
├── tangen.config.ts          # the CLI anchor: project name and schema path
├── config/                   # how the server runs - never schema, never hooks
│   ├── extensions.ts         #   which extensions this project declares
│   ├── auth.ts               #   site-user authentication
│   ├── storage.ts            #   where media lives
│   ├── mail.ts               #   the mailer
│   └── localization.ts       #   locales and fallbacks
├── workspaces/
│   ├── index.ts              # the workspace registry
│   └── <slug>/
│       └── workspace.config.ts
├── content-objects/          # your content model, one folder per type
│   ├── index.ts              #   barrel, maintained by `tangen add object`
│   └── <name>/
│       ├── schema.ts         #     required - defineObjectType + field.*
│       ├── hooks.ts          #     optional - content hooks
│       └── access.ts         #     optional - field-level access
├── globals/index.ts          # workspace-level singletons
├── fields/                   # reusable field groups
├── forms/                    # code-first form definitions
├── hooks/                    # site-wide content hooks
├── jobs/                     # scheduled jobs
└── generated/                # written by the CLI - do not edit
```

## The line that matters

**`config/` is for how the server runs. `content-objects/` is what your content
looks like.** Putting a content type in `config/` or a database URL in a schema
file is the most common structural mistake, and the two are validated
separately.

## The files you edit most

| file | when |
|---|---|
| `content-objects/<name>/schema.ts` | adding or changing a content type |
| `globals/index.ts` | adding a site-wide singleton |
| the deployment's `.env` | a new database, or a changed URL |
| `config/extensions.ts` | declaring an extension |

## The files you do not edit

`app/generated/` is written by `tangen push` and `tangen types`. Editing it is
pointless - the next push overwrites it. See
[Generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types).

## Where content types live

One folder per type, and `tangen add object <name>` creates it:

```bash
bun run tangen add object article
```

That writes `content-objects/article/schema.ts` and adds it to the barrel. It
does **not** touch the database - `tangen push` does that.

## Related

- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration) - every key in every
  config file
- [Generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types)
- [Your first content type](/build/content-modeling/content-types)
- [CLI reference](/reference/cli)

---

# Configuring a project

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/getting-started/configuration
Section: Build with Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> Which config file to reach for, what the deployment supplies, and where secrets go.

# Configuring a project

Every config file exports through a `define*` helper, so the shape is checked
before anything runs.

## Which file

| you want to | edit |
|---|---|
| point at a database, or change a URL | the deployment's `.env` (`DATABASE_URL`, `SERVER_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL`) |
| declare an extension | `config/extensions.ts` |
| turn on site-user accounts | `config/auth.ts` |
| move media to S3 | `config/storage.ts` |
| send mail | `config/mail.ts` |
| add a language | `config/localization.ts` |
| add a site-wide setting | `globals/index.ts` |

## Deployments

The workspace config says what the site is. Where it runs is the
deployment's `.env`: one database, one role, its URLs.

```bash .env  (development, the laptop)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/my_site_dev
# TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE is unset: development, localhost URLs
```

```bash .env  (production, the server)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://.../my_site_prod
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
SERVER_URL=https://cms.example.com
FRONTEND_URL=https://example.com
ADMIN_URL=https://admin.example.com
```

```ts app/tangen.config.ts  (values every deployment shares)
server: { cors: { origins: ['https://example.com'] } },
frontend: { previewUrl: 'https://example.com/preview?id={id}' },
```

There are exactly three roles - `development`, `staging`, `production` - and
each is a deployment of its own. Nothing on a request or a command selects
between them. See [Deployments](/reference/deployments).

## Secrets

Config files are committed. Secrets are not. A config file names the
variable; the deployment supplies the value:

```ts
ai: { apiKey: { anthropic: 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY' } },   // a name, never a value
```

Never put a connection string, a key or a client secret in the file itself.

## Verify

```bash
bun run tangen check
```

`check` validates the schema and configuration without touching the database.

## Common mistakes

- **A content type in `config/`.** Content types live in `content-objects/`.
- **`dev` instead of `development`.** The role is the slug.
- **A literal secret in a config file.** It is committed the moment you save it.
- **Expecting a config change to reach the database.** Schema changes need
  `tangen push`; server config is read at boot.

## Related

- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration) - every key
- [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables)
- [Deployments](/reference/deployments)
