# Generated types

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/getting-started/generated-types
Section: Build with Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> What the CLI generates, when, where it lives, and why your queries are typed without generics.

# Generated types

Your content model is TypeScript, and so is everything derived from it. The CLI
turns `app/content-objects/` into types your editor and your build understand.

## What is generated

| artifact | where | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| **types declaration** | `app/generated/tangen-types.d.ts` | an interface per content type, per global and per custom table, plus the registry augmentation |
| **content tables** | `app/generated/content-tables.ts` | the drizzle table objects, for your own code and the types. The server builds its runtime tables from the registry of its database, so this file never decides what a process reads |
| **custom tables** | `custom-tables.ts`, when you have any | the same, for `customTables` |

## When it happens

| command | regenerates |
|---|---|
| `tangen push` | all of it, **after** the schema is applied |
| `tangen types` | the types declaration only |
| `tangen schema` | the generated registry |

`push` writes the files in its final step, after the DDL has committed. So the
generated files always describe a schema that actually exists - they are never
ahead of the database.

## What you get

```ts app/generated/tangen-types.d.ts
// DO NOT EDIT - generated by `tangen types`

export interface TangenSystemFields {
  id: string
  title: string | null
  slug: string | null
  status: 'draft' | 'published' | 'archived'
  publishedAt: string | null
  scheduledAt: string | null
  createdAt: string
  updatedAt: string
  createdBy: string | null
  updatedBy: string | null
}

/** Content type "article" (Article) */
export interface Article extends TangenSystemFields {
  subtitle?: string | null
  body?: string | null
}
```

Every content type extends `TangenSystemFields`, so `id`, `slug`, `status` and
the timestamps are always there without you declaring them.

## Why your queries are typed without generics

The file ends with a **module augmentation** against `@tangen/types`:

```ts
declare module '@tangen/types' {
  interface TangenRegistry {
    content: TangenContentTypes
    globals: TangenGlobals
    tables: TangenTables
    locales: 'en' | 'fr' | 'de'
    roles: 'owner' | 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
    extensions: 'forms' | 'seo'
  }
}
```

That is what makes this work with no generic parameter:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('article').limit(10).get()
//                                    ^ a literal union - a typo is a compile error
//      ^ data is Article[]
```

It also types `globals('site_settings')`, custom tables, locale codes and role
names. **You never write `objects<Article>('article')`** - if an example shows
that, it is out of date.

## When to regenerate

Any time the model changes:

- a field added, renamed, retyped or removed
- a content type added or removed
- a global, a custom table, a locale or a role added
- a workspace's extensions changed

`tangen push` does it for you. Run `tangen types` on its own when you have
changed the model but are not ready to touch the database - your editor catches
up without a schema change.

**If your editor disagrees with your schema file, you have not regenerated.**
That is almost always the cause.

## Do not edit generated files

They carry a `DO NOT EDIT` header and the next push overwrites them. Commit
them - your build and your CI need them - but change them only by changing the
model.

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [CLI reference](/reference/cli) ·
  [Your first content type](/build/content-modeling/content-types) ·
  [Using the SDK](/build/querying/sdk)

---

# The schema workflow

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/getting-started/schema-workflow
Section: Build with Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> check, diff, push - and how to read the plan before you apply it.

# The schema workflow

Your content model is code. The database catches up when you tell it to.

```bash
bun run tangen check     # is the model valid?
bun run tangen diff      # what would change?
bun run tangen push      # apply it
```

## Read the plan

`push` prints its plan and then applies it. The plan names every statement in
order, and marks anything destructive.

```text
Plan for development
  + CREATE TABLE "article"
  + ADD COLUMN  "article"."subtitle" TEXT
  - DROP COLUMN "article"."teaser"   [guarded: recoverable until purged]
```

**Read it.** It is the last point at which a mistake is cheap.

To see the plan without applying:

```bash
bun run tangen push --plan
bun run tangen push --plan --json    # for a script
```

## Destructive changes

Removing a field or a type can lose data, so it needs an explicit approval that
names the operation:

```bash
bun run tangen push --approve drop-field:article.teaser
```

Four rules, and none of them has an override:

1. **Every destructive operation needs its own token.** Approving one never
   approves another.
2. **Production refuses destructive operations**, whatever you approve.
3. **A drop is guarded** - renamed aside and recoverable until an approved
   purge, not deleted.
4. **Ambiguous operations never apply.** Safe operations in the same plan still
   do.

Push tells you the exact tokens it wants.

## Renaming without losing data

Do not delete and recreate. Declare the old name:

```ts
subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', previousName: ['teaser'] }),
```

The plan then shows a rename, and the data moves with it.

## After a push

`push` regenerates the types and the table artifacts as its final step, so your
editor is correct the moment it finishes. If it disagrees, run `tangen types`.

## Taking a change forward

Each deployment has its own database. Push on development, then on staging,
then on production - the same code, applied three times from wherever can
reach each database, with the plan read each time.

## Common mistakes

- **Approving a drop to "get past" a refusal in production.** It will not work,
  and it is not meant to.
- **Editing `app/generated/`** instead of the model.
- **Assuming a push moved content.** It moves *schema*. Content moves through a
  [Release](/build/deployments).

## Related

- [CLI reference](/reference/cli) · [Deployments](/reference/deployments) ·
  [Fields reference](/reference/fields) ·
  [Generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types)

---

# Content types

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/content-types
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: executable

> Defining a content type, what the system gives you, and what to put in it.

# Content types

A content type is one file.

```bash
bun run tangen add object article
```

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
import { defineObjectType, field } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineObjectType({
  name: 'article',
  label: 'Article',
  fields: {
    subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', validation: { required: true } }),
    body: field.richtext({ label: 'Body' }),
    heroImage: field.media({ label: 'Hero image' }),
    publishedOn: field.date({ label: 'Publish date' }),
  },
})
```

Then:

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

## Fields are a map, not a list

The field's **name is the key**. Every builder takes exactly one object:

```ts
fields: {
  subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle' }),   // correct
}
```

`field.text('subtitle', { … })` is not the API.

## What you get without asking

Every type has `id`, `title`, `slug`, `status`, `publishedAt`, `scheduledAt`,
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy` and `updatedBy`. Do not declare them, and
do not model your own `published` boolean - `status` is the one Tangen and the
Admin both use.

## Naming

`name` is the identifier: lowercase, singular, and stable. It becomes the table
name, the SDK's `objects('article')` key and part of every URL. `label` is what
editors see and can change freely.

Renaming a type is a schema change. Declare `previousName` so the data moves
rather than being dropped.

## How big should a type be

One type per thing a person would call a thing. An article is a type; its
author is a different type reached by a [relation](/build/content-modeling/relations);
its SEO metadata is a [group](/build/content-modeling/structuring-content) on the
article.

Signs you have gone wrong:

- **Fields that are only ever set together and only for some rows.** That is a
  component or a second type.
- **A `type` or `kind` select that changes which other fields matter.** Usually
  two types.
- **Thirty fields.** Group them, or split them.

## Verify

```bash
bun run tangen check
bun run tangen push
```

Then open the Admin: the type appears under Content with its fields in the
order you declared them.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the wrong builder signature.** One object, name as the key.
- **Declaring `title` or `status`.** They already exist.
- **Deleting a field to rename it.** Use `previousName`.
- **Expecting a schema change to appear without a push.**

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [Choosing a field](/build/content-modeling/choosing-fields)
  · [The schema workflow](/build/getting-started/schema-workflow)

# Choosing a field

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/choosing-fields
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: source

> Which of the 28 field types fits, and the ones people reach for wrongly.

# Choosing a field

The full list, with options and validation, is
[Reference → Fields](/reference/fields). This page is about picking.

## By what you are storing

| you want | use |
|---|---|
| a headline, a name, a short label | `text` |
| a paragraph of plain text | `textarea` |
| formatted body copy | `richtext` |
| a URL segment | `slug` |
| an email, a URL, a phone number | `email`, `url`, `phone` - they validate |
| a number | `number`; `currency` for money, `rating` for a score, `range` for a pair |
| yes or no | `boolean` |
| one of a fixed set | `select` |
| several of a fixed set | `multiselect` |
| open-ended keywords | `tags` |
| a date, or a date and time | `date` |
| an image, a PDF, a video | `media` |
| a link to another object | `relation` |
| a destination that might be internal **or** external | `link` |
| repeating rows of the same shape | `repeater` |
| a reusable block used across types | `component` |
| related fields shown together | `group` |

## The ones people get wrong

**`text` where `slug` belongs.** `slug` is unique per type, URL-safe, and can
derive itself: `field.slug({ label: 'Slug', config: { source: 'title' } })` - `source` names
the sibling field the editor's Generate button derives from.

**`text` holding a URL to another page.** If the destination is your own
content, that is a [`link`](/build/content-modeling/links) or a `relation`. A
stored URL breaks the moment a slug changes.

**`json` as an escape hatch.** It stores anything and validates nothing, cannot
be filtered meaningfully, and gives editors a textarea full of braces. Reach for
`repeater`, `component` or `group` first. `json` is right for data another
system owns.

**`multiselect` where a `relation` belongs.** If the options are content someone
edits - categories, authors, products - they are a type, not a list of strings.

**`boolean` for status.** Every type already has `status`.

## Required, and validation

```ts
subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', validation: { required: true } }),
excerpt:  field.textarea({ label: 'Excerpt', validation: { maxLength: 200 } }),
```

`required: true` is shorthand for `validation: { required: true }`. Required
means required **to publish**: a draft may be incomplete, and publishing an
incomplete object is refused with a `422` naming the field.

Validate what actually matters. A `maxLength` that exists because a designer
guessed becomes an editor's problem at 5pm.

## Localizing

`localized: true` per field. Decide it when you model - see
[Modeling for localization](/build/content-modeling/localization).

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [Relations](/build/content-modeling/relations)
  · [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links) ·
  [Errors](/reference/errors)

---

# Structuring content

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/structuring-content
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: executable

> Groups, repeaters and components: which one to use for nested and repeating content, and how a component differs from a block on a page.

# Structuring content

Three ways to nest, and they are not interchangeable.

| | use when |
|---|---|
| **`group`** | related fields belong together **on this type**, once |
| **`repeater`** | rows of the same shape, many of them, on this type |
| **`component`** | a block reused **across types**, chosen from a palette |

## Group

Fields shown together, stored as ordinary columns on the same row.

```ts
seo: field.group({
  label: 'SEO',
  fields: {
    metaTitle: field.text({ label: 'Meta title' }),
    metaDescription: field.textarea({ label: 'Meta description' }),
  },
}),
```

A group is presentation and grouping. Because its children are flat columns,
they filter and sort like any other field.

**The column takes the child's own name, not a prefixed one.** The group above
adds `metaTitle` and `metaDescription` to the table - not `seo_metaTitle`. So a
child may collide with a top-level field, or with a child of another group on
the same type, and the group name will not save you. Name group children as if
they sat at the top level, because in the database they do.

## Repeater

An ordered list of rows.

```ts
faqs: field.repeater({
  label: 'FAQs',
  // Rows are plain sub-field objects under config.fields; the field.* builders describe top-level fields.
  config: { fields: [
    { name: 'question', label: 'Question', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
    { name: 'answer', label: 'Answer', fieldType: 'textarea' },
  ] },
}),
```

Rows keep their order and are addressed by a stable key, so reordering does not
rewrite them.

Use a repeater when the rows only make sense **inside this object**. If a row
is a thing in its own right - something you would list, link to, or reuse - it
is a content type and a [relation](/build/content-modeling/relations).

## Component

A reusable block, defined once and offered on any type that accepts it. This is
how page builders work: a page has a `blocks` field, and an editor picks Hero,
Feature Grid or Quote.

```ts
blocks: field.component({ label: 'Blocks', config: { components: ['hero', 'featureGrid', 'quote'] } }),
```

Components are the right answer when the **shape varies per row** and an editor
chooses which shape. A repeater is one shape repeated; a component field is
several shapes in a sequence.

## Choosing

```text
Does the shape vary per row, chosen by an editor?   → component
Same shape, many rows, only meaningful here?        → repeater
A few fields that belong together, once?            → group
A thing you would list or link to on its own?       → its own type + relation
```

## Common mistakes

- **A repeater of one row** because a group felt too plain.
- **A component used on exactly one type** and never reused - a repeater is
  simpler.
- **Nesting three levels deep.** Editors stop being able to see the page.
- **`json` instead of any of these**, which loses validation and the editor.

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [Relations](/build/content-modeling/relations)
  · [Querying relations](/build/querying/relations)

---

# Relations

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/relations
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: executable

> Connecting content types, one and many, and what it costs to read them.

# Relations

A relation points at other content.

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
author:     field.relation({ label: 'Author', config: { targetType: 'person' } }),
categories: field.relation({ label: 'Categories', config: { targetType: 'category', many: true } }),
```

## Reading them costs depth

A relation is an id until you ask for more:

```ts
await tangen.objects('article').depth(0).get()   // author is an id
await tangen.objects('article').depth(1).get()   // author is the person object
await tangen.objects('article').depth(2).get()   // and the person's own relations expand
```

**The ceiling is 5**, and each level is another expansion pass. Ask for what
you render:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .depth(1)
  .populate('author', ['id', 'title', 'slug'])   // project the expanded record
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```

`populate` narrows the expanded record; `props` narrows the row itself.

A cycle stops at the object already on the path, so a mutual relation cannot
loop.

## Filtering across one

A dotted path filters by a field on the related record, **one level deep**:

```ts
.where({ 'author.title': { contains: 'jane' } })
.where({ 'categories.slug': 'engineering' })
```

Deeper paths are refused. If you need two levels, query the middle type first.

## Finding what points at you

`_referencedBy` selects objects that a **many** relation points at:

```ts
await tangen.objects('person')
  .where({ _referencedBy: { type: 'article', field: 'contributors' } })
  .get()
```

It works through many relations only, and it refuses `link` fields - links do
not participate in backlink discovery.

## Relation or link

| | |
|---|---|
| **relation** | a structural connection you query, filter and expand. An article *has* an author |
| **link** | a destination an editor chose, which may be external. A CTA *points at* something |

Use a relation when the connection is part of the model. Use a
[link](/build/content-modeling/links) when it is an editorial choice.

## Modeling notes

- **Put the relation where the cardinality is natural.** An article has one
  author; a person has many articles. Declare it on the article.
- **A many-relation you always expand is a depth cost on every read.** Consider
  whether the list view needs it.
- **Required relations affect publishing.** Publishing an object whose required
  relation points at a draft is refused with `NEEDS_CASCADE`. Publish the
  dependency, or publish with the cascade.

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Querying relations](/build/querying/relations)
  · [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links) ·
  [Errors](/reference/errors)

---

# Links and navigation

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/links
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: executable

> Modeling destinations that survive a slug change, and resolving them to URLs in your app.

# Links and navigation

A `link` field holds a destination an editor chose: either your own content or
an external URL.

**An internal link stores identity, not a URL.** That is the whole point. An
editor renames `/about-us` to `/about`, and every menu item, button and inline
link still resolves - because none of them stored the old path.

## Model it

```ts app/globals/index.ts
import { defineGlobals } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineGlobals([
  {
    name: 'navigation',
    label: 'Navigation',
    fields: [
      {
        name: 'primary', label: 'Primary menu', fieldType: 'repeater',
        config: {
          fields: [
            { name: 'label', label: 'Label', fieldType: 'text', required: true },
            {
              name: 'target', label: 'Target', fieldType: 'link',
              config: { allowedTargets: ['page', 'article'] },
            },
          ],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
])
```

Globals and container fields both take their sub-fields as an **array** whose
entries name themselves - the keyed `field.*` map is for a content type's
top-level fields. See [Globals](/build/globals).

`allowedKinds` restricts to internal or external; `allowedTargets` restricts
which content types an internal link may point at; `anchor` and `query` toggle
those inputs.

## Resolve it in your app

Tangen gives you identity and the target's current facts. **Your router builds
the URL** - Tangen does not know your routes, and inventing one is the thing it
refuses to do.

```ts app/lib/link.ts
import { isInternalLink, isExternalLink, isLinkResolved, linkSuffix } from '@tangen/sdk'
import type { ResolvedLink } from '@tangen/sdk'

export function hrefFor(link: ResolvedLink): string | null {
  if (!isLinkResolved(link)) return null
  if (isExternalLink(link)) return link.href
  if (isInternalLink(link) && link.target) {
    const path = link.target.type === 'page'
      ? `/${link.target.slug}`
      : `/${link.target.type}/${link.target.slug}`
    return `${path}${linkSuffix(link)}`
  }
  return null
}
```

`linkSuffix()` returns the `?query#anchor` part, or `''`. There is no
`hrefOf()` that handles both branches, and there will not be.

## Render an unresolved link as text

`target` is `null` when the destination is missing, deleted, or not published in
this read. That is normal, not an error:

```tsx
const href = hrefFor(item.target)
return href
  ? <a href={href}>{item.label}</a>
  : <span>{item.label}</span>
```

A link to nowhere is worse than no link. `targetRef` survives even then, so an
editor can see and repair it in the Admin.

## Anchors, query and locale

- `anchor` is stored without the `#` and appended by `linkSuffix()`.
- `query` is structured, and merged into the href for external links.
- `locale` on an internal link says **which locale of the target to resolve**.
  It is metadata about the destination, not a routing instruction - your app
  still decides what a French URL looks like.

## Common mistakes

- **Storing a URL in a `text` field** for internal content. It breaks silently
  on the first rename.
- **Treating `target === null` as an error.** Render text.
- **Building the URL from `targetRef`** instead of `target`. `targetRef` is the
  authored identity and carries no slug.
- **Expecting to filter on a link.** `link` is not filterable in v1.

## Related

- [Link reference](/reference/link) - the exact shapes and every edge case
- [Relations](/build/content-modeling/relations) - when a relation is the right
  answer instead
- [Frontend integration](/build/frontend)

---

# Modeling for localization

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content-modeling/localization
Section: Build with Tangen / Content modeling
Verification: executable

> Deciding which fields translate, before you have translations.

# Modeling for localization

Localization is **per field, opt-in**:

```ts
subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', localized: true }),
body:     field.richtext({ label: 'Body', localized: true }),
sku:      field.text({ label: 'SKU' }),                      // not localized
```

A localized field's values live in a per-type side table; the default locale's
value stays on the main row.

## What to localize

**Yes:** anything a person reads. Titles, body copy, labels, meta descriptions,
alt text, button text.

**No:** identifiers and data. SKUs, prices in a single currency, dates, external
URLs, and anything another system owns.

**It depends:** slugs. A localized slug gives you `/fr/a-propos`; an
unlocalized one gives you `/fr/about`. Both are legitimate - decide by whether
your URLs are content or infrastructure.

## Media does not need the flag

Media localizes at the **asset** level - per-locale variants of the same field.
Do not put `localized: true` on a media field.

## Decide early

Adding `localized: true` later is a schema change that moves data into a side
table. It works, and `tangen push` shows you the plan, but it is easier to
decide while you are modeling.

If you are unsure whether a site will ever be multilingual, localize the
obvious text fields now. An unused side table costs nothing; a retrofit costs a
migration.

## Related

- [Localization](/build/localization) - configuring locales and querying
- [Fields reference](/reference/fields)

# Drafts and publishing

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content/publishing
Section: Build with Tangen / Content
Verification: executable

> Draft and published status: why a newly created entry is invisible to the Delivery API until it is published, and what a reader sees.

# Drafts and publishing

Every object has a `status`: `draft`, `published` or `archived`. An API key
reads **published** content unless you ask otherwise and hold the right to.

## What a reader sees

```ts
await tangen.objects('article').get()                    // published only
await tangen.objects('article').status('draft').get()    // needs objects: read_draft
await tangen.objects('article').status('any').get()       // needs objects: read_draft
```

`objects: read` does **not** include drafts. That separation is what lets you
give a public frontend a key that cannot leak unpublished work.

Publishing takes a **snapshot**. A published object serves what it looked like
when it was published, so an editor's in-progress changes do not appear on the
live site until they publish again.

## Publishing

```ts
await tangen.objects('article').publish(id)
await tangen.objects('article').unpublish(id)
```

Both need `objects: publish`.

**Publishing validates.** Required fields must be filled, and a `422
VALIDATION_ERROR` names each one that is not. A draft may be incomplete; a
published object may not.

## Required relations and cascade

If an object's required relation points at something still in draft, publishing
is refused with **`409 NEEDS_CASCADE`**. Either publish the dependency first, or
ask for a preflight and publish together:

```ts
const plan = await tangen.objects('article').publishPreflight(id)
// plan lists what else would publish, and what blocks it
```

`CASCADE_BLOCKED` means the cascade itself cannot proceed - something in the
chain is invalid, not merely unpublished.

## Unpublishing

Unpublish takes the object offline: the published snapshot is cleared, and it
disappears from published reads. **The draft is untouched** - unpublishing is
not deleting, and republishing restores it.

Any per-object data an extension stores goes offline with it.

## Archiving

`archived` is content you keep but do not serve. It is not in published reads
and it is not deleted.

## Versions

Publishing creates a version. Past versions are readable, and restorable from
the Admin.

## Common mistakes

- **Giving a public frontend `read_draft`.** It leaks unpublished content.
- **Modeling your own `published` boolean.** `status` is the one the platform
  and the Admin use.
- **Expecting an edit to appear live.** Edits land in the draft; publishing
  moves them.
- **Treating `NEEDS_CASCADE` as a bug.** It is the platform refusing to publish
  a page with a broken required link.

## Related

- [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions)
  · [Errors](/reference/errors) · [Preview](/build/content/preview)

---

# Scheduling

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content/scheduling
Section: Build with Tangen / Content
Verification: executable

> Publishing at a future time, and what happens when that time arrives.

# Scheduling

```ts
await tangen.objects('article').schedule(id, '2026-10-01T09:00:00Z')
await tangen.objects('article').unschedule(id)
```

Needs **both `objects: write` and `objects: publish`**. A key with only one gets
a `403` naming the other, which is the fastest way to tell them apart.

On the wire the field is `scheduledAt`:

```http
POST /api/v1/objects/<id>/schedule?type=article&env=development
{ "scheduledAt": "2026-10-01T09:00:00Z" }
```

A scheduled object takes the status **`scheduled`** - not `draft` - and carries
`scheduledAt`. It is still invisible to the Delivery API, which serves published
content only, so a default read will not find it. When its time arrives the
platform publishes it: no request of yours, and no cron of yours.

## What is checked, and when

Scheduling **validates as if publishing now**: an object that could not publish
cannot be scheduled. That means the failure lands while a person is looking at
it, rather than at 3am.

At the scheduled moment the validation runs again. If the object has become
invalid since - a required relation was unpublished, a required field cleared -
it is **left scheduled** rather than published, and it retries on a later tick.
Nothing publishes incomplete.

## Time

Timestamps are absolute. Send UTC and let your frontend format for the reader.

## Verify

`scheduledAt` is on every object. A scheduled article is `status: 'scheduled'`
with a `scheduledAt` in the future; after publication `scheduledAt` is cleared and
`publishedAt` is set.

## Related

- [Drafts and publishing](/build/content/publishing) ·
  [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) · [Fields reference](/reference/fields)

---

# Writing content from code

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content/writing
Section: Build with Tangen / Content
Verification: executable

> Creating and updating objects, and not overwriting somebody else's edit.

# Writing content from code

Most content is written by people in the Admin. Sometimes your application
writes it: an import, a form that creates a submission record, a sync from
another system.

```ts
const created = await tangen.objects('article').create({
  title: 'Launch day',
  subtitle: 'What we shipped',
})

await tangen.objects('article').update(created.id, { subtitle: 'Revised' })
await tangen.objects('article').delete(created.id)
```

`create` and `update` need `objects: write`; `delete` needs `objects: delete`.

A created object is a **draft**. Publishing is a separate call.

## Validation

A write that violates the model is refused with `422 VALIDATION_ERROR`, and
`fieldErrors` names each field. Draft writes are more permissive than
publishing: `required` is enforced at publish.

## Not overwriting somebody else

Every read returns an **`ETag`**. Send it back as `If-Match` and your write
applies only if nothing changed in between:

```ts
const res = await fetch(`${api}/api/v1/objects/article/${id}`, {
  method: 'PATCH',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'If-Match': etag,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ subtitle: 'Revised' }),
})
```

If the row moved you get **`409 STALE_OBJECT`**, carrying the current ETag.
Reread, reapply your change, retry. Do not loop blindly - a stale write usually
means a human is editing the same object.

Omitting `If-Match` means "any version" and skips the check. That is the right
choice for an importer that owns the data, and the wrong one for anything a
person also edits.

## Slugs

A slug is unique per type. Two concurrent creates with the same slug: one wins,
the other gets a **`409 CONFLICT`**. Retry with a different slug, or let the
`slug` field derive itself from the title.

## Common mistakes

- **Expecting a created object to be live.** It is a draft.
- **Retrying a `STALE_OBJECT` with the same body.** Reread first.
- **Writing with a key that only has `read`.** That is a `403`, not an empty
  result.

## Related

- [SDK reference](/reference/sdk) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Drafts and publishing](/build/content/publishing) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions)

# Preview

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/content/preview
Section: Build with Tangen / Content
Verification: executable

> Showing draft content on your frontend without leaking it.

# Preview

An editor clicks Preview in the Admin and lands on **your** site showing the
draft. Three things make that work, and one of them is a credential you must
handle carefully.

## The flow

```text
Admin  ──mints a token──►  opens frontend.previewUrl with ?token=…&id=…&type=…
                                        │
Your frontend  ──GET /preview/object/:id with X-Tangen-Preview-Token──►  Tangen
                                        │
                            the draft object, no-store
```

The Admin mints the token; your frontend spends it. **Your frontend never mints
one** - minting needs a member session.

## Configure where Preview lands

```ts tangen.config.ts
{
  frontend: {
    url: 'http://localhost:4321',
    previewUrl: 'http://localhost:4321/preview?id={id}&type={type}&slug={slug}',
    previewUrls: {
      article: 'http://localhost:4321/blog/{slug}?preview=1&id={id}',
    },
  },
},
```

`{id}`, `{type}` and `{slug}` are substituted. `previewUrls` overrides per type
and falls back to `previewUrl`.

## Read the draft

```ts app/routes/preview.ts
import { fetchPreviewObject } from '@tangen/sdk'

const draft = await fetchPreviewObject({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  id, type, token,
  locale,                       // optional
})

if (!draft) {
  // token missing, expired, or scoped elsewhere - do not fall back to published
  return notFound()
}
```

It returns the object with media expanded and links resolved, or `null` on any
failure.

## Securing it

The token is a **draft-read credential**. Anyone holding it reads unpublished
content until it expires.

**Do this:**

- Read the token from the request on the **server**, use it there, and never
  send it to the browser.
- Set a short TTL. An editor previewing one article needs minutes, not a day.
- Prefer object-scoped tokens, which read that object and nothing else.
- Keep the preview route out of your sitemap, and return `X-Robots-Tag:
  noindex` from it.
- Fail closed. If the token is bad, render not-found - never the published
  version, which quietly makes preview look like it worked.

**Do not:**

- Put the token in a client-side bundle, a cookie readable by JavaScript, or a
  URL you log.
- Cache a preview response, or use it to warm a published cache. Tangen serves
  these `no-store` and so should you.
- Reuse one long-lived token as "the preview key".

## Caching

Preview responses are `no-store`. If your framework caches routes by default,
opt this route out - Next.js `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, or your
framework's equivalent. A cached draft is a leak with a long tail.

## Live preview

`onLivePreview` subscribes to changes as an editor types, so an iframe
re-renders without a fetch:

```ts
import { onLivePreview, isLivePreview } from '@tangen/sdk'

if (isLivePreview()) {
  onLivePreview({ onUpdate: (object) => render(object) })
}
```

Guard it with `isLivePreview()` so the listener does not run on the public site.

## Errors

| you get | means |
|---|---|
| `null` from `fetchPreviewObject` | any failure: no token, expired, wrong scope |
| `401 UNAUTHORIZED` | the header was missing or the token is not live |

Preview needs **Redis**, which is where tokens live with their expiry.

## Common mistakes

- **Falling back to published on a failed token.** The editor sees a stale page
  and believes it.
- **Rendering the token into HTML.**
- **Caching the preview route.**
- **Expecting an API key to read `/preview/object/:id`.** The header is the only
  credential that route accepts.

## Related

- [Preview reference](/reference/preview) - TTLs, scoping, the four endpoints
- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration) - `previewUrl`
- [Drafts and publishing](/build/content/publishing) ·
  [Frontend integration](/build/frontend)

---

# Globals

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/globals
Section: Build with Tangen / Globals
Verification: executable

> Site-wide singletons - settings, navigation, SEO defaults - and how to query them.

# Globals

A global is a **singleton**: one record for the whole workspace, not a list.
Site settings, the main menu, the footer, SEO defaults.

## Global or content type

| | |
|---|---|
| **global** | there is exactly one, forever. No slug, no list, no publish cycle of its own |
| **content type** | there are many, or there might be. It has a URL, or it appears in a list |

"Site settings" is a global. "Pages" is a type. A single About page is still a
type - one row today, two tomorrow.

## Defining

```ts app/globals/index.ts
import { defineGlobals } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineGlobals([
  {
    name: 'site_settings',
    label: 'Site settings',
    fields: [
      { name: 'siteName', label: 'Site name', fieldType: 'text', required: true, config: { localized: true } },
      { name: 'contactEmail', label: 'Contact email', fieldType: 'email' },
      { name: 'maintenanceMode', label: 'Maintenance mode', fieldType: 'boolean' },
    ],
  },
  {
    name: 'seo_defaults',
    label: 'SEO defaults',
    fields: [
      { name: 'titleTemplate', label: 'Title template', fieldType: 'text', config: { localized: true } },
      { name: 'description', label: 'Default description', fieldType: 'textarea', config: { localized: true } },
      { name: 'socialImage', label: 'Default social image', fieldType: 'media' },
    ],
  },
])
```

Then import it in your workspace config as `globals` and run `tangen push`.

> A Global's `fields` is an **array**, not the keyed builder map content types
> use: each entry names itself with `name` and states its `fieldType`. Every field
> type is available - but the per-field options a `field.*` builder would fold in
> for you go under `config` here, which is why `localized` is nested. That is the
> whole difference between the two authoring shapes.

## Querying

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()
console.log(data.values.siteName)      // 'My Blog'
```

The values sit at `data.values` - one unwrap, unlike `objects(...)` which
returns its rows at `data`. Sites usually wrap it once:

```ts
const global = async (name: string) => (await tangen.globals(name).get()).data.values
```

**The name is not typed.** `tangen push` augments the registry with your
content types only - the generated file declares `content` and nothing else - so
`globals('site_settings')` takes a plain string and its result is `unknown`.
Narrow it yourself at the boundary:

```ts
interface SiteSettings { siteName: string; tagline?: string }
const settings = (await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()).data.values as SiteSettings
```

A typo in the name is therefore a runtime miss, not a compile error. Keep the
names in one module rather than repeating string literals across your site.

### A global has no `depth`

A relation or media field on a **content object** expands into the full record
under `.depth(1)`. A global has no depth option, so the same field comes back
as the **bare id string**:

```ts
const settings = (await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()).data.values
settings.logo                              // 'med_2ab66f04…', not an object
tangen.media.transformUrl(settings.logo, { w: 32, format: 'webp' })
```

That is enough to render an image, because a transform only needs the id. If
you want the asset's own `altText`, `width` or `height`, fetch it:
`tangen.media.get(settings.logo)`.

The key needs the **`globals:read`** scope - a key with only `objects: read`
gets a 403 that names the missing scope.

Needs `globals: read`. Writing needs `globals: write`.

## Navigation

The common pattern: a repeater of items, each with a label and a
[link](/build/content-modeling/links).

```ts
{
  name: 'navigation',
  label: 'Navigation',
  fields: {
    primary: field.repeater({
      label: 'Primary menu',
      // A repeater's rows are plain sub-field objects under config.fields;
      // the field.* builders describe top-level fields only.
      config: { fields: [
        { name: 'label', label: 'Label', fieldType: 'text', required: true, localized: true },
        { name: 'target', label: 'Target', fieldType: 'link', config: { allowedTargets: ['page', 'article'] } },
      ] },
    }),
    footer: field.repeater({ label: 'Footer menu', config: { fields: [ /* … */ ] } }),
  },
}
```

Then in your app:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.globals('navigation').get()
const items = data.values.primary.map((item) => ({ label: item.label, href: hrefFor(item.target) }))
```

Because the target is a link, renaming a page's slug does not break the menu.

Header and footer are the same pattern - two repeaters on one global, or two
globals. One global with several menus is usually easier for editors to find.

## Localization

`localized: true` works on a global's fields exactly as it does on a type's.
Read a locale by passing it to your client, and the fallback rules are the
same.

## Caching

A global is read on nearly every page render. Cache it in your frontend for the
life of a request at minimum; a short TTL is usually safe, because a settings
change is not urgent to the second.

## Common mistakes

- **Modeling a one-row content type as a global** when it might become many.
- **Reading a global per component** instead of once per request.
- **Storing URLs as text in a menu.** Use a link.
- **Expecting a media or relation field to arrive expanded.** Globals have no `depth`; you get the id.

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links)
  · [Querying](/build/querying) · [Localization](/build/localization)

- [Relations](/build/querying/relations) - depth, projection and cost

# Your first query

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/first-query
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Creating a client and reading a list and a single object.

# Your first query

> The Delivery API serves **published** content. A draft is invisible to an API
> key however it is queried - so an empty result is far more often an unpublished
> object than a wrong filter. See [Publishing](/build/content/publishing).


## Create a client once

```ts app/lib/tangen.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

export const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
})
```
**Keep the key on the server.** It is not a user credential, and a browser
bundle is a public place.

## A list

```ts
const { data, meta } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```
`data` is typed `Article[]` from your generated types - no generic parameter.
`meta` carries `total`, `limit`, `offset`, `cursor` and `hasMore`.

You get **published** content. Drafts need `objects: read_draft` and an
explicit `.status()`.

## One object

```ts
const article = await tangen.objects('article').find(id)
const bySlug  = await tangen.objects('article').findBySlug('launch-day')
```
`findBySlug` is what a page route usually wants, because a slug is what is in
the URL.

## Only the fields you render

```ts
const { data } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .props(['id', 'title', 'slug', 'publishedAt'])
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```
A list of cards does not need the body of every article.

## Verify

Ask the API the same question your code is asking, with the same key:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$TANGEN_API_URL/api/v1/objects/article/query" \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TANGEN_API_KEY" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"limit":5}'
```

If that returns rows and your code does not, the difference is in your code. If
it returns none, the usual causes are that nothing is published yet, the key
was issued on another deployment, or the key is missing an action - and a missing
action is a `403`, never a silent empty list.

## Common mistakes

- **The key in client-side code.**
- **`objects('articles')`** - the type name is what you declared, usually
  singular, and a typo is a compile error.
- **Expecting drafts.** A default read is published only.

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Filtering and sorting](/build/querying/filtering)
  · [Using the SDK](/build/querying/sdk)

---

# Filtering and sorting

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/filtering
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Narrowing a result set with operators and boolean groups, and ordering it.

# Filtering and sorting

A filter is an object. **Every condition ANDs.**

```ts
await tangen.objects('article')
  .where({ featured: true, views: { gt: 100 } })
  .get()
```

A bare value means equals, and `null` means absent:

```ts
.where({ slug: 'launch-day' })      // equals
.where({ excerpt: null })            // has no excerpt
```

## The operators you will use

```ts
.where({ views: { gte: 50 } })                    // gt gte lt lte
.where({ status: { in: ['published'] } })          // in, nin
.where({ title: { contains: 'launch' } })          // case-insensitive
.where({ slug: { startsWith: 'guide-' } })         // case-insensitive prefix
.where({ heroImage: { exists: true } })            // presence
```

`contains`, `ncontains` and `startsWith` are case-insensitive. On a
`multiselect`, `in` **overlaps** rather than compares - `{ tags: { in: ['blue'] } }`
matches any row tagged blue.

The full operator list is in [Reference → TangenQL](/reference/tangenql).

## Or, and grouping

```ts
.where({ _or: [{ featured: true }, { views: { gt: 1000 } }] })
```

Conditions **inside one branch AND together**, and a top-level condition ANDs
with the whole group:

```ts
// (featured AND views < 10) OR (views = 50)
.where({ _or: [{ featured: true, views: { lt: 10 } }, { views: { eq: 50 } }] })

// (views > 90 OR views = 0) AND published this year
.where({ _or: [{ views: { gt: 90 } }, { views: { eq: 0 } }], publishedAt: { gte: '2026-01-01' } })
```

Groups nest four levels deep.

## Filtering by a related field

```ts
.where({ 'author.title': { contains: 'jane' } })
.where({ 'categories.slug': 'engineering' })
```

**One level only.** For two, query the middle type first.

## Sorting

```ts
.sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
```

Use the name from your content model - `createdAt`, `publishedAt`, `title`, or
any field you declared. camelCase is canonical. The default is `createdAt`
descending.

## A realistic query

```ts
const { data, meta } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .where({
    'categories.slug': 'engineering',
    heroImage: { exists: true },
    _or: [{ featured: true }, { views: { gt: 500 } }],
  })
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .props(['id', 'title', 'slug', 'publishedAt'])
  .limit(12)
  .get()
```

## Common mistakes

- **An array as a condition.** `{ views: [1, 2] }` is refused; use `in`.
- **A string operator on a number.** Refused, not coerced.
- **A two-level relation path.** Refused.
- **Expecting `contains` to be case-sensitive.** It is not.

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Pagination](/build/querying/pagination)
  · [Query troubleshooting](/build/querying/troubleshooting)

---

# Pagination

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/pagination
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Offset paging, cursors, and when to skip the count.

# Pagination

```ts
const { data, meta } = await tangen.objects('article').limit(20).offset(40).get()
```

`meta` carries `total`, `limit`, `offset`, `cursor` and `hasMore`.

## Offset, for page numbers

Right when the reader picks a page and expects "Page 3 of 12".

```ts
const page = 3, perPage = 20
const { data, meta } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .limit(perPage)
  .offset((page - 1) * perPage)
  .get()

const totalPages = Math.ceil((meta.total ?? 0) / perPage)
```

Offset gets slower as it grows: the database still walks the rows it skips.

## Cursors, for feeds

Right for infinite scroll, a "load more" button, or walking everything.

```ts
let cursor: string | undefined
do {
  const { data, meta } = await tangen
    .objects('article')
    .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
    .limit(100)
    .after(cursor)
    .get()

  process(data)
  cursor = meta.hasMore ? meta.cursor : undefined
} while (cursor)
```

A cursor walks the same order as your sort and does not degrade with depth.
**Do not mix a cursor with `offset`** - that is refused.

## Skip the count

```ts
.total(false)
```

The count is a second query over the whole table. On a large type it can cost
more than the page itself.

`total` comes back `null`, and **`hasMore` is still exact** - it is not an
estimate. Use this whenever your UI shows "load more" rather than a page count.

## Rule of thumb

| your UI | use |
|---|---|
| page numbers | `offset`, with `total` |
| load more, infinite scroll | `after`, with `total: false` |
| exporting everything | `after`, with `total: false` |

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Performance](/build/performance)

---

# Querying relations

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/relations
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Expanding related content with depth, and keeping the cost down.

# Querying relations

A relation is an id until you ask for more.

```ts
await tangen.objects('article').depth(0).get()   // author: "obj_01H…"
await tangen.objects('article').depth(1).get()   // author: { id, title, … }
await tangen.objects('article').depth(2).get()   // and the author's relations expand
```

**The ceiling is 5.** Asking for more is refused with a `422` naming the field;
over REST the gateway clamps instead and reports it in `meta.clamped`.

## Ask for what you render

```ts
const { data } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .depth(1)
  .populate('author', ['id', 'title', 'slug'])
  .props(['id', 'title', 'slug', 'author'])
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```

`props` narrows the row; `populate` narrows the **expanded** record. A card grid
needs the author's name, not their biography.

## What depth does not affect

- **Media** expands at every depth, including `0`. It is always resolved, and
  it resolves on the object you asked for rather than on expanded targets.
- **`object` fields** are values on the row at every depth.
- **Links** consume no depth at all - a link resolves the same at `depth(0)`.

So `depth` is about **relations**, and nothing else.

## Cycles

An article's author whose latest article is that article stops at the object
already on the path. You cannot loop, however deep you ask.

## Cost

Each level is another expansion pass. A list of 50 articles at `depth(2)` is
three passes over widening sets.

Practical shapes:

| view | depth |
|---|---|
| a card grid | `0` or `1` with `populate` |
| an article page | `1` |
| a page needing the author's employer | `2` |
| anything deeper | query the middle type separately |

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Relations](/build/content-modeling/relations)
  · [Performance](/build/performance)

---

# Using the SDK

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/sdk
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Configuring the client, cancelling requests, handling errors, and what the SDK does not do.

# Using the SDK

```ts app/lib/tangen.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

export const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
  timeoutMs: 10_000,
  retries: 2,
})
```

One client per process. Creating one per request throws away nothing important
but is pointless.

`retries` adds attempts for 429, 502, 503, 504 and network failures. It does
**not** retry a 4xx that is your fault.

## Browser or server

The root entry is browser-safe - it imports no `node:` module. But **the API key
is not**: a key in a browser bundle is a public key. Read on the server and pass
data down.

`@tangen/sdk/node` holds the Node and Bun SSR helpers.

## Cancelling

```ts
const controller = new AbortController()
const promise = tangen.objects('article').limit(50).get({ signal: controller.signal })
controller.abort()
```

Aborting cancels the request **and stops the retry loop**, so a cancelled read
does not quietly retry three more times. Every method takes `{ signal }`.

## Errors

```ts
import { TangenError } from '@tangen/sdk'

try {
  await tangen.objects('article').create({ title: '' })
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof TangenError) {
    if (e.code === 'VALIDATION_ERROR') return showFieldErrors(e.fieldErrors)
    if (e.code === 'NOT_FOUND') return notFound()
    if (e.code === 'FORBIDDEN') return serverError('key is missing an action')
  }
  throw e
}
```

Switch on `code`, never on the message.

## Globals, media, search

```ts
const settings = (await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()).data.values
const assets   = await tangen.media.list({ limit: 20 })
const hits     = await tangen.search('pricing')
const locales  = await tangen.locales()
const maps     = await tangen.extensionSettings('maps')   // an extension's settings marked public, e.g. a Maps browser key
```

`tangen.media` is read-only. Uploading is a REST call.

## What the SDK does not do

**Site authentication.** There is no `tangen.auth`. Registering, logging in,
refreshing and reading the current site user are REST calls your application
makes with `fetch`. See [Site authentication](/build/auth).

Media **uploads**, form **submissions** and schema operations are also REST or
CLI.

## Related

- [SDK reference](/reference/sdk) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Site authentication](/build/auth) · [Query troubleshooting](/build/querying/troubleshooting)

---

# Query troubleshooting

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/querying/troubleshooting
Section: Build with Tangen / Querying
Verification: executable

> Reading a TangenQL refusal and finding the cause.

# Query troubleshooting

TangenQL refuses rather than guesses. Every refusal is a `422
VALIDATION_ERROR` naming the offending field.

| symptom | cause | fix |
|---|---|---|
| "unknown field" | a typo, or the field is not pushed to this deployment | check the model, then `tangen push` |
| "unknown operator" | an operator that does not exist, e.g. `between` | use `gte` and `lte` together |
| a bare array is refused | `{ views: [1, 2] }` | `{ views: { in: [1, 2] } }` |
| a string operator refused | `contains` on a number | use `eq`, or the right operator for the type |
| "unknown type" | a typo, or the type is not on this deployment | `tangen push` |
| a relation path is refused | more than one level deep | query the middle type separately |
| depth is refused | over the ceiling of 5, where no clamp runs (the local client, an extension) | reduce it, or query in two steps |
| a cursor is refused | `after` (the wire key for a cursor) combined with `offset` | use one or the other |

## A read that quietly did less than you asked

A REST read does not refuse an over-limit `depth` or `limit`; the gateway
**clamps** it and says so in `meta.clamped`:

```json
{ "meta": { "clamped": { "depth": { "requested": 9, "applied": 5 } } } }
```

If a query looks like it ignored you, read `meta` before changing the query.

## Empty results with no error

| cause | check |
|---|---|
| the content is a draft | a default read is published only |
| wrong deployment | the key was issued on another deployment |
| the type is not pushed here | `tangen doctor` |
| a filter is stricter than you think | remove conditions until rows appear |

## `403` rather than empty

A key missing an action gets `403 FORBIDDEN`, never a silent empty list. If a
query works on one deployment and 403s on another, compare the two keys'
actions.

## Types disagree with the schema

Regenerate:

```bash
bun run tangen types
```

Your editor is reading `app/generated/`, which only changes when you push or
regenerate.

## Related

- [Errors reference](/reference/errors) · [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql)
  · [Permissions](/reference/permissions) ·
  [Generated types](/build/getting-started/generated-types)

# Frontend integration

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/frontend
Section: Build with Tangen / Frontend
Verification: executable

> Connecting a frontend to Tangen - fetching, routing, rendering, caching and errors.

# Frontend integration

Tangen is headless and framework-neutral. It serves content over HTTP; your
application owns everything about how that content becomes pages.

## The division

| Tangen owns | your application owns |
|---|---|
| the content model and its data | routes and URL shapes |
| publication state | which URL a piece of content lives at |
| media storage and delivery | rendering, layout, components |
| link **identity** | resolving a link to an href |
| localized **content** | locale routing (`/fr/…`, a subdomain, a header) |
| SEO **data** | emitting `<meta>` and `<link>` tags |

If you find yourself asking "what URL does Tangen give this page?", the answer
is that it does not. You do.

## Fetch on the server

```ts app/lib/tangen.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

export const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
})
```

The API key must stay server-side. Fetch in a server component, a loader, or a
route handler, and pass data to the browser.

Client-side fetching is possible but needs a key the browser can hold - which
means a key scoped to published reads only, and even then you are publishing a
credential. Prefer the server.

## Routing

Look content up by the thing that is in the URL:

```ts
const article = await tangen.objects('article').findBySlug(slug)
if (!article) return notFound()
```

For a static build, list the slugs first:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('article').props(['slug']).total(false).limit(500).get()
const paths = data.map((a) => ({ slug: a.slug }))
```

## Rendering links

Never store or render a URL Tangen gave you for internal content - it does not
give you one. Resolve identity with your own router:

```ts
import { isInternalLink, isExternalLink, isLinkResolved, linkSuffix } from '@tangen/sdk'
```

See [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links).

## Caching

Tangen caches server-side; your frontend caches too, and the two are
independent.

- **Published content** is safe to cache. Choose a TTL, or revalidate on a
  webhook.
- **Preview** is `no-store`. Never cache it.
- **Globals** are read on nearly every render - cache them for at least the
  life of a request.
- **Localized content** varies by locale: the locale must be in your cache key.

## Errors and not-found

```ts
import { TangenError } from '@tangen/sdk'

try {
  const article = await tangen.objects('article').findBySlug(slug)
  if (!article) return notFound()
  return render(article)
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof TangenError && e.code === 'NOT_FOUND') return notFound()
  throw e   // a real failure should be a 500, not a blank page
}
```

Distinguish "no such content" from "the CMS is unreachable". The first is a
404; the second is your problem and should page someone.

## Metadata

Read your SEO fields and emit the tags yourself. Tangen holds the data; the
`<head>` is your framework's.

## A framework example

The following is **an example, not a contract** - Tangen does not require
Next.js, and every other framework does the equivalent.

```tsx app/[slug]/page.tsx
import { tangen } from '@/lib/tangen'
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation'

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const { data } = await tangen.objects('page').props(['slug']).total(false).limit(500).get()
  return data.map((p) => ({ slug: p.slug! }))
}

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const page = await tangen.objects('page').findBySlug(params.slug)
  return page ? { title: page.title, description: page.seo?.metaDescription } : {}
}

export default async function Page({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const page = await tangen.objects('page').findBySlug(params.slug)
  if (!page) notFound()
  return <article>{/* … */}</article>
}
```

`@tangen/nextjs` and `@tangen/astro` exist as opt-in helpers. Both are
**experimental** - see [Public contract](/reference/public-contract).

## What has actually been proven

Being framework-neutral is a claim about the API, not evidence about a
framework. This is what has been built and run end to end, and what has not:

| integration | status |
|---|---|
| a plain HTTP server (`Bun.serve`) reading through `@tangen/sdk` | **PROVEN** - the whole [Enterprise Website](/learn/enterprise-website), 13 routes, three locales, media, forms |
| any framework that can call `fetch` on a server | **GENERICALLY COMPATIBLE** - the SDK is ordinary async code with no runtime assumptions beyond `fetch` |
| `@tangen/nextjs`, `@tangen/astro` | **UNPROVEN** - experimental helpers, not yet built end to end from their own documentation |
| client-side-only rendering | **NOT APPLICABLE** - the API key is a server credential |

The distinction that matters: the **Tangen contract** is the SDK call and the
shape it returns. The **framework integration** is where you put that call.
Everything in the Enterprise Website moves to another framework by changing the
second and none of the first.

## Related

- [Using the SDK](/build/querying/sdk) · [Preview](/build/content/preview) ·
  [Media](/build/media) · [Localization](/build/localization) ·
  [Performance](/build/performance)

# Media

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/media
Section: Build with Tangen / Frontend
Verification: executable

> Uploading, reading and rendering media, and what transforms are available.

# Media

Media is a library of assets. A `media` field on a content type points at one.

```ts
heroImage: field.media({
  label: 'Hero image',
  config: { mimeTypes: ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'] },
}),
```

## Reading

Media is **always resolved**. It expands at every depth, including `depth(0)`,
so an article's `heroImage` is an object with a URL without you asking:

```ts
const article = await tangen.objects('article').findBySlug(slug)
// article.heroImage → { id, url, alt, width, height, mimeType, … }
```

`props` is the opt-out: a projection that omits the field returns no media.

```ts
const assets = await tangen.media.list({ limit: 20 })
```

`tangen.media` is **read-only by design**: list, read, and build asset URLs.

## Uploading

Uploading is a REST call, not an SDK method. It needs `media: write`:

```ts
const body = new FormData()
body.append('file', file)

await fetch(`${process.env.TANGEN_API_URL}/api/v1/media/upload`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY}` },
  body,
})
```

Most media arrives through the Admin. Upload from code when your application
ingests files - a user avatar, an import.

## Transforms

```http
GET /api/v1/media/transform?id=<id>&w=800&format=webp&quality=70
```

| parameter | does |
|---|---|
| `w`, `h` | target width and height |
| `fit`, `position` | how the image fills the box |
| `format` | `webp`, `avif`, and the rest |
| `quality` | encoder quality |
| `blur` | blur radius |
| `variant` | a named variant declared on the field or workspace |

Transforms serve **without a key** so a browser can load them directly, and
they are cached immutably.

Named variants are usually better than ad-hoc parameters: declare them once on
the field and every consumer gets the same rendition.

```ts
heroImage: field.media({
  label: 'Hero image',
  config: {
    variants: [
      { name: 'hero', width: 1600, format: 'avif', quality: 60 },
      { name: 'card', width: 640, format: 'webp', quality: 70 },
    ],
  },
}),
```

**Transforms are images.** A PDF or a video is served as it was uploaded.

## Rendering

`transformUrl` is a method on the client's `media` accessor, not a free
import - alongside `list`, `get` and `fileUrl`. It builds a URL and issues no
request. Its options are `width`, `height`, `format`, `quality` and `fit`,
which it serializes to the `w` and `h` the route reads:

```tsx
<img
  src={tangen.media.transformUrl(article.heroImage.id, { width: 1200, format: 'webp' })}
  alt={article.heroImage.altText ?? ''}
  width={article.heroImage.width}
  height={article.heroImage.height}
/>
```

The alt text is **`altText`** on the asset, not `alt`. Always render it, and
always render intrinsic `width` and `height` - they are on the asset too, and
omitting them causes layout shift.

Use `tangen.media.fileUrl(id)` for anything that is not an image: a transform
of a PDF is a mistake, and the file URL serves the bytes as uploaded.

## Localization

Media localizes at the **asset** level: a field can hold a different rendition
per locale without `localized: true`. Alt text follows the asset.

## Storage

Where bytes live is `config/storage.ts` - local disk or S3-compatible. Changing
the adapter does **not** move existing files, and delivery always goes through
the current adapter, so assets uploaded before a switch 404 until you copy
them.

## Common mistakes

- **Expecting `tangen.media.upload()`.** Uploading is REST.
- **Importing `transformUrl` from `@tangen/sdk`.** It is `tangen.media.transformUrl`.
- **Reading `.alt`.** The asset carries `altText`.
- **Requesting a transform of a PDF.**
- **Omitting `alt`.**
- **Switching storage adapters and not copying the files.**

## Related

- [Fields reference](/reference/fields) · [SDK reference](/reference/sdk) ·
  [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) · [Performance](/build/performance)

# Localization

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/localization
Section: Build with Tangen / Capabilities
Verification: executable

> Configuring locales, localizing content and globals, querying, fallbacks and routing.

# Localization

Tangen owns **localized content**. Your application owns **URLs and routing**.
Neither side crosses that line, and knowing where it is saves most of the
confusion.

## Enable it

```ts app/config/localization.ts
import { defineLocalizationConfig } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineLocalizationConfig({
  enabled: true,
  defaultLocale: 'en',
  locales: [
    { code: 'en', label: 'English' },
    { code: 'fr', label: 'Français' },
    { code: 'de', label: 'Deutsch' },
  ],
})
```

The default locale's values live in the main content table; other locales live
in per-type side tables that `tangen push` manages.

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

## Localize fields

Per field, opt-in:

```ts
subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', localized: true }),
body:     field.richtext({ label: 'Body', localized: true }),
sku:      field.text({ label: 'SKU' }),                       // one value, all locales
```

Globals work the same way.

Media does **not** need the flag - it localizes at the asset level.

## Query a locale

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('article').locale('fr').limit(20).get()
const settings = await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()
```

```ts
const { data: locales } = await tangen.locales()
// { enabled: true, locales: [...], defaultLocale: 'en' }
```

`locales()` returns `{ enabled: false }` when localization is off, which is the
honest way to build a language switcher that disappears rather than breaks.

## Fallbacks

A field with no translation falls back to the default locale, so a partly
translated page renders rather than showing gaps. That is usually what you
want - and it means **you cannot tell "translated" from "fallen back" by
looking at the value**. If a UI needs to say "not yet translated", check for the
translation explicitly rather than comparing strings.

## Routing is yours

Tangen does not choose between `/fr/about`, `fr.example.com` and an
`Accept-Language` header. Pick one, and read the locale from it:

```ts app/[locale]/[slug]/page.tsx
export default async function Page({ params }: { params: { locale: string; slug: string } }) {
  const page = await tangen.objects('page').locale(params.locale).findBySlug(params.slug)
  if (!page) notFound()
  return render(page)
}
```

## Localized slugs

If `slug` is localized you get `/fr/a-propos`; if it is not you get
`/fr/about`. Both are legitimate. Localized slugs are better for search and
for readers; unlocalized slugs are simpler and stable across languages.

Whichever you choose, look content up by the slug **for that locale** - a
French URL resolved against English slugs finds nothing.

## Links across locales

An internal link can name a `locale`: which locale of the **target** to
resolve. It is metadata about the destination, not a routing instruction - your
router still decides the path.

## Caching

**The locale must be in your cache key.** A cache keyed on slug alone will
serve French content to English readers, and it will do it intermittently,
which is the worst kind of bug to find.

## A language switcher

```ts
const { data: info } = await tangen.locales()
if (info.enabled) {
  const options = info.locales.map((l) => ({ code: l.code, label: l.label, href: `/${l.code}/${slugFor(l.code)}` }))
}
```

Switching should land on the **same content** in the new locale, not the home
page. That means knowing the target's slug per locale, which is why localized
slugs need a little more work in the router.

## Preview

Preview takes a locale: `fetchPreviewObject({ …, locale })`. An editor
previewing the French draft should see French.

## Common mistakes

- **Localizing a SKU or a price.**
- **Forgetting the locale in a cache key.**
- **Resolving a French URL against default-locale slugs.**
- **A switcher that always goes home.**
- **Adding `localized: true` to media.**

## Related

- [Modeling for localization](/build/content-modeling/localization) ·
  [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Globals](/build/globals) ·
  [Frontend integration](/build/frontend)
