# Site authentication

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/auth
Section: Build with Tangen / Capabilities
Verification: executable

> Accounts for your site's users through the Site users extension, and calling its REST endpoints.

# Site authentication

Accounts for **your site's end users** - not your team's Admin logins, and not
your application's API key. The three are separate systems; see
[Reference → Authentication](/reference/authentication) for the full map.

Site users is a bundled **extension** (`@tangen/ext-auth`, it arrives with
`@tangen/cms`). Its tables exist only where it is installed, and its routes
live under `/api/v1/ext/auth`.

> **This is REST-only in v1.** `@tangen/sdk` has no `auth` namespace. You call
> the endpoints below with `fetch`. That is a real limitation, stated here so
> you do not go looking for an SDK method that does not exist.

## Install and configure

```bash
bun run tangen extension install auth
```

The options go on the extension's entry in `app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'
import { defineAuthOptions } from '@tangen/ext-auth'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-auth', options: defineAuthOptions({
    allowRegistration: true,
    profileFields: [
      { name: 'display_name', label: 'Display name', fieldType: 'text' },
      { name: 'bio', label: 'Bio', fieldType: 'textarea', config: { validation: { maxLength: 500 } } },
    ],
    token: { accessTtl: '15m', refreshTtl: '30d' },
  }) },
])
```

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

**Profile fields become real columns**, so adding one is a schema change and
needs a push. Their names must be **snake_case**, and that is checked at
compile time - `displayName` is a type error naming the field, before push
runs.

## Sign-in methods

Password, one-time codes by **email or SMS**, single sign-on, and guest
sessions - each on by configuration:

```ts
otp: { channels: ['email', 'sms'] },
sms: { send: async (to, message) => { /* your SMS provider */ } },   // needed for the sms channel
allowAnonymous: true,
providers: [
  { name: 'google', clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID!, clientSecret: 'GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET' },
  { name: 'github', clientId: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_ID!, clientSecret: 'GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET' },
  { name: 'oidc', id: 'okta', issuer: 'https://acme.okta.com', clientId: '…', clientSecret: 'OKTA_CLIENT_SECRET' },
],
ssoRedirectUrl: 'https://example.com/auth/callback',
```

`clientSecret` is the **name** of the deployment variable holding the secret,
never the secret itself. Send the browser to `/api/v1/ext/auth/sso/google`
(with the site key); Tangen completes the flow and redirects to
`ssoRedirectUrl` with `?accessToken=…&refreshToken=…`. The Admin's
**Sign-in methods** page prints the exact callback URL to register with each
provider. `oidc` covers any OpenID Connect issuer (Okta, Entra, Auth0,
Keycloak).

Codes by email go through the workspace mailer unless an `onOtpSend` hook
delivers them itself.

## Every call carries your site key

The sign-in endpoints are **keyed**, not anonymous. Send `X-Tangen-Key` (or
`Authorization: Bearer tgn_…`) with a key granted **Site users → sessions**:

```jsonc
{ "permissions": { "objects": { "actions": ["read"] }, "extensions": { "auth": { "actions": ["sessions"] } } } }
```

Without the header you get `401 API key required`; with a key that lacks the
grant, `403 This API key cannot sign users in`. These calls therefore belong
on your **server**, where the key lives.

## Register and log in

```ts app/lib/site-auth.ts
const API = process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!
const KEY = process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!
const headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-Tangen-Key': KEY }

export async function register(email: string, password: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/ext/auth/register`, {
    method: 'POST', headers, body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
  })
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('register failed')
  return (await res.json()).data          // { id, email, name }
}

export async function login(email: string, password: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/ext/auth/login`, {
    method: 'POST', headers, body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
  })
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('login failed')
  return (await res.json()).data          // { accessToken, refreshToken, expiresIn, user }
}
```

Everything comes back under **`data`**, like the rest of the API. A
validation failure is `422` with `error.fieldErrors` naming each field.

## The current user

```ts
export async function me(accessToken: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/ext/auth/me`, {
    headers: { 'X-Tangen-Key': KEY, Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` },
  })
  return res.ok ? (await res.json()).data : null
}
```

`PATCH /api/v1/ext/auth/me` updates the name and the profile fields you
declared.

## Refreshing

The access token is short-lived - 15 minutes by default. Exchange the refresh
token at `POST /api/v1/ext/auth/refresh` when it expires. Each refresh returns
a **new** refresh token and spends the old one; store it and discard the old
one.

## Protecting a route

Verify on the **server**, on every request that matters:

```ts
const user = await me(getAccessTokenFromSession(request))
if (!user) return redirect('/login')
```

Do not trust a client-side flag. The access token is the credential; a
`loggedIn` boolean in local storage is a suggestion.

A Tangen custom route declaring `auth: 'user'` does this for you:
`ctx.requireAuth()` answers the site user or 401.

## Storing tokens

Put the refresh token where your framework puts sessions - an httpOnly,
`Secure`, `SameSite` cookie, or a server session. Keep it out of
JavaScript-readable storage.

## Other endpoints

One-time codes (`otp/send`, `otp/verify`), password reset
(`password-reset/request`, `password-reset/confirm`), guest sessions
(`anonymous`, `anonymous/convert`), logout, and the SSO pair per provider.
The full list is in [Reference → Authentication](/reference/authentication).

## Site users are not API keys

A signed-in site user does **not** get to read your content directly. Your
server reads content with the API key and decides what that user may see. A
site-user token is not accepted by the content endpoints.

## Common mistakes

- **Looking for `tangen.auth.login()`.** It does not exist.
- **camelCase profile field names.** Compile error, by design.
- **Storing the refresh token in `localStorage`.**
- **Ignoring rotation** and reusing a spent refresh token.
- **Confusing site users with Admin members.**
- **Registering the SSO callback without its `?workspace=` query string.**

## Related

- [Authentication reference](/reference/authentication) - every endpoint and
  every option
- [Permissions](/reference/permissions) · [Errors](/reference/errors)

---

# Search

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/search
Section: Build with Tangen / Capabilities
Verification: executable

> Adding search to your site - what is indexed, how you query it, and its limits.

# Search

To add search to your site you query it: there is nothing to install, no index
to build and no third-party service to run. Search is part of the platform,
backed by PostgreSQL full-text search, with one engine.

## There is nothing to enable

Search is part of the platform and answers as soon as you have published
content. There is no `tangen enable search`; the enableable features are `auth`,
`forms`, `localization`, `graphql` and `ai`, and asking for any other name is
refused with that list.

What you do need is a key with the **`search: read`** scope:

```jsonc
{ "permissions": { "objects": { "actions": ["read"] },
                   "search":  { "actions": ["read"] } } }
```

## What is indexed

Published content, indexed as it changes. Publishing, unpublishing, updating and
deleting all update the index in the same transaction as the write - so a
published article is findable immediately, and an unpublished one stops being
found immediately.

Indexing is per **workspace, on each deployment**. Staging content is not in
production's index.

## Search

```ts
const results = await tangen.search('pricing')
```

Needs `search: read`.

Results are ranked, hydrated into full objects, and grouped by type internally
so hydration is one batch per type rather than one query per hit.

## Audiences

Search providers declare an audience. A key granted the `public` audience
searches content; `internal` reaches provider surfaces meant for the Admin.
**Give a public frontend the public audience** - the internal one exists for
Admin search and reaches things a visitor should not see.

## Tuning

| variable | default | does |
|---|---|---|
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_FUZZY` | `false` | typo tolerance via `pg_trgm`. Only the exact string `true` enables it |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS` | `100` | ceiling on rows one search returns |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_OFFSET` | `1000` | the deepest page a caller may request |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | statement timeout for a search |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_CONCURRENT` | `4` | concurrent searches per process |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_PER_WORKSPACE` | `2` | concurrent searches per workspace |

The concurrency limits exist so a search storm cannot starve content reads.
A search over the limit waits, and a search over the timeout is cut off -
both by design.

## Limits

- **Full-text, not semantic.** It matches words, not meaning. For meaning, the
  Knowledge capability does retrieval over embeddings - a different feature with
  its own requirements.
- **Published content only.** Drafts are not indexed.
- **Not a query engine.** Use [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) for filtering and
  sorting; use search for a search box.
- **Offset is capped.** Deep paging through results is refused rather than
  allowed to get slow.

## Common mistakes

- **Using search where a filter belongs.** "All articles in this category" is a
  TangenQL query.
- **Expecting drafts.**
- **Giving a public key the internal audience.**
- **Assuming search is on.** It is a capability; check before you build a UI
  that depends on it.

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions)
  · [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables) ·
  [Performance](/build/performance)

# Deployments in practice

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/deployments
Section: Build with Tangen / Ship it
Verification: executable

> Developing on one deployment, taking schema and content to the next, and staying safe in production.

# Deployments in practice

Three roles - `development`, `staging`, `production` - and each is a
deployment of its own: one process, one database (`DATABASE_URL`), one
role (`TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE`), one `.env`. Nothing is shared implicitly,
and nothing on a request or a command line selects between them.

## Day to day

You work on the development deployment. Your model changes there, your test
content lives there, and your local frontend points at it.

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

## Taking a schema change forward

Each deployment has its own database, so the same code is applied three
times - from wherever can reach each database:

```bash
bun run tangen push                    # on your laptop: the development database
# in CI, with staging's .env:          tangen push
# on a host inside the network:        tangen push   (production's .env)
```

Read the plan each time. The plan for production is not the plan for
development, because the two databases are in different states.

**Production refuses destructive operations.** Remove a field on
development, verify on staging, and take the removal to production as a
reviewed migration - there is no flag that skips this.

## Taking content forward

Schema and content move by different mechanisms, and conflating them is the
usual confusion:

| moving | mechanism |
|---|---|
| **schema** - types, fields, tables | `tangen push` on each deployment |
| **content, media, extension data** between deployments | **Porter**: export a bundle and import it, or an instance-to-instance transfer |
| **a reviewed set of drafts**, published together on one deployment | a **Release** |

A push never moves content. A Release never crosses a database.

### Porter

Porter moves data as a bundle: export, import, and instance-to-instance
transfer. Ids are stable across deployments and a slug match updates in
place, so a re-import is idempotent. Credentials, sessions and API keys
never travel.

### Releases

A Release is a reviewed, frozen set of drafts of one workspace that
publishes together, in place. **Releases are created, approved and applied
in the Admin or over the API.** The CLI is read-only on them:

```bash
bun run tangen release list                      # status, approval, schedule
bun run tangen release status <id>               # items in apply order, outcomes
```

That split is deliberate: applying a release is an approval-gated act, not
something a script should be able to do because it had a terminal.

The properties that matter to you:

- **The approved payload is frozen.** What was reviewed is what publishes;
  the drafts cannot drift between approval and application.
- **One object belongs to at most one open Release.**
- **Preflight runs first**, and reports what would block.
- **There is no force apply.** A release that cannot apply is fixed and
  retried, not overridden.
- **History is kept**, so what was published when is answerable.

Releases can be scheduled and retried.

## Configuration that differs

The workspace config says what the site is; the deployment's variables say
where it runs:

```bash .env  (the production deployment)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://.../northwind_prod
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
SERVER_URL=https://cms.example.com
FRONTEND_URL=https://example.com
ADMIN_URL=https://admin.example.com
```

Keys, media storage, cache and extension installation state are all per
deployment. An extension enabled on development is not enabled on production
until someone enables it there.

## Capabilities differ too

A capability can be `on` on one deployment and `off` or `unavailable` on
another. Code that assumes search exists will fail where it does not -
check, and degrade.

## Testing on staging

Staging exists to rehearse. Push the schema there first, import the content
there first, and look. A production incident that staging would have caught
is the most expensive kind.

## Common mistakes

- **`--env` anything.** There is no such flag; run the command from the
  deployment you mean.
- **Expecting a push to bring content with it.**
- **Approving a destructive operation to "force" production.** It refuses
  regardless.
- **Assuming extension state travels.** Install and enable are per
  deployment.

## Related

- [Deployments reference](/reference/deployments) ·
  [The schema workflow](/build/getting-started/schema-workflow) ·
  [CLI reference](/reference/cli) · [Deploying](/operate/deployment)

---

# Performance

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/performance
Section: Build with Tangen / Ship it
Verification: executable

> Caching, query cost, and finding what makes a page slow.

# Performance

Most slow Tangen pages are one of four things: too much depth, no projection,
a missing cache, or an exact count on a large type.

## Query cost

**Depth.** Each level is another expansion pass. A card grid at `depth(2)` does
three passes over a widening set to render a name.

```ts
.depth(1).populate('author', ['id', 'title', 'slug'])
```

**Projection.** `props` narrows what is selected and serialized; `populate`
narrows **one named relation's** expanded record. A list of 50 articles does not
need 50 bodies.

`populate` takes **two arguments**: the relation field, then its columns. The
one-argument form typechecks against a loose signature and silently narrows
nothing, so you keep paying the cost you were trying to avoid.

**Counting.** `total` is a second query over the whole table.

```ts
.total(false)     // hasMore is still exact
```

Use it whenever the UI shows "load more" rather than a page count.

**Paging.** `offset` walks the rows it skips. For feeds and exports use a
cursor:

```ts
.after(meta.cursor)
```

## Caching

Three layers, and they are independent:

| layer | caches | you control |
|---|---|---|
| **Tangen** | content reads, per workspace | TTLs in the workspace config |
| **your frontend** | rendered pages and fetched data | your framework |
| **the browser or CDN** | responses | your headers |

Rules that save real incidents:

- **The locale must be in your cache key.** Otherwise a French reader gets
  English intermittently.
- **Preview is `no-store`.** Never cache it, and never let a preview response
  warm a published cache.
- **Globals are read on nearly every render.** Cache them at least per request.
- **Invalidate on publish**, not on a timer, when freshness matters. A webhook
  on `object.published` is the usual mechanism.

## Modeling for speed

- **A many-relation you always expand** is a cost on every read of that type.
- **Filtering on a field you did not model as filterable** - `link` is not
  filterable - means doing it in your application over a larger result set.
- **Deeply nested repeaters** serialize on every read whether you render them
  or not. `props` is the escape.

## Performance Monitor

The Admin's Devspace has a **Performance Monitor**: per-request SQL with real
execution and pool-queue time, duplicate and N+1 detection, page vitals, and
captured console errors.

It is on in development by default. The process variable that forces it
keeps its older name:

```bash
TANGEN_QUERY_MONITOR=1    # force on
TANGEN_QUERY_MONITOR=0    # force off
```

The Admin toggle wins over the variable. The bootstrap flag is
`queryMonitorEnabled`. **The product is Performance Monitor**; those two
identifiers are the implementation's, and they are what you type.

**It is not Telemetry.** Telemetry is a separate operator-facing capability
that keeps recent operational events in memory. Performance Monitor is a
developer tool for one request at a time.

## Debugging a slow page

1. Open the page with Performance Monitor on.
2. Look at **statement count** first. A page doing 40 queries has an N+1, not a
   slow query.
3. Look for **duplicates** - the same statement several times usually means a
   global read inside a loop.
4. Check **depth and projection** on the query behind it.
5. Only then look at individual timings.

## Related

- [TangenQL reference](/reference/tangenql) · [Pagination](/build/querying/pagination)
  · [Querying relations](/build/querying/relations) ·
  [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables)

# Testing your application

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/testing
Section: Build with Tangen / Ship it
Verification: executable

> What to test around a Tangen site, and what not to.

# Testing your application

You are testing **your site**, not Tangen. The platform has its own suite; your
tests should fail when your code is wrong, not when Tangen changes an internal.

## What is worth testing

| test | because |
|---|---|
| your **queries** return what the page needs | a filter or a projection is easy to get subtly wrong |
| your **link resolution** builds the right href | it is your router, not Tangen's |
| your **routing** finds content by slug, and 404s when it should | the most common page bug |
| **locale** routing and fallbacks | quiet, intermittent failures otherwise |
| **form** submit and validation display | your markup against the server's answer |
| **preview** fails closed | a leak, if it does not |
| **auth-protected routes** actually redirect | verified on the server |

## What is not

- **That Tangen validates a required field.** It does; that is its test.
- **That `depth(1)` expands a relation.** Same.
- **Internal shapes** - the schema cache, the query compiler, the runtime
  registry. Those are not your contract and will change.

A test that breaks when Tangen changes something you never call is a test that
will be deleted in six months.

## Test data

Seed a **dedicated deployment** (its own database) and commit the seed. Deterministic data means
a failing assertion is a real failure rather than yesterday's content.

```bash
bun run tangen push
```

Then seed content the way your application writes it - through the SDK with a
key that has `objects: write`, from a script you can re-run. That keeps the
seed and your application on the same path, so a seed that works proves the
write path works.

Point tests at that deployment's key, and never at production.

## Querying tests

```ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'bun:test'
import { tangen } from '../app/lib/tangen'

describe('article listing', () => {
  it('returns published articles, newest first', async () => {
    const { data } = await tangen.objects('article')
      .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
      .limit(5)
      .get()

    expect(data.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)
    expect(data.every((a) => a.status === 'published')).toBe(true)
  })
})
```

Assert on **what your page needs**: the field is present, the order is right,
the draft is absent.

## Preview

The valuable preview test is the negative one:

```ts
it('renders not-found for a bad preview token, never the published page', async () => {
  const res = await fetchPage('/preview?id=obj_1&type=article&token=prev_bogus')
  expect(res.status).toBe(404)
})
```

Falling back to published is the failure mode that makes a leak look like a
success.

## Browser tests

Use a browser for the two things only a browser answers: **what the layout does
at a width**, and **where focus goes**. Everything else is cheaper as a unit
test.

Serve fixed content, so a layout assertion fails because the layout changed and
not because an editor did.

## Deployments

Run against the development deployment locally and staging in CI. Never
against production, and never with a key that can write there.

Test **that your app handles a deployment difference** - a capability off in
one place - rather than testing the deployments themselves.

## When you need a real database

Only if your application owns tables of its own through custom tables. Reading
Tangen content is an HTTP call, and a running Tangen against a seeded
database is the honest test double.

## Common mistakes

- **Testing against production.**
- **Asserting on generated internal shapes** instead of the fields you render.
- **A shared mutable database** where one test's write breaks another's read.
- **Mocking the SDK so thoroughly** that the test passes with a query that
  would 422.

## Related

- [Querying](/build/querying) · [Preview](/build/content/preview) ·
  [Deployments in practice](/build/deployments) · [Errors](/reference/errors)

# Cache lifecycle

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/build/performance/cache
Section: Build with Tangen / Cache & performance
Verification: executable

> What a read costs the second time, what publishing invalidates, and what you have to do about it.

# Cache lifecycle

Delivery reads are cached. You do not configure it, warm it, or clear it after
an edit.

## The whole lifecycle

Measured against a real project, reading one product through the SDK:

```text
cold read              571.7 ms   "Streaming ingestion that does not drop events"
warm read                9.1 ms   "Streaming ingestion that does not drop events"

  -- edit the tagline, publish --

read after publish      42.7 ms   "Ingestion that never drops an event"
read again               5.6 ms   "Ingestion that never drops an event"
```
Three things to take from that:

1. A repeated read is served from cache.
2. **Publishing invalidates.** The next read returns the new value, not a stale
   one, with no action from you.
3. The read after a publish costs more than a warm read and less than a cold
   one - it refills.

This was measured without Redis, on the PostgreSQL fallback. Redis makes the
numbers smaller; the lifecycle is the same.

## What invalidates

Publishing and unpublishing an object invalidate the reads that could return
it. Saving a draft does not - a draft is not in the published view that
Delivery serves.

If you edit and do not publish, the Delivery API is *correct* to keep returning
the old value.

## Controlling it

**The SDK query builder has no cache method.** Caching is automatic and the
platform's defaults are what the measurements above show. There is nothing to
call and nothing to configure per query through `@tangen/sdk`.

A caller posting to the Delivery API directly can state what staleness it will
accept, because `cacheStrategy` is a key on the query body:

```json
{
  "query": { "slug": { "eq": "gridlock" } },
  "cacheStrategy": { "ttl": 60, "swr": 300 }
}
```
`ttl` is how long a result stays fresh; `swr` is how long a stale result may be
served while a fresh one is fetched behind it. Most sites never need it - the
default plus publish-invalidation is the whole story.

## Related

- [Publishing](/build/content/publishing)
- [Your first query](/build/querying/first-query)

# Extensions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions
Section: Extensions / Overview
Verification: executable

> Using the extensions that ship with Tangen - Forms, Flow, SEO: what each one does, and the three separate steps between a package being available and a feature being on.

# Extensions

An extension adds capability to a workspace: server routes, Admin screens, Flow
actions and triggers, content types of its own. Some ship with Tangen. Others
you write, or install from a registry.

This section is about **using** them. If you want to build one, go to
[Extend Tangen](/extend).

## Three steps, not one

The single most common confusion is treating availability, installation and
activation as one thing. They are three, they happen on different surfaces, and
the CLI reports them separately.

```text
declare   →   install   →   enable
 config        database     database
             per env       per env
```
### Declare

A project lists the extensions it may use in `app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-seo' },
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows' },
])
```
Declaring makes an extension **available**. It does not turn anything on, and it
is workspace-wide - the same declaration serves every deployment.

Options go here too, and they are read by the extension itself:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: { runRetentionDays: 14 } }
```
See [Extension options](/extend/configuration) for what an extension does with
them.

### Install

Installing writes a row in this deployment's database:

```sh
tangen extension install seo
```
Nothing about your files changes. The extension's `onInstall` runs, its tables
(if it declares any) are migrated, and the deployment now knows about it.

### Enable

Installing leaves an extension enabled. Disabling and re-enabling is a separate
action, also per deployment:

```sh
tangen extension list
#  seo    SEO     0.1.142   installed, enabled
#  flows  Flows   0.1.143   installed, enabled
```
An extension that is declared but not installed contributes nothing: no routes,
no Flow actions, no Admin screens. That is not a bug, it is the point - you can
run an extension in development and not in production.

## Bundled extensions

**SEO** and **Flow** arrive with `@tangen/cms`. You never install their
packages, and there is no supported add command for either - putting
`@tangen/ext-seo` in your own dependencies is not an instruction this
documentation will give you.

They are already in your `node_modules` because the platform brought them. A
scaffolded project declares both for you. You still install and enable them per
deployment like anything else.

## What ships

| extension | package | how you turn it on | documented |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Forms](/extensions/forms) | core capability - no package | `tangen extension install forms` | yes |
| [SEO](/extensions/seo) | `@tangen/ext-seo`, bundled | `tangen extension install seo` | yes |
| [Flow](/extensions/flow) | `@tangen/ext-flows`, bundled | `tangen extension install flows` | yes |

**Forms is the odd one.** It is a core capability with no package, enabled with
`tangen extension install forms` rather than installed. Everything else in this section is
an extension and follows declare / install / enable.

Other packages exist under `extensions/` in the Tangen repository - Porter,
Review, Variants, Studio, and a kitchen-sink reference. They are not published
for external installation in v1 and are not documented here. Seeing a package
name in a repository is not a supported install.

## Related

- [Extension options](/extend/configuration) - what your `options` reach
- [Extend Tangen](/extend) - building one
- [CLI reference](/reference/cli) - every `tangen extension` command

---

# Forms

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/forms
Section: Extensions / Forms
Verification: executable

> Defining forms in code or the Admin, rendering them, and handling submissions.

# Forms

> Forms is a **core capability**, not an installed extension - so it is enabled
> differently from SEO or Flow. Run `tangen extension install forms` once; there is no
> `tangen extension install` step. See [Extensions](/extensions) for how the two
> mechanisms differ.


Forms is a **built-in capability**, not an extension. There is nothing to
install: configure it, and it is there.

A form has fields, validation and submissions. Editors can build one in the
Admin; you can define one in code. Both end up in the same place.

## Define one in code

```ts app/forms/newsletter.ts
import { defineForm } from '@tangen/cms'

export const newsletterForm = defineForm({
  name: 'Newsletter signup',
  slug: 'newsletter-signup',
  isLive: true,
  fields: [
    { id: 'email', type: 'email', name: 'email', label: 'Email', required: true, placeholder: 'you@example.com' },
    { id: 'name',  type: 'text',  name: 'name',  label: 'Name' },
    {
      id: 'frequency', type: 'radio', name: 'frequency', label: 'How often?',
      options: [
        { label: 'Weekly', value: 'weekly' },
        { label: 'Monthly', value: 'monthly' },
      ],
    },
  ],
})
```
```ts app/forms/index.ts
import { newsletterForm } from './newsletter'

export default [newsletterForm]
```
`tangen push` upserts each definition on its slug. A code-first form is
**read-only in the Admin builder** - code is its source of truth.

## Dynamic options

Options can be a function, resolved server-side at render and submit:

```ts
{
  id: 'topic', type: 'select', name: 'topic', label: 'Topic',
  options: async ({ tangen }) => {
    const r = await tangen.objects('category').status('published').limit(50).get()
    return r.data.map((c) => ({ label: c.title, value: c.slug ?? c.id }))
  },
}
```
The function is stripped at push and never reaches the browser.

## Render it

Fetch the schema and render it with your own components:

```ts
const res = await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/forms/newsletter-signup/schema`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
})
const { data: form } = await res.json()
// form.fields → id, type, name, label, required, placeholder, options
```
Needs `forms: read`. Tangen gives you the definition; the markup is yours.

## Submit

```ts
await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/forms/newsletter-signup/submit`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ email, name, frequency }),
})
```
Needs `forms: submit` - a separate action from `read`, so a public key can
submit without listing submissions.

Validation runs server-side against the definition. A `422 VALIDATION_ERROR`
names each field. **Validate in the browser for the experience, and never trust
it** - the server's answer is the one that counts.

## When a form is closed

| code | means |
|---|---|
| `FORM_DISABLED` | the form is not live |
| `FORM_CLOSED` / `FORM_NOT_OPEN` | it exists and is not accepting submissions |
| `ENTRY_LIMIT` | it reached its configured submission limit |

These are not your bug. Render the message the form is configured with.

## Reading submissions

```ts
const res = await fetch(`${API}/api/v1/forms/newsletter-signup/submissions`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
})
```
Needs `forms: read`. **Do not give a public frontend key that action** - it is
everyone's email addresses.

## Hooks

Run code after a submission - send mail, create content, call another system:

```ts app/forms/index.ts
import { defineFormHooks } from '@tangen/cms'

export default [
  defineFormHooks('contact-us', {
    afterSubmit: async (submission, form, ctx) => {
      // runs as a queued job; ctx has a Tangen client for content changes
    },
  }),
]
```
`defineFormHooks` attaches to **any** form by slug, including one an editor
built in the Admin, without creating a definition.

## Notifications

Form notification email goes through the workspace mailer - `config/mail.ts`.
Without a transport configured, notifications do not send.

## Common mistakes

- **Calling it "the Forms extension."** It is a capability.
- **Editing a code-first form in the Admin.** It is read-only there.
- **Giving a public key `forms: read`** when it only needs `submit`.
- **Trusting client-side validation.**

## Related

- [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions)
  · [Errors](/reference/errors) · [Configuration](/reference/configuration)

---

# Reading submissions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/forms/submissions
Section: Extensions / Forms
Verification: executable

> Who may read a form submission, and the narrow accessor that resolves one by id.

# Reading submissions

## Who may read one

| caller | result |
|---|---|
| a member with the grant | the submissions |
| a Delivery API key | **403** |
| nobody | **401** |

A Delivery key is for reading published content. It cannot read what people
submitted, whatever its other scopes say. This is not configurable, and it is
why a public frontend never holds a key that could.

## Resolving one by id

Server-side code with a Tangen client - a custom route, a content hook, an
extension - can resolve a single submission:

```ts
const submission = await tangen.forms.submission(submissionId)
// {
//   id: 'sub_1',
//   formId: 'frm_1',
//   values: { company: 'Meridian Group', companySize: '500+' },
//   createdAt: '2026-09-02T00:00:00.000Z',
// }
```
Scoped to the client's own workspace. That scoping is not a
filter you can widen - a submission from another workspace is simply not
found.

### What it returns, and what it leaves behind

Returned: `id`, `formId`, `values`, `createdAt`.

Deliberately not returned: the submitter's IP address, the request metadata
(user agent, captcha score), and the internal `notes` field. Those are
operational and lead-management data. Something reacting to a submission needs
what was submitted, not who submitted it from where.

### Missing submissions

`null`. A deleted id, an id from another workspace, a malformed id and an
empty string all return `null` rather than throwing, so a caller handles one
case instead of four.

## Why this exists

The `form.submitted` event carries identifiers only, on purpose: values must not
ride the general event bus where every subscriber would see them. Something with
the id and the authority resolves them here.

Flow uses exactly this to hydrate its trigger - see
[Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration).

## Related

- [Forms](/extensions/forms)
- [Flow security and retention](/extensions/flow/security)

---

# Flow

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> Automations that run when something happens - a form submitted, content published, a schedule elapsing.

# Flow

Flow runs work when something happens. A demo request arrives and a lead is
created. An article is published and a cache is purged. A schedule elapses and
a digest goes out.

A flow is a graph. One **trigger** starts it; **nodes** do the work; **edges**
decide what runs next.

```text
trigger  →  condition  →  action  →  action
                 │
                 └──────→  action
```

Every node writes an output, and every later node can read it.

> Flow is an extension. It ships with Tangen but is installed and enabled per
> deployment - see [Extensions](/extensions). Nothing below works until
> `tangen extension install flows`.

## What a flow is made of

| kind | does |
|---|---|
| **trigger** | starts the flow. Exactly one per flow |
| **action** | the work: HTTP, content, email, code, a contributed action |
| **condition** | a yes/no branch |
| **switch** | a many-way branch on one value |
| **transform** | builds an object from expressions, without calling anything |
| **loop** | runs its body once per item in a collection |
| **wait** | parks the run and resumes it later |

## How data moves

A node's result is addressable by the node's id:

```text
{{trigger.…}}                     what started the flow
{{steps.<nodeId>.output.…}}       any earlier node's result
{{item}} {{itemIndex}}            inside a loop body
```

So a node that returns `{ lead: { id: 'nw_123' } }` is read downstream as
`{{steps.createLead.output.lead.id}}`. See
[Data and expressions](/extensions/flow/concepts).

## Runs are durable

A run is queued, not executed inline with whatever triggered it. It survives a
restart, retries on failure, and can park at a `wait` for days and pick up
where it left off. Every run keeps a per-step log with timings, which is what
you read when something did not happen.

## Extensions can add to it

An extension contributes its own actions and triggers, and they appear on the
canvas next to the built-in ones. A contributed action runs with **its own**
extension's context and storage - Flow invokes it, it does not own it.

Building one is [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions).

## Where to go next

- [Getting started](/extensions/flow/getting-started) - a flow that runs, in five minutes
- [Data and expressions](/extensions/flow/concepts)
- [Triggers](/extensions/flow/triggers)
- [Logic nodes](/extensions/flow/logic)
- [Actions](/extensions/flow/actions)
- [Runs, retries and failures](/extensions/flow/runs)
- [Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration)
- [Security and retention](/extensions/flow/security)

# Getting started with Flow

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/getting-started
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> Build a flow that runs, read its run log, and reference one node's output from another.

# Getting started with Flow

You will build a flow with a manual trigger, a step that computes something,
and a step that reads what the first one produced. It needs no external
service.

## Before you start

Flow must be installed on the deployment you are working on:

```bash
tangen extension install flows
tangen extension list
#  flows   Flows   installed, enabled
```

## The flow

Three nodes:

```text
manual trigger  →  transform  →  log
```

**Trigger** - choose *Manual*. It starts only when you press Run, which is what
you want while building.

**Transform** - a node that builds an object out of expressions without calling
anything. Give it:

```json
{ "greeting": "hello", "answer": 42 }
```

**Log** - reads the transform's output:

```text
{{steps.shape.output.greeting}} the answer is {{steps.shape.output.answer}}
```

`shape` is the transform node's id. Every reference is
`{{steps.<nodeId>.output.<field>}}`, so give your nodes ids you will recognise.

Connect trigger → transform → log, and enable the flow.

## Run it

Press **Run**. Then open the run:

```json
{
  "status": "completed",
  "path": ["start", "shape", "done"],
  "log": [
    { "step": "shape", "action": "transform", "ok": true, "ms": 0, "output": { "greeting": "hello", "answer": 42 } },
    { "step": "done",  "action": "log", "ok": true, "ms": 1, "attempt": 1, "output": { "message": "hello the answer is 42" } }
  ]
}
```

`path` is the route the run actually took - the fastest way to see which branch
ran. `log` is one entry per step with its output and duration.

## Try it without doing it

A flow that calls something real can be tested without calling it:

```text
POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/<id>/test
```

Write-actions are simulated. An `http` node makes no request and returns

```json
{ "dryRun": true, "wouldDo": { "url": …, "method": … }, "response": { "status": 200, "body": {} } }
```

That `response` is a **stub, always 200**. A downstream branch on
`{{steps.fetch.output.response.status}}` therefore takes the success path in
every test run - a test proves the shape of your flow, not how it behaves when
the call fails. Read [Testing a flow](/extensions/flow/runs#testing).

## What you just used

`{{steps.<id>.output.…}}` is the whole data model, and it works the same for a
transform, an HTTP response, a code step or a contributed action. The next page
is that model in full.

## Related

- [Data and expressions](/extensions/flow/concepts)
- [Triggers](/extensions/flow/triggers) - replacing Manual with something real

---

# Data and expressions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/concepts
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> The scope a flow sees, how one node reads another's output, and what happens when a path is missing.

# Data and expressions

Every node can read what came before it. There is one scope and one syntax.

## The scope

| path | is |
|---|---|
| `trigger` | what started the run: the event, and whatever the trigger resolved |
| `steps.<nodeId>.output` | an earlier node's result |
| `item`, `itemIndex` | the current element, inside a loop body only |

```text
{{trigger.submission.values.company}}
{{steps.createLead.output.lead.id}}
{{item}}   {{itemIndex}}
```

## Nested paths work

A node's output is an object, and the path goes as deep as the object does. An
action returning:

```json
{ "lead": { "id": "nw_q96aczht", "tier": "enterprise", "company": "Meridian Group" } }
```

is read as:

```text
{{steps.createLead.output.lead.id}}
{{steps.createLead.output.lead.tier}}
```

Both resolved in a real run, producing
`lead nw_q96aczht tier enterprise for Meridian Group`.

## A single token keeps its type

A string that is *only* a token keeps the raw value - an array stays an array,
a number stays a number:

```text
{{steps.query.output.items}}       →  ["a","b","c"]
found {{steps.query.output.count}} →  "found 3"
```

The second is interpolation, so it is a string. That distinction matters when
you feed a value into a `loop` or an action expecting a list.

## A missing path is empty, never an error

```text
{{trigger.nope.deep}}   →  ""
```

Flow does not throw on a path that is not there. That keeps a flow running when
one optional field is absent - and it means a branch that silently never
matches is usually a misspelled path. When a value matters, test it with a
condition rather than assuming.

## Where output comes from

Two different things share the word:

- **Runtime output** - what a node actually returned. This is what
  `{{steps.…}}` reads.
- **Declared output metadata** - what a contributed action *says* its result
  contains, so the builder can offer the tokens. It never changes the value.

Metadata is `{ key, label?, type? }`, where `key` is a dot-path into the
result - `lead.id`, `response.status`. Declaring it is optional; a `code` step
declares nothing and its output is simply opaque to the picker while remaining
fully readable by hand.

See [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions) for declaring it.

## Related

- [Logic nodes](/extensions/flow/logic)
- [Runs and history](/extensions/flow/runs)

# Triggers

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/triggers
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: source

> What can start a flow, what each kind puts on the trigger scope, and what that means for security.

# Triggers

Every flow has exactly one trigger. It decides when the flow runs and what
`{{trigger.…}}` contains.

## Platform events

Thirteen event types, from content, media, members and site users:

```text
object.created     object.updated     object.published
object.unpublished object.deleted     object.scheduled
media.uploaded
member.invited     member.created     member.updated
form.submitted
site_user.registered   site_user.login
```

For a content event the trigger carries the live row as `trigger.data`, the
object's identity as `trigger.typeName` and `trigger.objectId`, its operational
labels as `trigger.labels`, and - for an update - the changed field names as
`trigger.changed` and their previous values under `trigger.prev`.

```text
{{trigger.data.title}}
trigger.changed contains price
```

A content trigger can be narrowed to one content type, and to a condition, so a
flow on "published" need not wake for every publish.

## Form submitted

`form.submitted` resolves the submission, giving
`trigger.submission = { id, formId, formSlug, values, createdAt }`. This has its
own page, because what does and does not travel matters:
[Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration).

## Manual

Runs only when someone presses Run. The right trigger while you are building,
and for anything an operator invokes deliberately.

## Schedule

Runs on a recurrence rather than an event. The run's `triggerType` records that
it was scheduled, and cancelling a flow's schedule cancels its parked runs.

## Webhook

An external system starts the flow by calling a per-flow URL. Treat that URL as
a credential: anyone who has it can start the flow.

## Extension triggers

An extension declares its own event types, namespaced `ext:<id>:<name>`:

```text
ext:crm:lead-created
```

They appear alongside the built-in ones once the contributing extension is
active in that workspace, and disappear when it is not. Their payload is
whatever the extension emitted, read as `{{trigger.payload.…}}` - proven with a
flow that branched on `trigger.payload.tier`.

A site can declare `custom:` types the same way without writing an extension -
see [site helpers](/reference/flow-contract).

## What a trigger does not do

A trigger does not authenticate anything. Who a run acts as is the flow's
`runAs`, not the trigger: `owner` (the default) runs with the current authority
of the member who owns the flow, `initiator` runs as the member or key whose
event triggered it (and refuses an event with nobody behind it, such as a public
form submission), and `identity` runs as a service or agent identity. A flow
never holds rights of its own: if its owner may not publish, the flow's publish
step is refused, and an owner who was suspended or lost the grant makes the run
fail with `AUTHORITY_LOST` rather than fall back to elevated rights. The run
record names the actor and the initiator.

## Related

- [Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration)
- [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions)

# Logic nodes

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/logic
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> Condition, switch, transform, loop and wait - the nodes that decide and shape rather than call.

# Logic nodes

## Condition

A yes/no branch. Two outlets: **yes** and **no**.

```text
path:  trigger.submission.values.companySize
op:    eq
value: 500+
```

Operators:

| operator | true when |
|---|---|
| `eq` | equal |
| `neq` | not equal |
| `gt` · `lt` | greater / less than |
| `contains` · `not_contains` | the value contains the operand |
| `exists` | the path resolves to something |

Several conditions on one node are combined; a path that is missing simply does
not match, so `exists` is how you ask whether a field arrived at all.

## Switch

A many-way branch on one value.

```text
path:  trigger.payload.tier
cases: ["enterprise", "1-50"]
```

Each case gets an outlet named `case:<value>`; anything unmatched takes
`default`. Connect the outlets you care about - an unconnected branch ends the
run, which is normal.

A real run: `{"value": "enterprise", "outlet": "case:enterprise"}`.

## Transform

Builds an object from expressions. It calls nothing, which makes it the right
place to reshape data between two nodes:

```json
{ "queue": "priority", "lead": "{{trigger.payload.leadId}}" }
```

Output: `{"lead": "nw_6ea0icx5", "queue": "priority"}`, read downstream as
`{{steps.shape.output.queue}}`.

## Loop

Runs its body once per item.

```text
path: steps.seed.output.rows
```

The body connects on the **`body`** outlet - a loop with nothing on `body` is
refused when you enable the flow, by name.

Inside the body, `{{item}}` is the element and `{{itemIndex}}` is its position.
Steps are logged per iteration:

```text
path: ["start","seed","each","body","body","body"]
  each         loop       { "items": 3 }
  body[0]      log        { "message": "item 0 = a" }
  body[1]      log        { "message": "item 1 = b" }
  body[2]      log        { "message": "item 2 = c" }
```

**A loop runs at most 20 items.** A longer collection is truncated and the run
records `truncatedFrom`, so a silent partial pass is visible rather than
guessed at. An empty collection runs the body zero times and continues.

## Wait

Parks the run and resumes it later.

```text
minutes: 1        (also hours, days - they add up)
```

**The minimum is 60 seconds.** A shorter wait is rounded up to it.

The run's status becomes `waiting` and stays that way until it is due; then it
continues from the node after the wait. Proven end to end: a run parked at
`["start","pause"]`, and on resume logged `resumed after 60s` from
`{{steps.pause.output.waited}}`.

A parked run survives a restart - the wait is durable queue state, not a timer
in memory.

> If a flow started by a form waits, the submission is resolved again on
> resume, from the small event. It is not carried in the parked state. See
> [Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration).

## Related

- [Actions](/extensions/flow/actions)
- [Data and expressions](/extensions/flow/concepts)

# Actions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/actions
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> The built-in actions, the code sandbox, HTTP and its network guard, and calling one flow from another.

# Actions

## The built-in set

| action | does | output |
|---|---|---|
| `http` | an outbound request | `response.status`, `response.body` |
| `content` | create, update or publish content | `updated.typeName`, `updated.objectId`, `result` |
| `query` | read content | `count`, `items` |
| `email` | send mail | `sent.to`, `sent.subject` |
| `label` | add or remove an operational label | `entityType`, `entityId` |
| `run_flow` | run another flow | the child flow's output |
| `log` | write a line into the run history | `message` |
| `code` | run JavaScript in a sandbox | whatever you return |

Extensions add more, and they behave the same way -
[Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions).

## HTTP, and the network guard

```text
method: POST
url:    https://api.example.com/hook
headers, body: JSON, with {{tokens}}
```

**Private and loopback addresses are refused.** A flow pointed at
`http://localhost:3990/api/health` fails with:

```text
http action refuses private/loopback targets (localhost)
```

That guard is on by default and exists so a flow cannot be turned into a probe
of your internal network. A workspace can lift it for local development:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows' }
// then, in the Admin: Settings, Extensions, Flows, "Allow private networks" - it
// takes effect only under the optional network:private grant
// (tangen extension upgrade flows --approve-optional network:private)
```

With it set, the same flow reaches the address and reports the real response.
Leave it off in production.

The guard is about *destination*, not authentication. It does not inspect
bodies or redact headers you supply.

## Code

`code` runs your JavaScript in a **QuickJS WebAssembly isolate**. It is not
server-side Node.

```js
return { doubled: input.steps.a.n * 2 }
```

- `input` holds `{ trigger, steps, item?, itemIndex? }`.
- Your return value becomes the step's output. A primitive or array is wrapped
  as `{ value: … }`; an object is used as-is; returning nothing gives `{}`.
- **You cannot return a promise.** The isolate is synchronous and has nothing
  to await; a promise is refused by name.

Measured limits and absences:

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | interrupted at ~1 second |
| output | refused over **64KB** |
| memory | bounded; an unbounded allocation is stopped |
| `process`, `Bun`, `require`, `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `setTimeout` | all `undefined` |
| `import(...)` | refused |

A real run confirms it: `typeof process` returns `"undefined"` inside a code
step. Use `code` for shaping and arithmetic. For anything that must reach the
world, use `http` or an extension action.

> This is an isolate, not a defence against a QuickJS or WebAssembly escape.
> What is guaranteed is that Flow passes no host object across the boundary and
> grants no host global.

## Subflows

`run_flow` runs another flow and returns its output:

```text
flowId: fl_…
```

The child's output is the step's output **directly**:

```text
{{steps.call.output.echoed}}
```

not nested under a second `output`. A parent that ran a child returning
`{ echoed: 'child ran' }` read exactly that.

**Depth is limited to 5.** Exceeding it fails the run with a message naming
recursion. A child containing a `wait` cannot be used as a subflow, and says so
rather than hanging.

## Content and query

`content` writes and `query` reads, both through the same content model your
site uses - a flow cannot see anything an API key could not. Content actions
default to the object that triggered the flow, so a flow on "any content type"
can label or update whatever fired it without naming the type in advance.

## Related

- [Runs, retries and failures](/extensions/flow/runs)
- [Security and retention](/extensions/flow/security)

---

# Runs, retries and failures

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/runs
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> What a run records, when Flow retries, how a failure is reported, and how to test a flow without doing anything.

# Runs, retries and failures

## What a run records

```json
{
  "status": "completed",
  "path": ["start", "gate", "createLead", "hot"],
  "ms": 6,
  "attempts": 1,
  "startedAt": "…",
  "runAs": "owner",
  "actor": { "kind": "member", "id": "mem_…" },
  "initiator": null,
  "correlationId": "…",
  "log": [
    { "step": "gate", "action": "condition", "ok": true, "ms": 0, "output": { "result": "yes" } },
    { "step": "createLead", "action": "crm_create_lead", "ok": true, "ms": 4,
      "output": { "lead": { "id": "nw_q96aczht", "tier": "enterprise" } }, "attempt": 1 }
  ]
}
```

`path` is the route taken, which answers "which branch ran" faster than reading
the log. `runAs`, `actor` and `initiator` say who the run was: the flow's
`runAs` mode, the member, key or identity whose authority it used, and the
member or key behind the triggering event when there was one. A run refused
because that authority was lost records `failure.code: "AUTHORITY_LOST"`. Each log entry carries its step id, the action, whether it succeeded,
its duration, its attempt number and its output.

Statuses you will see: `completed`, `error`, `waiting`, `waiting_retry`,
`skipped`, `cancelled`.

## Retries

**Nothing is retried unless you ask for it.** A node's default policy is
`maxAttempts: 1`, so a failed step fails - once. Flow cannot know whether the
action you wired up is safe to repeat, so it does not guess.

Declare a policy on the node to opt in:

```json
{ "retry": { "maxAttempts": 3, "backoff": "exponential", "baseDelaySeconds": 30 } }
```

| field | default | bounds |
|---|---|---|
| `maxAttempts` | `1` | 1 to **5** - a node needing six tries needs a different design |
| `backoff` | `exponential` | `exponential` or `fixed` |
| `baseDelaySeconds` | `30` | 1 to **3600** - further out than an hour is a schedule, not a retry |

An unusable declaration (`maxAttempts: 99`) is reported, not quietly clamped.

Only a failure **declared retryable** is retried. `unknown` is not treated as a
maybe: it is not retried. The log records one entry per attempt with its
`attempt` number, and each entry carries `failure.retryable` so you can see why
a step stopped where it did.

Between attempts the run parks as `waiting_retry`. That is **durable queue
state**, not an in-memory timer: a run waiting to retry survives a restart.

If a node has an **on error** outlet connected, the branch is taken once the
attempts are spent - not on the first failure - and it reads the message as
`{{steps.<id>.output.error}}`. A node with `maxAttempts: 3` and an on-error
branch records three failed entries and then the branch, and `path` shows the
node once per attempt:

```json
{ "status": "completed", "path": ["start", "call", "call", "call", "rescue"] }
```

The run's own status is `completed`, because the flow handled its failure.

A flow that keeps failing trips a circuit breaker and is disabled, with the
reason written into its history. The threshold is configurable:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: { failureThreshold: 10 } }
```

### Idempotency is yours to honour

A contributed action's handler receives an `idempotencyKey` and an `attempt`
number in its third argument. Flow does not deduplicate for you - it gives an
action that reaches an external system the identity it needs to deduplicate
itself. An action that ignores the key will act twice if it is retried.

## Failures

Failure messages are bounded and redacted - bearer and token-shaped strings are
stripped before a message reaches history. A failure carries a stable code and
whether it was retryable, so a run that stopped tells you whether trying again
would have helped.

An unhandled crash closes its run rather than leaving it open, and a crashed
run is never silently re-run.

## Cancelling a run

```text
POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/<flowId>/runs/<runId>/cancel
```

A parked run (`waiting`, `waiting_retry`) is cancelled immediately. A run that
is executing records the request and stops at its next boundary - in-flight work
is not interrupted mid-step. A finished run cannot be cancelled and says so.

> The `runId` in that path is the run's `executionId` **without its `exec_`
> prefix**. The runs listing returns `executionId: "exec_mtjmah4q5ktdjd"`; the
> route wants `mtjmah4q5ktdjd`. Tracked as FLOW-G5-1.

## Testing {#testing}

```text
POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/<flowId>/test
```

Runs the flow and returns the complete log **inline**, rather than queuing it.
Write-actions are simulated:

```json
{ "step": "call", "action": "http", "ok": true,
  "output": { "dryRun": true, "wouldDo": { "url": "https://example.invalid/hook", "method": "POST" },
              "response": { "status": 200, "body": {} } } }
```

No request was made. The `dryRun` and `wouldDo` fields are how you tell a
simulated step from a real one, and the run continues past it so you can see the
whole path.

The `response` is a **stub and always reports 200**, so a condition on
`{{steps.call.output.response.status}}` takes its success outlet in every test
run. A test proves the flow's shape and expressions; it does not exercise how
the flow behaves when the call fails. For that, point the node at a URL that
really fails and run it for real.

## Retention

Runs are pruned on a window, **30 days** by default:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: { runRetentionDays: 7 } }
```

Shorten it if your flows touch personal data - a step's own output is stored.
See [Security and retention](/extensions/flow/security).

## Related

- [Actions](/extensions/flow/actions)
- [Security and retention](/extensions/flow/security)

# Forms and Flow

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/forms-integration
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> Branching a flow on what somebody submitted, and what the platform deliberately does not put on the event bus.

# Forms and Flow

A form submission can start a flow, and that flow can branch on what was
submitted.

## The trigger

Choose **Form submitted** and name the form. The trigger resolves the
submission and puts it on the scope:

```ts
trigger.submission = {
  id: 'sub_1',
  formId: 'frm_1',
  formSlug: 'request-a-demo',
  values: { company: 'Meridian Group', companySize: '500+', businessEmail: '…' },
  createdAt: '2026-09-02T00:00:00.000Z',
}
```
Every submitted field is under `values`, keyed by the field's `name`.

**Only declared fields arrive.** The submit route is public, so the pipeline
drops any key that is not one of the form's fields before it stores, notifies
or emits. A flow condition on something the form does not declare will never
match - add it as a `hidden` field on the form if the site needs to carry it
through.

## Branching on a value

A condition reads the same dot-path any other Flow expression uses:

```text
trigger.submission.values.companySize   eq   500+
```
and an action interpolates it:

```text
ENTERPRISE lead from {{trigger.submission.values.company}}
```
A worked run, from a public submission with no credential:

```text
submit { company: "Meridian Group", companySize: "500+" }
  → gate      condition   → yes
  → lead      crm_create_lead   { leadId: "nw_iuctpr90" }
  → hot       log   "ENTERPRISE Meridian Group lead nw_iuctpr90"

submit { company: "TinyCo", companySize: "1-50" }
  → gate      condition   → no
  → cold      log   "standard TinyCo size 1-50"
```
## What the event carries, and what it does not

The `form.submitted` event is **identifiers only**:

```ts
{ formId, formSlug, submissionId }
```
Submitted values are not on it, and that is deliberate. Every subscriber to the
event bus - webhooks included - would otherwise receive the contents of every
form on your site.

Flow resolves the values itself, **after** it has matched a flow to the event.
An unrelated event costs nothing, and a workspace with no form flows never reads
a submission at all.

## When there is nothing to resolve

A deleted submission, or a lookup that fails, leaves `trigger.submission`
undefined and the flow runs anyway. Conditions reading a missing path evaluate
against an empty value rather than throwing, so a flow degrades instead of
erroring. If a branch matters, test the field you depend on.

## Related

- [Flow security and retention](/extensions/flow/security) - **read this before
  logging a submitted value**
- [Forms](/extensions/forms)
- [Reading a submission](/reference/sdk#forms) - resolving one yourself

---

# Flow security and retention

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/flow/security
Section: Extensions / Flow
Verification: executable

> Where submitted values can end up, what the sandbox does and does not guarantee, and how long a run is kept.

# Flow security and retention

> **Warning**
>
> A flow step's own output is written to run history. If a step logs or
> interpolates a submitted value, that value is stored for the retention period.
> Nothing redacts it for you.

## Where submitted values travel

| place | carries values | why |
|---|---|---|
| the `form.submitted` event | **no** | identifiers only, so no other subscriber sees form contents |
| the durable task queue | **no** | a run parked at a Wait re-resolves on resume from the small event |
| the run record's trigger | **no** | a run stores status, log and path |
| **a step's own output** | **yes, if you put it there** | this is the one to think about |

So this is safe:

```text
condition   trigger.submission.values.companySize eq 500+
```
and this stores an email address for as long as the run is kept:

```text
log   "New lead: {{trigger.submission.values.businessEmail}}"
```
Branch on sensitive fields freely. Think before you interpolate one into an
output.

## Retention

Runs are pruned on the extension's retention window, **30 days** by default:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: { runRetentionDays: 7 } }
```
Shorten it if your flows touch personal data.

## What the code step guarantees

The `code` action runs in a QuickJS WebAssembly isolate with no host bindings.
Measured, not asserted:

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `process`, `Bun`, `require`, `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `setTimeout` | all `undefined` |
| `globalThis` own properties | the ECMAScript intrinsics, plus `input` |
| `import("node:fs")` | refused |
| `while (true) {}` | interrupted at ~1s |
| unbounded allocation | stopped, out of memory |
| output over 64KB | refused |

**What is not claimed:** this is an isolate, not a defence against a QuickJS or
WebAssembly escape. What is guaranteed is that the platform passes no host
object across the boundary and grants no host global. Treat a code step as
untrusted-input-safe, not as a security boundary against a hostile author.

## Outbound requests

The `http` action refuses private and loopback addresses. A workspace can opt
out for local development:

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows' }
// then, in the Admin: Settings, Extensions, Flows, "Allow private networks" - it
// takes effect only under the optional network:private grant
// (tangen extension upgrade flows --approve-optional network:private)
```
Leave it off in production. It exists so a developer can reach a local
receiver, not so a flow can reach your internal network.

## The four places, named

The distinction that matters, in order of durability:

| | carries submitted values | lives |
|---|---|---|
| the `form.submitted` event | no | in memory, for the moment it is dispatched |
| trigger hydration | yes | in the run's scope, for the run |
| a step's own output | **only what you put there** | run history |
| run history | whatever the outputs held | `runRetentionDays`, default 30 |

Hydration is not the event; a step's output is not hydration; history is not
either. A flow can read a submitted email in a condition and store nothing.

## Related

- [Forms and Flow](/extensions/flow/forms-integration)
- [Runs, retries and failures](/extensions/flow/runs)
- [Extension options](/extend/configuration)

# SEO

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extensions/seo
Section: Extensions / SEO
Verification: executable

> Sitemaps, canonical URLs, OpenGraph metadata and a robots policy per deployment role: what Tangen holds for SEO, what your application owns, and how the bundled SEO extension is installed and configured.

# SEO

> SEO is an extension. Before the steps below work it must be **declared,
> installed and enabled** on the deployment you are working on - three separate
> actions. See [Extensions](/extensions).


> **Availability.** Tangen's SEO capability ships as a first-party extension
> that is **not currently published as an npm package**, so an external project
> has no supported way to install it. This page documents the model and the
> boundary; it does not tell you to install something you cannot. See
> [what is not installable](#what-is-not-available-yet).

## The division

**Tangen owns SEO data and artifacts. Your application owns routing.**

| Tangen | your application |
|---|---|
| the metadata an editor writes per object | which URL that object lives at |
| defaults, and how a page inherits them | emitting `<title>`, `<meta>`, `<link rel="canonical">` |
| the sitemap's contents | serving `/sitemap.xml` |
| robots policy per deployment role | serving `/robots.txt` |
| the redirect table | performing the redirect |

Tangen never learns your routes. It asks **you** for them, once, through a URL
resolver you supply - and if your resolver returns nothing for an object, that
object is **omitted** from the sitemap and left without a canonical, rather
than given a guessed address.

## What you can do today without the extension

Everything here is core, works in any project, and is what most sites need:

**Model your own SEO fields.**

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
seo: field.group({
  label: 'SEO',
  fields: {
    metaTitle: field.text({ label: 'Meta title', localized: true }),
    metaDescription: field.textarea({ label: 'Meta description', localized: true }),
    socialImage: field.media({ label: 'Social image' }),
    noindex: field.boolean({ label: 'Hide from search engines' }),
  },
}),
```
**Hold defaults in a global.**

```ts app/globals/index.ts
{
  name: 'seo_defaults',
  label: 'SEO defaults',
  fields: {
    titleTemplate: field.text({ label: 'Title template', localized: true }),
    description: field.textarea({ label: 'Default description', localized: true }),
    socialImage: field.media({ label: 'Default social image' }),
  },
}
```
**Emit the tags yourself**, falling back to the defaults:

```ts
const [page, defaults] = await Promise.all([
  tangen.objects('page').findBySlug(slug),
  tangen.globals('seo_defaults').get(),
])

const title = page?.seo?.metaTitle ?? page?.title
const description = page?.seo?.metaDescription ?? defaults.description
```
**Build a sitemap** from a query:

```ts
const { data } = await tangen.objects('page')
  .props(['slug', 'updatedAt'])
  .total(false)
  .limit(1000)
  .get()
// map to your own URLs, and serve as XML from your framework
```
**Model redirects as content** if you need editor-managed ones: a small type
with `from`, `to` and `permanent`, read by your middleware.

This is more work than the extension, and it is entirely supported.

## The SEO extension

SEO ships with the platform. A scaffolded project already declares it in
`app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-seo' },
])
```
You never install it yourself. There is no `add` command for it, and there is
not meant to be one - it arrives with the platform or not at all.

Declaring it makes it available. Turning it on is per deployment and lives in
its database, like every other extension:

```sh
tangen extension install seo
tangen extension list
```
Once enabled it adds resolved metadata, canonical URLs, a robots policy that
differs by deployment role, a generated sitemap and sitemap index, a redirect
manager in the Admin, and structured data - all driven by the one `resolveUrl`
function you supply. Its public routes mount under `/api/v1/ext/seo/`,
including `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`.

## Supplying `resolveUrl`

It goes in the extension's **options**, in `app/config/extensions.ts`. That is
also where every other SEO helper lives:

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
export default defineExtensions([
  {
    resolve: '@tangen/ext-seo',
    options: {
      siteUrl: 'https://example.com',
      locales: ['en', 'fr', 'de'],
      sitemapTypes: ['product', 'article'],
      resolveUrl: ({ type, slug, locale }) => {
        if (!slug) return null
        const prefix = locale && locale !== 'en' ? `/${locale}` : ''
        const path = { product: `/products/${slug}`, article: `/blog/${slug}` }[type]
        return path ? `https://example.com${prefix}${path}` : null
      },
      robotsTxt: {
        groups: [{ userAgents: ['*'], allow: ['/'] }],
        sitemaps: ['https://example.com/sitemap.xml'],
      },
    },
  },
])
```

| option | is |
|---|---|
| `siteUrl` | the site's origin |
| `resolveUrl` | how this application builds a URL for one object |
| `resolveMediaUrl` | how it builds an absolute media URL |
| `locales` | locales offered as sitemap alternates |
| `sitemapTypes` | content types eligible for the sitemap; absent means all |
| `fallback` | last-resort title and description |
| `structuredData` | site-wide JSON-LD |
| `robotsTxt` | the policy on a **production** deployment |
| `nonProductionRobotsTxt` | everywhere else; absent means disallow everything |

`robotsTxt` groups take **`userAgents`, a list**. A group written with the
singular `userAgent` is dropped without an error, and you ship a robots.txt with
no rules in it.

### What `resolveUrl` receives

`{ workspaceId, type, id, slug, locale }` - **not the object's fields**.
A content type routed by anything other than its slug cannot be resolved here,
so either derive that type's route from its slug or leave it out of
`sitemapTypes` and serve it from your own sitemap route.
## Common mistakes

- **Storing a canonical URL on the object.** It goes stale the moment a slug
  changes. Derive it from the route.
- **Expecting Tangen to serve `/sitemap.xml`.** Your framework serves it;
  Tangen supplies the contents.
- **Letting staging get indexed.** Your robots policy must differ by
  deployment role, whichever way you produce it.

## Related

- [Globals](/build/globals) · [Frontend integration](/build/frontend) ·
  [Links and navigation](/build/content-modeling/links) ·
  [Public contract](/reference/public-contract)
