# What is an extension?

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/introduction/what-is-an-extension
Section: Extend Tangen / Getting started
Verification: source

> What an extension can contribute, when to build one, and what is not an extension.

# What is an extension?

An extension is a **package** that declares what it contributes to Tangen and
is installed per workspace on each deployment. It can add content types, tables,
server routes, Admin pages, panels, field types, jobs, hooks and permissions.

The manifest **declares**; the platform decides when any of it runs.

## When to build one

| build an extension | put it in your application |
|---|---|
| the behaviour belongs with the **content**, and editors need it in the Admin | the behaviour belongs to your **site** |
| you want it in more than one workspace or project | it is used once |
| it needs server-side lifecycle - hooks on publish, queued jobs, its own tables | a request-time concern your frontend handles |
| an operator should be able to switch it off | it is not optional |

A review workflow that gates publishing is an extension. A pricing calculator on
your marketing site is application code.

## What is not an extension

**Not every optional Tangen feature is one.** Several things you configure and
switch off are **platform capabilities** with no package to install:

| capability | not an extension |
|---|---|
| **Forms** | configured in `app/config/forms.ts` and code-first definitions. There is nothing to install |
| **Search** | part of the platform; nothing to enable or install |
| **Media**, **Mail**, **Realtime**, **Scheduler**, **Webhooks** | core capabilities |
| **AI**, **MCP**, **Knowledge** | optional capabilities, credential- and package-gated |
| **Telemetry** | a Core capability with no persistence. There is no `ext:telemetry` |

If a page or a colleague calls one of these "the X extension", that wording is
out of date. The list of registered capabilities is in
[Reference → Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest#dependencies).

## Three states, not two

An extension is `on`, `off` or `unavailable`, per workspace on each
deployment. "Installed" is not the same as "running":

| | means |
|---|---|
| **installed** | it exists on this deployment, and its migrations have run |
| **enabled** | an operator switched it on here |
| **active / on** | installed, enabled, code loaded in this process, and everything it requires is available |
| **unavailable** | it cannot run here - a required capability is missing, a dependency is not active, migrations are pending, or this process has not loaded its code |

Design for all of them. See
[Capabilities and dependencies](/extend/contract/capabilities).

## What an extension may not assume

- **That it is running.** An operator can disable it, and a missing dependency
  can make it unavailable.
- **That it may touch the database freely.** No runtime DDL. Tables come from
  declared migrations, at install and upgrade.
- **That it can reach platform internals.** Extensions import from
  `@tangen/cms` and nothing else. See
  [Public contract](/reference/public-contract).
- **That configuration is present.** An operator may not have filled it in.
- **That it owns the request.** Its routes are gated by the same permissions
  everything else is.

## Related

- [Your first extension](/extend/introduction/first-extension) ·
  [Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest) ·
  [Extension lifecycle](/reference/extension-lifecycle)

---

# Your first extension

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/introduction/first-extension
Section: Extend Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> The smallest extension that installs, runs and can be verified.

# Your first extension

The smallest useful extension: one server route, one Admin page, no database of
its own.

## Scaffold

```bash
bun run tangen extension create
```

It writes the manifest, the entries and a `package.json`, and appends the
extension to `app/config/extensions.ts`.

## The manifest

```ts extensions/hello/tangen.extension.ts
import type { TangenExtensionManifest } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  id: 'acme.hello',
  name: 'Hello',
  version: '0.1.0',
  description: 'A minimal Tangen extension.',

  config: {
    greeting: { type: 'string', label: 'Greeting', default: 'Hello' },
  },

  server: './src/server.ts',

  pages: [
    {
      path: '',
      component: 'HelloPage',
      nav: { label: 'Hello', icon: 'IconPuzzle', section: 'extensions' },
    },
  ],
} satisfies TangenExtensionManifest
```

`pages[].component` is the **name of a named export** of the browser entry, not
a function. The manifest holds no functions.

## The server entry

```ts extensions/hello/src/server.ts
import type { TangenExtensionServer } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  adminRoutes: [
    {
      method: 'GET',
      path: 'greeting',
      auth: 'member',
      handler: async (req, ctx) => {
        const greeting = (ctx.options?.greeting as string) ?? 'Hello'
        return { greeting, role: ctx.deploymentRole?.() ?? null }
      },
    },
  ],
} satisfies TangenExtensionServer
```

That mounts at `GET /api/v1/admin/ext/acme.hello/greeting` and answers to
member sessions only.

## The browser entry

```tsx extensions/hello/src/index.ts
export { HelloPage } from './pages/HelloPage'
```

```tsx extensions/hello/src/pages/HelloPage.tsx
import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom'

export function HelloPage() {
  const { workspaceId, env } = useParams<{ workspaceId: string; env: string }>()
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello</h1>
      <p>Workspace {workspaceId}.</p>
    </div>
  )
}
```

A page gets **no injected props**. Read the workspace from the route with
`useParams()`, because it is the identity everything else is scoped by.

## Declare, install, enable

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '../../extensions/hello', options: { greeting: 'Hi' } },
])
```

```bash
bun run tangen extension install acme.hello
bun run tangen extension enable  acme.hello
bun run tangen extension list
```

Declaring makes it available. Installing and enabling are separate acts, per
deployment, and they are an operator's to make.

## Verify

The page appears in the Admin sidebar under Extensions, at
`/:workspaceId/:env/extensions/acme.hello`. The route answers:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <member session>" \
  https://localhost:3000/api/v1/admin/ext/acme.hello/greeting
```

Disable it and both disappear:

```bash
bun run tangen extension disable acme.hello
```

That is the property worth checking first: a disabled extension contributes
**nothing** - no nav item, no page, no route.

## What to add next

- [Migrations](/extend/data/migrations) if it needs tables
- [Secrets](/extend/data/secrets) if it calls an external service
- [Capabilities](/extend/contract/capabilities) if it depends on media, search
  or another extension

## Related

- [Extension structure](/extend/introduction/structure) ·
  [Admin contributions](/extend/contributions/admin) ·
  [Server routes](/extend/contributions/routes) ·
  [Local development](/extend/shipping/local-development)

---

# Extension structure

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/introduction/structure
Section: Extend Tangen / Getting started
Verification: executable

> The files an extension has, which are required, and what each one is for.

# Extension structure

```text
my-extension/
├── package.json
├── tangen.extension.ts      # required - the manifest, default export
└── src/
    ├── index.ts             # optional - the BROWSER entry: Admin components
    ├── server.ts            # optional - the SERVER entry: routes, hooks, tasks
    └── migrations.ts        # optional - ledgered SQL migrations
```

**Only the manifest is required.** An extension that declares a content type and
nothing else needs one file.

## `tangen.extension.ts`

The manifest, as the default export. It is **data**, not behaviour: ids,
versions, dependencies, and the *names* of things it contributes. It never
holds a function that renders UI.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
import type { TangenExtensionManifest } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  id: 'acme.reviews',
  name: 'Reviews',
  version: '1.0.0',
  server: './src/server.ts',
} satisfies TangenExtensionManifest
```

## `src/server.ts`

Server behaviour: routes, event subscriptions, queued tasks, content hooks,
custom field type servers, install and uninstall callbacks. Named in the
manifest's `server` field.

It runs on the server only. It must not import anything browser-facing, and
**nothing in it may run at import time**.

## `src/index.ts` — the browser entry

Admin components, as **named exports**. The manifest refers to them by name;
the Admin build resolves those names statically at build time.

```ts src/index.ts
export { ReviewPanel } from './components/ReviewPanel'
export { ReviewsPage } from './pages/ReviewsPage'
```

This entry must be **browser-safe**: no `node:` imports, no database, no
secrets. It ends up in the Admin bundle.

## `src/migrations.ts`

An ordered array of `{ id, sql }`. SQL only, so the checksum is the truth of
what ran.

## `package.json`

```jsonc
{
  "name": "@acme/tangen-reviews",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "./src/index.ts",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./src/index.ts",
    "./server": "./src/server.ts"
  },
  "peerDependencies": { "@tangen/cms": "*" }
}
```

`@tangen/cms` is a **peer** dependency: the host project supplies it, and two
copies would mean two registries.

## The two-entry rule

Keeping the browser and server entries apart is not style. The browser entry is
bundled into the Admin and shipped to every editor's laptop; the server entry
holds your secrets and your database access. A single entry means one of those
two things is in the wrong place.

## Declaring it in a project

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@acme/tangen-reviews', options: { moderation: true } },
  { resolve: '../../extensions/my-local-extension' },
])
```

`resolve` is an npm package name or a path in the project. Declaring makes it
**available**; installing and enabling are separate, per-deployment acts.

## Related

- [Your first extension](/extend/introduction/first-extension) ·
  [Writing a manifest](/extend/contract/manifest) ·
  [Extension manifest reference](/reference/extension-manifest)

# The contract

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contract
Section: Extend Tangen / The contract
Verification: source

> Manifest, lifecycle, capabilities and versioning.

# The contract

Manifest, lifecycle, capabilities and versioning.

See [Extend Tangen](/extend) for the full map.

---

# Writing a manifest

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contract/manifest
Section: Extend Tangen / The contract
Verification: executable

> Authoring a manifest that installs, with the decisions that matter.

# Writing a manifest

Every field, with its type, is in
[Reference → Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest). This page is
about the choices.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
import type { TangenExtensionManifest } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  id: 'acme.reviews',
  name: 'Reviews',
  version: '1.0.0',
  description: 'Customer reviews on any content type.',
  author: 'Acme Inc',
  homepage: 'https://acme.example/reviews',
  license: 'MIT',

  requires: { capabilities: ['media'] },

  config: {
    moderation: { type: 'boolean', label: 'Hold reviews for moderation', default: true },
    webhookUrl: { type: 'string', label: 'Notify URL' },
  },
  secrets: ['ACME_REVIEWS_KEY'],
  // deploymentRoles: ['development', 'staging'],   // omit: every deployment
  migrations: './src/migrations.ts',

  capabilities: [
    { id: 'reviews:read', label: 'View reviews' },
    { id: 'reviews:moderate', label: 'Moderate reviews', implies: ['reviews:read'] },
  ],

  server: './src/server.ts',
  pages: [{ path: '', component: 'ReviewsPage', nav: { label: 'Reviews', icon: 'IconStar' } }],
  sidebarPanels: [{ id: 'reviews', label: 'Reviews', component: 'ReviewPanel', types: ['product'] }],
} satisfies TangenExtensionManifest
```

## Choose the id once

`id` is `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*` and it is **forever**. It is the install
identity, the route prefix (`/api/v1/ext/<id>/`), the page path
(`/extensions/<id>`), the capability id (`ext:<id>`), and the key in an
operator's install state.

**Namespace it**: `acme.reviews`, not `reviews`. A bare noun will collide.

Changing it later is not a rename - it is a different extension, and the old
one's data stays behind.

## Version means something

`version` drives UPGRADE. Bump it when you ship, because that is what makes new
migrations run.

## Say who wrote it

`author`, `homepage` and `license` are what an operator reads on
**Settings > Extensions** before trusting your extension: the table shows the
author with the website as a link, and the sheet shows the licence beside
them. All three are optional and none is guessed at - an undeclared one reads
"Not declared".

`homepage` is rendered as a link, so it must be an `http(s)` URL; anything
else fails manifest validation rather than reaching a browser.

That screen also compares the version a workspace RUNS with the one your
package ships (an upgrade the operator runs) and, on request, with your
package's `dist-tags.latest` at the registry (an update they install). Both
read the version from this manifest, so keep it in step with your
`package.json`.

## Declare capabilities the roles editor can see

`capabilities` are **RBAC capabilities your extension defines** - not runtime
capabilities you require. They appear in the roles editor for workspaces where
you are installed, and your routes and pages gate on them.

Ids are namespaced `scope:name`. `implies` saves an operator ticking two boxes:

```ts
{ id: 'reviews:moderate', label: 'Moderate reviews', implies: ['reviews:read'] }
```

## Components are names, not functions

`pages[].component` and `sidebarPanels[].component` are the **names of named
exports** of your browser entry. The Admin build resolves them statically.

The manifest is data. It is read by the CLI, the server and the Admin build, and
a function value in it cannot survive any of those.

## Panels: scope them

```ts
sidebarPanels: [{ id: 'reviews', label: 'Reviews', component: 'ReviewPanel', types: ['product'] }]
```

Omitting `types` shows the panel on **every** content type. Editors of every
type will see it, including the ones it makes no sense for. List the types.

## Content types and tables

| you want | declare |
|---|---|
| content editors manage in the Admin | `contentTypes` |
| tables `tangen push` plans and creates | `customTables` |
| tables you evolve yourself with SQL | `migrations` |

Do not reach for `migrations` when `customTables` fits - a declared table is
planned, reported and drift-checked.

## Validate it

```bash
bun run tangen extension install acme.reviews
```

An invalid manifest fails here, naming the field. Required config with no value
fails at install too, which is where you want it.

## Related

- [Extension manifest reference](/reference/extension-manifest) ·
  [Capabilities and dependencies](/extend/contract/capabilities) ·
  [Admin contributions](/extend/contributions/admin) ·
  [Configuration](/extend/data/configuration)

# The lifecycle in practice

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contract/lifecycle
Section: Extend Tangen / The contract
Verification: executable

> Declare, package, publish, install, enable, upgrade, disable, uninstall: what an extension author must do, and must not do, at each of the eleven stages.

# The lifecycle in practice

```text
REGISTER → INSTALL → ENABLE → MOUNT → START → STOP → DISABLE → UPGRADE → UNINSTALL → PURGE → DISPOSE
```

The stage list and its scopes are in
[Reference → Extension lifecycle](/reference/extension-lifecycle). This page is
about what you write.

## Nothing runs at import

The rule that catches people first. Importing your manifest, your server entry,
registering, installing, or running `onInstall` must not:

- open a database connection or a socket
- start a timer, worker or subscriber
- call an external service
- read a secret

```ts
// wrong - runs the moment the module is imported
const client = new SomeClient(process.env.ACME_KEY)

export default {
  adminRoutes: [{ method: 'GET', path: 'x', handler: async () => client.get() }],
}
```

```ts
// right - created when a request needs it
let client: SomeClient | undefined
const getClient = () => (client ??= new SomeClient(process.env.ACME_KEY))

export default {
  adminRoutes: [{ method: 'GET', path: 'x', handler: async (req, ctx) => getClient().get() }],
}
```

A secret's **value** comes from `process.env`, read at the point of use. The
manifest's `secrets: []` declares the variable **names** you read, not their
values, and there is no `ctx.secrets`. See [Secrets](/extend/data/secrets).

Background work belongs to START, which only happens when the extension is
actually available and wanted here.

## The six callbacks

Your server entry may export six lifecycle callbacks, and each maps to exactly
one stage.

| callback | stage | scope | for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `onInstall(ctx)` | INSTALL | workspace | non-schema setup. Runs **after** migrations, with **no database handle** |
| `onStart(ctx)` | START | workspace | timers, subscribers, consumers, connections |
| `onStop(ctx)` | STOP | per started scope | cease new work. **Idempotent by contract** |
| `onUpgrade(ctx, info)` | UPGRADE | workspace | non-schema upgrade work. Runs after migrations, before the new version is recorded |
| `onUninstall(ctx)` | UNINSTALL | workspace | advisory cleanup. **Your data is not deleted** |
| `onDispose()` | DISPOSE | once per process | release what `onStart` shared across scopes |

```ts src/server.ts
export default {
  onStart: (ctx) => {
    const timer = setInterval(() => sweep(ctx), 60_000)
    return () => clearInterval(timer)          // the cleanup runs at STOP
  },
  onUpgrade: async (ctx, info) => {
    // info: { from: string | null, to: string }
    if (info.from === null) return              // first install; nothing to migrate
    await migrateStoredOptions(ctx)
  },
  onDispose: () => { /* release process-wide handles */ },
} satisfies TangenExtensionServer
```

**`onStart` is where background work belongs** - never at import, and never in
`onInstall`. It is called once per workspace where the extension
is active, and again when a scope becomes active while the process runs.

Return a cleanup function and it runs at STOP; that is usually simpler than
writing `onStop`. **A throw in `onStart` marks that scope's runtime as failed
and starts nothing else of the extension there** - so make it defensive.

`onUpgrade` is not a schema escape hatch: DDL belongs in `migrations`. A throw
leaves the old version on the row, and the next upgrade retries the hook alone.

**There is no `onEnable` and no `onDisable`.** Enabling and disabling are
operator state; your code is not called. You do not need them - a disabled
extension contributes nothing, so its routes 404 and its pages are gone.

## What uninstall takes with it

Uninstall retires your row and stops your runtime; the platform then
revokes the connections made through your connectors (their material is
cleared), cancels your queued jobs, and announces `extension.uninstalled`
with the Flow action and trigger names you contributed, so flows built on
them are paused with a reason instead of failing later. Your stored data
stays until the operator purges.

## Disable is not uninstall

| | happens | your data |
|---|---|---|
| **DISABLE** | an operator switches it off on one deployment | untouched |
| **UNINSTALL** | it is removed from that deployment | **retained** - tables, rows, ledger and content types all survive, and a reinstall adopts them |
| **PURGE** | the separate, approved deletion | gone |

Write your extension so a reinstall is a resumption, not a fresh start. Rows
you left behind will still be there, and they will still have your `workspace_id`
on them.

## Operator state wins

Re-declaring the extension in `app/config/extensions.ts` does **not** re-enable
one an operator disabled, and does not reinstall one they uninstalled.
Declaring makes it available; the rest is their decision, per deployment.

Do not write code, docs or a setup script that assumes deploying re-enables
anything.

## Upgrade

Bumping `version` and deploying makes the new code available. **`UPGRADE`
runs new migrations** - the ones whose ids the ledger has not seen. Migrations
that already ran are never re-run, and must never be edited.

Write upgrades so an old row still makes sense: add columns with defaults,
tolerate an absent value, and do not assume every row was written by the
current version.

## Deployment awareness

Every stage except REGISTER and DISPOSE is per **workspace**, in the
database of the deployment the command runs on. An extension installed on
the development deployment is not installed on production until someone
installs it there.

Read `ctx.deploymentRole?.()` when the decision depends on production-ness:

```ts
const role = ctx.deploymentRole?.() ?? 'production'
if (role !== 'production') {
  // safe to do the noisy thing
}
```

A runtime that does not wire the seam answers `undefined`; treat that as
production and choose the cautious branch.

## Verify the lifecycle

```bash
bun run tangen extension install   acme.reviews
bun run tangen extension disable   acme.reviews   # contributes nothing
bun run tangen extension enable    acme.reviews
bun run tangen extension uninstall acme.reviews   # data retained
bun run tangen extension install   acme.reviews   # adopts it back
bun run tangen doctor                             # what was retained
```

## Related

- [Extension lifecycle reference](/reference/extension-lifecycle) ·
  [Migrations](/extend/data/migrations) ·
  [Capabilities and dependencies](/extend/contract/capabilities) ·
  [Testing an extension](/extend/shipping/testing)

# Capabilities and dependencies

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contract/capabilities
Section: Extend Tangen / The contract
Verification: source

> Declaring what you need, and designing for on, off and unavailable.

# Capabilities and dependencies

Your extension runs in deployments you did not configure. Declare what you need,
and degrade honestly when it is not there.

## Declaring

```ts tangen.extension.ts
requires: {
  capabilities: ['media', 'search'],
  extensions: [{ id: 'acme.core', version: '^1' }],
},
optional: {
  extensions: ['acme.analytics'],
},
```

| | means |
|---|---|
| `requires.capabilities` | runtime capabilities that must be **available** in the process. One missing makes your extension `unavailable` with a safe reason, and it **never starts** |
| `requires.extensions` | extensions that must be installed **and enabled in the same workspace** |
| `optional.extensions` | used when present; your extension works without them |

Capability ids you may require include `media`, `search`, `mail`, `knowledge`,
`redis`, `realtime`, `scheduler` and `webhooks`. The full registered list is in
[Reference → Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest#dependencies).

Declare only what you genuinely need. A `requires.capabilities: ['redis']` you
added defensively makes your extension unavailable in every Redis-less
deployment.

## The three states

| state | means | who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| `on` | installed, enabled, code loaded, everything it requires available | - |
| `off` | not installed here, or switched off | an operator |
| `unavailable` | it cannot run here | an operator, by fixing the condition |

**Never write "if installed, it is running".** Installed is one of four
conditions that must all hold.

## Optional dependencies

Check at runtime, and mean it:

```ts
const handler = async (req, ctx) => {
  if (await ctx.hasExtension?.('acme.analytics')) {
    // the richer path
  }
  // the path that always works
}
```

`hasExtension` answers for **this workspace**. Absent on a
runtime that does not wire it - so `?.` and a sensible default, not an
assumption.

## Degrading honestly

Three bad patterns, and what to do instead:

**Silently doing nothing.** A feature that quietly stops is a support ticket.
Say what is missing.

**Crashing.** A missing optional dependency is not an exception.

**Pretending it worked.** Returning an empty list where you meant "search is
off here" is the worst of the three, because nobody investigates it.

```ts
if (!(await ctx.hasExtension?.('acme.analytics'))) {
  return { available: false, reason: 'Analytics is not enabled in this workspace.' }
}
```

Give the caller a reason an operator could act on, and never a stack trace or a
credential.

## Capability is not permission

A capability is about the **deployment**; a permission is about the **caller**.

- `search` `off` - nobody can search here, whatever their role.
- `search` `unavailable` - it cannot run here at all; an operator fixes it.
- no `search: read` action - **this caller** cannot search, while others can.

They are three different answers and they need three different messages. A page
that says "you do not have permission" because a capability is off tells a user
something false about their own account.

## Your extension is a capability too

Yours appears in the platform's capability list as `ext:<id>` - so
`acme.reviews` is `ext:acme.reviews`. That is how the Admin knows whether to
render your pages, and it is why a disabled extension's UI disappears rather
than erroring.

You do not register that yourself and you do not read the registry directly.
Declare in the manifest, and the platform does the rest.

## Typed services are not capabilities

A **capability** is a platform feature this deployment has or lacks. A
**service** is an implementation another extension offers you, with a type:
`requires: { services: ['seo.service@^1'] }` and `ctx.services.get<SeoService>('seo.service@^1')`.
The rules are the same shape - required blocks you, optional degrades - but
the provider is an extension, the version is a range, and the answer is a
typed object rather than a yes or no. See
[Cross-extension](/extend/cross-extension#typed-services).

## Related

- [The lifecycle in practice](/extend/contract/lifecycle) ·
  [Extension manifest reference](/reference/extension-manifest) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions) ·
  [Permissions and security](/extend/contributions/permissions)

---

# Versioning and compatibility

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contract/versioning
Section: Extend Tangen / The contract
Verification: source

> Versioning an extension, upgrading it, and staying compatible with Tangen.

# Versioning and compatibility

## Your version

`version` in the manifest is yours. Bump it when you ship: it is what makes
UPGRADE run your new migrations.

Semver is the sensible convention, and what a **breaking** change means for an
extension is concrete:

| change | version |
|---|---|
| a new optional config key, a new page, a new route | minor |
| a migration that adds a column with a default | minor |
| a config key becoming required | **major** - installs will start failing |
| a route or page path changing | **major** - callers and bookmarks break |
| a declared capability id changing | **major** - operators' role assignments break |
| removing a content type or column | **major**, and it needs a purge story |

## Depending on another extension

```ts
requires: { extensions: [{ id: 'acme.core', version: '^1' }] }
```

Ranges accepted: `1.2.3`, `^1.2`, `~1.2.3`, `>=1.2.0`, `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0`, `*`.
A bare `'acme.core'` means any version.

If the installed version does not satisfy your range, your extension is
`unavailable` here with a reason naming the dependency. That is the correct
outcome - it never half-runs.

## Depending on Tangen

`@tangen/cms` is a **peer dependency**:

```jsonc
{ "peerDependencies": { "@tangen/cms": "^0.1" } }
```

The host project supplies it. Two copies would mean two registries and two sets
of types.

Pin a range, not `latest`. And read
[Public contract](/reference/public-contract): a surface marked **experimental**
can change in a minor, so an extension that leans on one should say so in its
own README.

## Migrations and versions

A migration that has run is **immutable**. Its id is in the ledger with a
checksum, and editing it is a corruption, not an update.

To change something a past migration created, write a new migration. To fix one
that has not shipped anywhere, you may edit it - but "not shipped anywhere"
includes nobody's development environment.

## When Tangen changes

The lifecycle stages, the manifest shape and the contribution types are v1
contracts. When they change, it is a major Tangen version with a deprecation
path.

Your extension should:

- **use `?.` on optional context seams.** `ctx.deploymentRole?.()`,
  `ctx.hasExtension?.()` and their kind are absent on runtimes that do not wire
  them, and an absent seam is a supported state rather than an error.
- **not depend on undocumented behaviour.** If it is not in the reference, it is
  not a contract.

## Related

- [Migrations](/extend/data/migrations) ·
  [Packaging and distribution](/extend/shipping/distribution) ·
  [Public contract](/reference/public-contract)

# Configuration

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/data/configuration
Section: Extend Tangen / Configuration and data
Verification: executable

> Declaring options an operator sets, and reading them safely at runtime.

# Configuration

Declare your options in the manifest so the platform can validate them at
install and upgrade, show them in the Admin, and know which ones never to print.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
config: {
  moderation: { type: 'boolean', label: 'Hold reviews for moderation', default: true },
  webhookUrl: { type: 'string', label: 'Notify URL', description: 'Posted to on each new review' },
  maxPerPage: { type: 'number', label: 'Reviews per page', default: 20 },
  blockedWords: { type: 'string[]', label: 'Blocked words' },
  apiToken: { type: 'string', label: 'API token', secret: true },
},
```

| key | means |
|---|---|
| `type` | `'string' \| 'number' \| 'boolean' \| 'string[]' \| 'json'`. **Required** |
| `label`, `description` | what an operator sees |
| `required` | install and upgrade **fail** without a value |
| `default` | used when the value is absent |
| `secret` | the value is a credential: redacted in logs and diagnostics, never echoed back |

## Values come from the project

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@acme/tangen-reviews', options: { moderation: false, maxPerPage: 50 } },
])
```

Configuration is per workspace. An operator can also edit declared options in
the Admin.

## Read it defensively

```ts
const handler = async (req, ctx) => {
  const moderation = (ctx.options?.moderation as boolean) ?? true
  const perPage = Number(ctx.options?.maxPerPage ?? 20)
}
```

`ctx.options` is the options object from this workspace's entry. **Read it with
a fallback every time**, even for a key with a `default`: a project may declare
you with no options at all, and a defensive read is one `??`.

A tidy pattern:

```ts src/config.ts
export interface ReviewsConfig { moderation: boolean; webhookUrl?: string; maxPerPage: number }

export function readConfig(options: Record<string, unknown> | undefined): ReviewsConfig {
  return {
    moderation: options?.moderation !== false,
    webhookUrl: typeof options?.webhookUrl === 'string' ? options.webhookUrl : undefined,
    maxPerPage: Number.isFinite(Number(options?.maxPerPage)) ? Number(options!.maxPerPage) : 20,
  }
}
```

One place that coerces, one type the rest of your code trusts, and it is a pure
function you can test.

## `required` is a real gate

```ts
webhookUrl: { type: 'string', label: 'Notify URL', required: true },
```

Install and upgrade fail without it. That is the right place for it - an
operator finds out while installing, not at 3am when the first review arrives.

Use `required` only for something with no sensible default. Everything else gets
a `default` and degrades.

## Site config your extension defines

`ctx.workspaceConfig?.()` returns the workspace's loaded config, so an
extension can read a settings key the site declares for it. **Read it
defensively**: the shape is whatever the site authored, the seam is absent on
runtimes that load no workspace config, and it is read-only by contract.

## Configuration is not secrets

A `secret: true` config value is a **per-workspace credential an operator
types**. A deployment-wide credential is a
[secret](/extend/data/secrets) - a deployment variable you declare by name.

If a value would be the same for every workspace on the deployment, it is a
secret, not config.

## Testing

```ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'bun:test'
import { readConfig } from '../src/config'

describe('config', () => {
  it('applies defaults when a project declares no options', () => {
    expect(readConfig(undefined)).toEqual({ moderation: true, webhookUrl: undefined, maxPerPage: 20 })
  })
  it('coerces a bad number rather than propagating NaN', () => {
    expect(readConfig({ maxPerPage: 'lots' }).maxPerPage).toBe(20)
  })
})
```

## Related

- [Secrets](/extend/data/secrets) · [Writing a manifest](/extend/contract/manifest)
  · [Extension manifest reference](/reference/extension-manifest)

# Secrets

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/data/secrets
Section: Extend Tangen / Configuration and data
Verification: source

> API keys and other credentials an extension reads: declaring them by name, reading their values from the environment, and not leaking them.

# Secrets

A secret is a **deployment-wide credential** the deployment's secret
provider resolves (self-hosted: the process environment). You declare the
variable **names**; the values never touch your manifest, your repository,
your options or your logs.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
secrets: ['ACME_REVIEWS_KEY', 'ACME_REVIEWS_WEBHOOK_SECRET'],
```

That is a list of variable names, and nothing else. Declaring them registers
`ext.<id>.secret.<NAME>` as a secret reference: the platform resolves it at
boot, reports whether it resolved, requires it in production, and never reads
the value into anything it might print.

## Secret or config

| | use |
|---|---|
| the same value for every workspace on this deployment - an API key for a service you own | **`secrets`** - a deployment variable |
| a different value per workspace, typed by an operator in the Admin | **`config`** with `secret: true` |

Getting this wrong is the common mistake. A vendor API key that is yours is a
secret. A customer's own webhook token is secret config.

## Reading one

Ask `ctx.secrets` for the name you declared, at the point of use:

```ts src/server.ts
export default {
  adminRoutes: [
    {
      method: 'POST', path: 'sync', auth: 'member', capability: 'reviews:moderate',
      handler: async (req, ctx) => {
        const key = ctx.secrets?.get('ACME_REVIEWS_KEY')
        if (!key) {
          ctx.log('ACME_REVIEWS_KEY is not set; sync is unavailable')
          return { ok: false, reason: 'This deployment has no Acme credential configured.' }
        }
        return { ok: true, synced: await sync(key) }
      },
    },
  ],
} satisfies TangenExtensionServer
```

**At the point of use, not at import.** `ctx.secrets` is scoped to your
extension (its declared `secrets` and its `secret: true` config fields) and
answers from the deployment's provider each time. A module-scope
`const KEY = process.env.…` would read the process when the file is imported -
the import-time work the lifecycle forbids - and would bypass the one reader
the platform accounts for. Extension code does not read `process.env`.

## Under grants

If your manifest declares [`grants`](/reference/extension-manifest#grants),
`ctx.secrets` answers your own declared names as before, and a platform-wide
secret only when a `secrets:<name>` grant names it. Reading one you were not
granted throws rather than returning `undefined`, so a missing grant is a
visible error and never a silent empty value.

## Absent is a normal state

A deployment may not have your secret. That is not an exception - it is a
capability that is unavailable here.

- **Say what is missing**, by variable name, in a message an operator can act
  on.
- **Do not throw** on a missing secret at boot.
- **Do not fall back** to a default credential.

## Never leak one

- **Never log a value.** Log the variable's *name* and that it is absent.
- **Never return one** in a route response, an error, or a diagnostic.
- **Never put one in your browser entry.** It ships to every editor's browser.
- **Never put one in a manifest, a config file or a test fixture.**
- **Never echo it back** from a settings page. `secret: true` config is
  write-only from the Admin's side, and yours should be too.

An error from an external service can contain the credential you sent it. Do
not pass a provider's message through:

```ts
catch (e) {
  ctx.log('acme sync failed')        // not e.message
  return { ok: false, reason: 'The Acme service rejected the request.' }
}
```

## Rotation

Secrets are read from the environment at the point of use, so rotating one is a
deployment concern: change the variable, restart. Your extension needs no
rotation logic - which is another reason not to cache the value in a
module-scope constant.

## Testing

Test both states, and use an obvious fake:

```ts
describe('sync', () => {
  it('reports unavailable when the credential is absent', async () => {
    delete process.env.ACME_REVIEWS_KEY
    const res = await route.handler(req, ctx)
    expect(res.ok).toBe(false)
    expect(res.reason).not.toContain('undefined')
  })

  it('never returns the credential', async () => {
    process.env.ACME_REVIEWS_KEY = 'test-not-a-real-key'
    const res = await route.handler(req, ctx)
    expect(JSON.stringify(res)).not.toContain('test-not-a-real-key')
  })
})
```

The second test is the one worth writing. It fails the day someone adds a debug
field to a response.

## Related

- [Configuration](/extend/data/configuration) ·
  [Permissions and security](/extend/contributions/permissions) ·
  [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables)

# Migrations

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/data/migrations
Section: Extend Tangen / Configuration and data
Verification: executable

> Owning tables safely - when migrations run, and the rules that never bend.

# Migrations

An extension may own tables. It creates them **only** through declared
migrations, which run at INSTALL and UPGRADE - the same for an extension inside
your project and one installed from a registry.

One declaration is enough: the manifest names the file and `files` ships it.
You do **not** add an `exports` entry for it.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
migrations: './src/migrations.ts',
```

```ts src/migrations.ts
import type { ExtensionMigration } from '@tangen/cms'

export default [
  {
    id: '0001_create_reviews',
    sql: `
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS acme_reviews (
        id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        workspace_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
        object_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
        rating        INTEGER NOT NULL,
        body          TEXT,
        created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
      );
      CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS acme_reviews_scope
        ON acme_reviews (workspace_id, object_id);
    `,
  },
] satisfies ExtensionMigration[]
```

## No runtime DDL. Ever.

Not in a route, not in a hook, not in `onInstall`, not "just this once behind a
flag". `onInstall` does not even receive a database handle, which is the
contract making itself hard to break.

The reason is not tidiness: a table created at runtime has no ledger entry, no
checksum, and no plan anyone read. It is invisible to `tangen doctor`, to drift
detection and to the guarded-drop machinery that makes a mistake recoverable.

If you find yourself wanting runtime DDL, you want a **migration** (for
schema you evolve) or **`customTables`** in the manifest (for schema the
platform plans).

## When they run

| stage | runs |
|---|---|
| **INSTALL** | every migration, in declared order |
| **UPGRADE** | the ones whose ids the ledger has not seen |
| import, REGISTER, ENABLE, START | **never** |

Each runs in its own transaction, and is recorded with a **checksum of its
SQL**. An extension whose migrations are pending is **not active**, and
the reason says so.

## The rules

**Never edit one that has run.** The ledger holds its checksum; changing the SQL
is a corruption, not an update. To change what it created, write a new one.

**Never reorder or renumber.** Order is position, and ids are identity.

**Write them idempotently.** `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, `ADD COLUMN IF NOT
EXISTS`, `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`. A migration may meet a partly-applied
database.

**Prefix your tables.** `acme_reviews`, not `reviews`. You share a database with
the platform, the site's content types and every other extension.

**Scope every row by `workspace_id`.** Several workspaces share one database,
and a query missing `workspace_id` reads one site's rows into another.

## Evolving

```ts
export default [
  { id: '0001_create_reviews', sql: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS acme_reviews (…);` },
  { id: '0002_add_status',     sql: `ALTER TABLE acme_reviews ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending';` },
]
```

Add with a default so existing rows stay valid. Bump your manifest `version`;
that is what makes UPGRADE apply it.

## Failure

A failing migration rolls back its own transaction and the extension does not
become active. Fix the SQL, bump the version, upgrade again.

Because ids are the identity, a migration that **never succeeded anywhere** may
be corrected in place. "Anywhere" includes a colleague's development database.

## Uninstall keeps your data

UNINSTALL does not drop your tables. Rows, ledger and content types are
retained, and a reinstall adopts them.

**PURGE** is the separate, approved deletion:

```bash
bun run tangen purge extension acme.reviews \
  --approve purge-extension:acme.reviews
```

It refuses in production. An owned table is kept aside as a guarded table once
no installation remains anywhere, and only `tangen purge guarded` drops it.

Design for adoption: on install, expect your tables to already exist and to have
rows.

## Migrations or `customTables`

| | use |
|---|---|
| a table shape you will evolve with SQL | `migrations` |
| a table the platform should plan, create and drift-check | `customTables` |
| content editors manage in the Admin | `contentTypes` |

Reach for `customTables` first. A declared table is planned, reported and
checked; a migration is yours to get right.

## Testing

```ts
import migrations from '../src/migrations'

it('has unique, ordered, non-empty ids', () => {
  const ids = migrations.map((m) => m.id)
  expect(new Set(ids).size).toBe(ids.length)
  expect([...ids].sort()).toEqual(ids)
})

it('is idempotent and scopes rows', () => {
  for (const m of migrations) {
    if (/CREATE TABLE/i.test(m.sql)) {
      expect(m.sql).toMatch(/IF NOT EXISTS/i)
      expect(m.sql).toMatch(/workspace_id/)
    }
  }
})
```

Then apply them against a real PostgreSQL - twice, to prove the second run is a
no-op.

## Related

- [Extension data](/extend/data/extension-data) - storage without a table ·
  [The lifecycle in practice](/extend/contract/lifecycle) ·
  [Extension manifest reference](/reference/extension-manifest)

# Extension data

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/data/extension-data
Section: Extend Tangen / Configuration and data
Verification: executable

> The extension store, and per-object data that follows publication.

# Extension data

Most extensions do not need a table. `ctx.store` is a key-value store scoped to
your extension and this workspace - no DDL, no migrations.

Rows live in the deployment's database, discriminated by workspace. Two
workspaces never see each other's entries, and another deployment has its
own store: extension data reaches it through Porter, not by itself.

```ts
await ctx.store.put('settings', { theme: 'dark' })
const settings = await ctx.store.get('settings')

await ctx.store.put('review:r_01', { rating: 5, body: 'Great' })
const reviews = await ctx.store.list('review:', { limit: 50 })

await ctx.store.remove('review:r_01')
const total = await ctx.store.count?.('review:')
```

| method | does |
|---|---|
| `get(key)` | one value, or `undefined` |
| `put(key, data)` | write |
| `remove(key)` | delete |
| `list(prefix, opts?)` | entries whose key starts with `prefix`. `opts`: `orderByDataKey`, `desc`, `limit`, `offset` |
| `count?(prefix)` | how many, without fetching payloads |

Scoping is automatic. You never write `workspace_id` yourself, and
you cannot read another workspace's rows.

## Choose keys with prefixes

`list` is prefix-based, so keys are your index:

```text
settings                       one row
review:<objectId>:<reviewId>   listable by object
index:pending:<reviewId>       a second access path
```

Design them before you write the first one. There is no query language here -
if you need one, use a [migration](/extend/data/migrations) and a real table.

## When the store is the wrong tool

| | use |
|---|---|
| a handful of values, settings, light per-object state | `ctx.store` |
| rows you filter, sort or join | a table via `migrations` or `customTables` |
| content editors manage in the Admin | `contentTypes` |

## Per-object data follows publication

**When the key is a content object's id**, that entry is per-object panel state,
and the platform maintains a **published snapshot** beside your draft.

```ts
const draft = await ctx.extensionData.get('acme.reviews', objectId)
const live  = await ctx.extensionData.getPublished('acme.reviews', objectId)
```

| happens | to the published snapshot |
|---|---|
| the object is **published** | your `data` is copied into it |
| the object is **unpublished**, archived, or moved out of published | it is **cleared** |
| the object stays published and you write again | unchanged until the next publish |

**A Delivery read of the object serves the published snapshot, never your
draft.** That is what lets an editor work on SEO metadata for a live page
without it appearing on the site.

`getPublished` returns **`null`** when the object has no published version -
never published, or unpublished. That is a different answer from `{}`, which is
a published object whose extension state is empty. Collapsing the two shows
blank published values for something that was never published.

```tsx
const live = await ctx.extensionData.getPublished('acme.reviews', objectId)
if (live === null) return <NotPublishedYet />
return <PublishedState value={live} />
```

## A member can write this row - sign what a decision depends on

One table serves both jobs on this page: your `ctx.store` and the per-object
panel data the Admin reads and writes. They share a key tuple, so **a member
with content-write permission on the object can overwrite your entry for it**,
through the Admin's panel-data route. That is by design - a panel saves its own
state - and for display state it costs nothing.

It costs something when the value **is** a decision. If your extension stores
"this was approved", "this passed the check", "the quota is 5", a member can
write that value directly and skip whatever produced it.

`ctx.sign` is the answer. It is a MAC over a string, keyed per extension from a
deployment secret no member can read, on both the server ctx and the
content-hook ctx:

```ts
// writing the decision
const verdict = { approvedBy: actor.id, contentHash: hashOf(row) }
await ctx.store.put(objectId, { ...verdict, mac: ctx.sign?.(JSON.stringify(verdict)) })

// acting on it, later and elsewhere
const row = await ctx.extensionData.get(EXT_ID, objectId)
const { mac, ...verdict } = row
if (!ctx.sign || mac !== ctx.sign(JSON.stringify(verdict))) {
  throw new Error('This approval can no longer be verified')
}
```

Three rules make it hold:

- **Sign the canonical form, not the object.** `JSON.stringify` of the same
  values in a different key order is a different string, and the two sides of
  the comparison usually reach the value by different read paths. Sort the keys,
  or hash a projection you control.
- **Fail closed when you cannot verify.** `ctx.sign` is optional, because a host
  predating it has none. Absent means "cannot verify", which means refuse -
  never fall back to comparing the bare value, which is the hole reopened.
- **Mark the format.** Prefix the stored signature (`v1:`), so a value written
  before you started signing is recognisable. It is unverifiable rather than
  wrong, and saying so lets you give an accurate message instead of accusing an
  editor of an edit they did not make.

The MAC is per extension, so a value signed for yours does not verify for
anyone else's, and it is deterministic, so the two sides of a comparison agree.
It proves the value came from your code. It does not keep the row private - a
member can still read it - so a secret still belongs in `ctx.secrets`.

## Draft and published in a panel

A panel usually shows both: what the editor is working on, and what the public
currently sees. Read both, label them, and never present the draft as live.

## Moving between deployments

Porter carries your per-object data with the object it belongs to, so an
object imported on another deployment arrives with its extension data
intact. A Release publishes in place and does not move data anywhere.

## Locales

The store has **no locale dimension**. If your data varies by locale, carry that
inside your own payload and say so in your own contract - do not assume the
platform will split it for you.

## Testing

```ts
it('clears the published snapshot when the object is unpublished', async () => {
  await publish(objectId)
  expect(await ctx.extensionData.getPublished('acme.reviews', objectId)).not.toBeNull()

  await unpublish(objectId)
  expect(await ctx.extensionData.getPublished('acme.reviews', objectId)).toBeNull()
  expect(await ctx.extensionData.get('acme.reviews', objectId)).toBeDefined()   // the draft survives
})
```

- [Migrations](/extend/data/migrations) · [Server contributions](/extend/contributions/server)
  · [Admin contributions](/extend/contributions/admin)

# Contributions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contributions
Section: Extend Tangen / Contributions

> Every supported server and Admin surface.

# Contributions

Every supported server and Admin surface.

---

# Server contributions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contributions/server
Section: Extend Tangen / Contributions
Verification: executable

> Every supported server-side surface an extension can contribute.

# Server contributions

Your server entry's default export declares these. All of them are optional.

| contribution | key | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Routes** | `adminRoutes` | HTTP endpoints. See [Server routes](/extend/contributions/routes) |
| **Content hooks** | `contentHooks` | `beforeChange`, `afterChange`, `beforeDelete`, `afterDelete` on content writes |
| **Event subscriptions** | `events` | platform events such as `object.published` |
| **Queued tasks** | `tasks` | durable background work, namespaced `ext:<id>:<name>` |
| **Publish policy** | `publishPolicy` | stand between a type and publication |
| **Custom field servers** | `fieldTypes` | validation and coercion for your field types |
| **Webhook triggers** | `webhookTriggers` | events site developers can subscribe webhooks to |
| **Search providers** | `searchProviders` | contribute results to search, per audience |
| **Porter providers** | `porterProviders` | rows your extension exports and imports; each call gets your own store as `scope.store` (on import, `ctx.store`) and the `db` handle only under `db:own` |
| **Flow triggers and actions** | `flowTriggers`, `flowActions` | usable in Flows where that extension is present |
| **MCP tools** | `mcpTools` | tools exposed over MCP, where that capability is on |
| **Lifecycle callbacks** | `onInstall`, `onStart`, `onStop`, `onUpgrade`, `onUninstall`, `onDispose` | see [The lifecycle in practice](/extend/contract/lifecycle) |

Every one is called **only for workspaces where the extension is installed**.

Some of these depend on a capability being available - `mcpTools` needs MCP,
`flowActions` needs the Flows extension. Declare the dependency, or degrade.

## Content hooks

A hook of an extension whose manifest declares `settings` also gets `ctx.settings.get()` (E.7), the same values its routes read.

```ts
export default {
  contentHooks: {
    afterChange: async (ctx) => {
      if (ctx.statusChange?.to !== 'published') return
      // …
    },
  },
} satisfies TangenExtensionServer
```

`beforeChange` and `beforeDelete` may **throw to abort**. `afterChange` and
`afterDelete` may not - their errors are logged, not surfaced.

Extension hooks run **before** site hooks, in install order. A site hook can
rely on yours having written already.

## Events

```ts
events: [
  {
    types: ['object.published', 'object.unpublished'],
    handler: async (event, ctx) => { /* … */ },
  },
],
```

`types` is a list of event type names, or `'*'` for everything. Subscribe
narrowly: `'*'` means your handler runs on every write in the workspace.

Handlers are for **reacting**, not for gating. To refuse a write, use a content
hook or `publishPolicy`.

## Queued tasks

```ts
tasks: [
  {
    name: 'reindex',
    description: 'Rebuild the review index',
    handler: async (payload, ctx) => { /* … */ },
  },
],
```

Namespaced as `ext:<extensionId>:reindex`. Durable: a task survives a restart
and is retried according to the platform's queue semantics. Use one for
anything slow, so a request does not wait on it.

## Publish policy

```ts
publishPolicy: async (ctx, input) => {
  // input: { typeName, objectId? }
  // return a refusal to stand between this type and publication
},
```

Called only for workspaces where you are installed. This is how a review
workflow gates publishing.

## Webhook triggers

`webhookTriggers` declares events a **site developer** can point a webhook at,
so your extension's happenings become part of their integration surface.

## Filters

`filters` registers transforms against a point another extension or the
platform runs:

```ts
filters: [
  { point: 'content.beforeWrite@^1', when: { contentType: 'review' }, priority: 50,
    transform: (record, c) => { if (typeof record.body === 'string') record.body = record.body.trim() } },
],
```

`content.beforeWrite@1` runs on every create and update (the record about to
be written, after content hooks, before validation) in draft mode: mutate
the record you are handed. `priority` orders (ascending), `when` narrows by
`contentType` and `locale`, and a transform that throws or takes longer than
`timeoutMs` (1000 ms) is skipped with a warning attributed to you - the write
continues. `content.validate@1` runs on every save and every publish: return
`{ fields: { path: message }, record: [message] }` (or nothing) and the
platform merges every extension's findings into its normal validation
error - field messages inline, record messages in the banner; `c.phase` tells
you whether this is a save or a publish, so a publish-only rule is one
condition. `content.publish@1` runs over the snapshot about to be published:
mutate it, or return `Filters.REJECT('why')` (from `@tangen/cms`) to veto the
publish with an error attributed to you. The Admin runs it as a dry run too
(`c.dryRun === true`: decide, do not act), so the veto shows on the Publish
button before anyone clicks - prefer it over `publishPolicy`, which is
deprecated onto this point. `content.serialize@1` runs over the
rows every read returns - REST, the content client, GraphQL - so a computed
field or a redaction reaches every transport once; `content.beforeDelete@1`
runs over the row about to be deleted and `Filters.REJECT('why')` vetoes it.
Under manifest `grants` you need `filters:content` for the platform's
content points. Declare and run points of your own with
`ctx.filters.declare` and `ctx.filters.apply`; see
[Cross-extension](/extend/cross-extension).

## Connectors

`contributions['connectors@1']` declares how an outside service is reached -
its auth kind (`oauth2`, `apiKey`, `basic`), the `hosts` it talks to, a
`request(conn, path, init)` that adds the credential, and a `health(conn)`.
The platform stores an operator's credentials for it, sealed, and hands
consumers an authed client through `ctx.connections.get(id)`; you need
`connections:contribute` to offer one and consumers need
`connections:<id>` to use it.

Operators add connections in Settings → Connections. For `apiKey` the
page asks for each of your `fields`; for `basic`, a username and
password; for `oauth2`, the client id and secret of the OAuth app they
registered with the provider (its redirect URL is the API's
`/api/v1/connections/oauth/callback`) - core runs the authorize redirect,
the state and PKCE, the code exchange at your `tokenUrl`, and seals the
tokens; your `request` then reads `conn.credentials.accessToken`. The
page's Test button runs your `health(conn)`, so declare one. When an
operator holds several connections of one connector they are told apart by
label: `ctx.connections.get(id, { label })`; without a label you get the
first active one.

Declare `revokeUrl` on an `oauth2` auth so a revocation in Settings reaches
the provider. Refresh is the platform's job: `conn.credentials.accessToken`
is always the current token, refreshed before expiry or after a 401 and the
request retried once, so never cache a token outside the call.

## GraphQL

`contributions['graphql.types@1']` (grant `graphql:contribute`) extends the
generated schema: `{ sdl, resolvers }` where the SDL adds your types,
`extend type Query { ... }`, `extend type Mutation { ... }` or
`extend type <ContentType> { ... }`, and `resolvers[Type][field]` covers
exactly the fields you added. A resolver gets `(source, args, context)`
with `context.ctx` your extension ctx bound to the caller.

## Translation engines

`contributions['translation.provider@1']` adds a machine-translation engine
(grant `translation:provide`): `{ id, label, languages?, translate(texts, opts) }`
returning `{ texts }` in order. The translate route takes it as `engine`,
refuses a target outside `languages`, and the locales route lists it for the
Admin. `google` and `ai` are core's ids.

## Storage providers

`contributions['storage.provider@1']` adds a storage adapter (grant
`storage:provide`): `{ id, label, description?, create(config) }` where
`create` returns a `StorageAdapter` from the resolved `storage.*` config.
The deployment picks it with `storage.adapter` / `STORAGE_ADAPTER=<id>`;
an id nothing provides is a boot error. `local` and `s3` are core's ids.

## AI providers

`contributions['ai.provider@1']` adds an AI provider (grant `ai:provide`):
`{ id, label, capabilities, models, text?, json?, image?, vision?, embeddings? }`
where `capabilities` names what you implement (`text.generate`,
`json.generate`, `image.generate`, `vision.describe`, `embeddings.generate`).
The platform routes each capability to the workspace's preferred provider
when it advertises it, else the first available one that does; a
definition advertising more than it implements is dropped with a warning.
Consumers call `ctx.ai.generateJSON` (`ai:generate`), `ctx.ai.vision.describe`
(`ai:vision`) and `ctx.ai.embeddings.generate` (`ai:embed`).

## When an operator changes your settings

```ts
onSettingsChange: async (ctx, { changed }) => {
  if (!changed.includes('searchConsoleProperty')) return
  await ctx.enqueue('sync-search-console', { once: true })
}
```

A setting is usually a pointer at the outside world, so this is where you act
on one moving instead of waiting for your next scheduled run. You are told
the KEYS that changed, never the values: read what you need with
`ctx.settings.get()`, so no secret reaches a hook payload. A key counts only
when its value actually differs (clearing counts; a secret counts whenever
one is submitted, because a re-seal is a different ciphertext).

It runs after the write is stored, under your extension's authority, and a
throw is logged rather than failing the operator's save. **Never block it** -
the Save button is waiting, so enqueue rather than calling a provider inline.
Only an operator's save fires it, so a write you make yourself cannot loop
back.

## Contributions by point

`contributions` is the explicit form of the well-known keys above:
`{ 'flow.actions@1': [...], 'mcp.tools@1': [...] }`. Both spellings reach a
host through `ctx.contributions(point)`; see
[Cross-extension](/extend/cross-extension).

## Not a contribution

**Telemetry is not an extension surface.** It is a Core capability with no
persistence and no public extension API. Use `ctx.log` for logging; audit
records are the platform's and are durable.

Do not build against anything not listed on this page, and do not infer a
surface from what a first-party extension does - some of them use internals
that are not part of the public contract.

## Related

- [Server routes](/extend/contributions/routes) ·
  [Extension data](/extend/data/extension-data) ·
  [Custom field types](/extend/contributions/fields) ·
  [The lifecycle in practice](/extend/contract/lifecycle)

# Server routes

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/extend/contributions/routes
Section: Extend Tangen / Contributions
Verification: executable

> Adding HTTP endpoints from an extension: member, key and public routes, their request context, capabilities and error handling.

# Server routes

An extension declares routes in its **server entry**, as data. You never touch
the HTTP framework.

```ts src/server.ts
import type { TangenExtensionServer } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  adminRoutes: [
    {
      method: 'GET',
      path: 'list',
      auth: 'member',
      capability: 'reviews:read',
      handler: async (req, ctx) => {
        const rows = await ctx.store.list('review:')
        return { data: rows.map((r) => r.data) }
      },
    },
  ],
} satisfies TangenExtensionServer
```

`method` is `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`. `path` is relative and may
contain `:param` segments.

## `auth` decides the mount

This is the most important field on the route, and the name `adminRoutes` is
misleading: only one of the three is an admin surface.

| `auth` | mounts at | who |
|---|---|---|
| `'member'` (default) | `/api/v1/admin/ext/<id>/<path>` | admin-panel member sessions. `req.memberId` is set |
| `'key'` | `/api/v1/ext/<id>/<path>` | a workspace API key. The workspace resolves from the key; `req.apiKeyId` is set |
| `'public'` | `/api/v1/ext/<id>/<path>` | **unauthenticated.** Workspace from the `X-Tangen-Workspace` header or the sole loaded workspace |

**Every mount 404s while the extension is uninstalled**, indistinguishable from
a route that was never declared. That is deliberate: an absent extension should
not be discoverable.

**Every route runs as its caller.** `ctx.tangen` is bound to the member, to the
key (or the identity the key is a credential of), or - on a `public` route - to
a reader holding only what the route declares in `authority`
(`{ objects: { actions: ['read'] } }` by default). A route may also declare
`access: { roles?, capability? }`, the same rule a page uses, and the server
decides it before your handler runs: owner and admin pass, a listed role
passes, a held capability passes. Declare `contract: 1` on the manifest to say
the extension is written against this.

## Choosing `auth`

Default to `'member'`. Reach for the others only with a reason:

- **`'key'`** when a customer's *server* calls you - a webhook receiver, a
  server-to-server integration.
- **`'public'`** when a *browser* must call you without a credential - an embed
  script, an unauthenticated form receiver. This is the one to be careful with:
  anyone on the internet can call it, and an unresolvable workspace is a 404
  rather than an error.

A public route must validate its own input, rate-limit itself, and return
nothing it would not put on a billboard.

## Capability gating

```ts
{ method: 'POST', path: 'approve/:id', auth: 'member', capability: 'reviews:moderate', handler }
```

`capability` is enforced **before your handler runs**, so a caller without it
never reaches your code. Declare the id in your manifest's `capabilities` so an
operator can grant it.

Inside the handler you can ask further questions:

```ts
handler: async (req, ctx) => {
  if (!req.can?.('reviews:moderate')) return { error: 'forbidden' }
  if (!req.actAsRole?.(['legal'])) return { error: 'legal review required' }
  if (!(await req.canWriteLocale?.(null))) return { error: 'base-language rights required' }
}
```

| helper | answers |
|---|---|
| `req.can(capability)` | does the caller hold this capability |
| `req.memberRole` | their workspace role on this deployment |
| `req.actAsRole(roles)` | do they satisfy a role restriction. `null` means no restriction; `owner` always satisfies one, so a restriction naming nobody still has a recovery path |
| `req.canWriteLocale(locale)` | may they write content in this language. `null` asks about the base language |

**Any route that writes content should ask `canWriteLocale`.** A capability
grant must never become a way around the locale model.

## Rate limiting

Available to `key` and `public` handlers:

```ts
await ctx.tangen.rateLimit(`reviews:${req.headers?.['x-forwarded-for'] ?? 'anon'}`, 10, 60)
```

## Context

The handler's second argument is your server context:

| | |
|---|---|
| `ctx.extensionId`, `ctx.workspaceId` | identity - scope every read and write by them |
| `ctx.options` | this workspace's configuration - the resolver's answer for your `config` keys |
| `ctx.secrets?.get(name)` | the material behind a declared `secrets` name or a `secret: true` config field, from this deployment's provider; never in `ctx.options` |
| `ctx.store` | your key-value storage |
| `ctx.http(url, init?)` | outbound HTTP with your extension's reach: fetch's shape, limited to the hosts your manifest `grants` name (`network:api.example.com`); an undeclared host, or one that resolves to a private address, is refused before any request (`code: 'NETWORK_REFUSED'`), redirects are re-checked hop by hop, and every call is audited. Use it instead of the global `fetch` - it is what an install review and an operator's audit can see |
| `ctx.tangen` | the content client, **bound to the caller**: it does what the member, the key or the public route's declared `authority` may, never more. A viewer's session cannot create through it; a key without `write` cannot write |
| `ctx.exec` | the caller's execution: `exec.actor.identity` (`{ kind: 'member' \| 'api_key' \| 'agent' \| 'service' \| 'extension', id }`), the workspace, the locale context, the request id and correlation id |
| `ctx.clientFor(exec)` | a content client bound to another execution - pair it with `resolveActor` to act as a recorded member, key or identity |
| `ctx.resolveActor(id)` | the CURRENT authority of a recorded member, key or identity id: `{ ok: true, actor }` or `{ ok: false, reason }` when it was suspended, removed or revoked. Under manifest `grants` it needs `delegation:act-as`; `ctx.db` needs `db:own`, `ctx.ai` needs `ai:generate`, `ctx.enqueue` needs `jobs:enqueue` |
| `ctx.deploymentRole?.()` | `development`, `staging` or `production` |
| `ctx.hasExtension?.(id)` | is another extension active here |
| `ctx.contributions?.(point, { except? })` | every item the active extensions contribute to a point (`'flow.actions@1'`), each with its contributor and a lender for the contributor's own ctx; throws on an unknown point |
| `ctx.connections?.get(id)` | an authed client for a configured connection (`connections:<id>` grant); see [Connectors](/extend/contributions/server#connectors) |
| `ctx.filters?.register(reg)` / `apply(point, value, { scope })` / `declare(def)` | filters: register a transform for this workspace (the handle withdraws), run one of your own points over a value, declare a point in your namespace |
| `ctx.services?.get<T>(ref)` / `resolve(ref)` / `provide(ref, impl)` / `dispatch(ref, { as })` | typed services between extensions: get `'seo.service@^1'` from the active provider (`undefined` when none satisfies), resolve adds who provides it, provide offers one of your declared services from `onStart`, dispatch instantiates a factory service for a caller under provider ∩ caller |
| `ctx.contribute?.(point, items)` | contribute at runtime (from `onStart`), scoped to this workspace; the returned handle withdraws early, and the host withdraws when the scope stops |
| `ctx.realtime?.publish(…)` | publish on a declared channel |
| `ctx.log(message)` | log a line |
| `req.requestId` | the correlation id, echoed as `X-Tangen-Request-Id`. Put it in your log lines |

## Errors

Return a value and it is the response body. Throw, and the platform reports a
failure to the client under the same `requestId` - **without your exception
text**.

Do not return a driver message, a stack trace, or the value that was rejected.

## Testing

```ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'bun:test'
import server from '../src/server'

const route = (m: string, p: string) => server.adminRoutes!.find((r) => r.method === m && r.path === p)!

describe('GET list', () => {
  it('is a member route gated on reviews:read', () => {
    const r = route('GET', 'list')
    expect(r.auth ?? 'member').toBe('member')
    expect(r.capability).toBe('reviews:read')
  })

  it('scopes its read to the calling workspace', async () => {
    const seen: string[] = []
    const ctx = {
      workspaceId: 'wsp_a', extensionId: 'acme.reviews',
      store: { list: async (p: string) => { seen.push(p); return [] } },
      log: () => {},
    }
    await route('GET', 'list').handler({ params: {}, query: {}, body: null }, ctx as never)
    expect(seen).toEqual(['review:'])
  })
})
```

The route table is plain data, so most of what matters is assertable without a
server.

## Related

- [Permissions and security](/extend/contributions/permissions) ·
  [Server contributions](/extend/contributions/server) ·
  [Admin contributions](/extend/contributions/admin) ·
  [Permissions reference](/reference/permissions)
