# Deploying Tangen

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/operate/deployment
Section: Develop & Operate / Deployment
Verification: executable

> Deploying Tangen to production: what runs, what to configure, the secrets you need, and the `tangen start` command that serves the API.

# Deploying Tangen

A Tangen deployment is **one API process**, **one PostgreSQL database**, and
somewhere to keep **media**. Redis is optional and enables several capabilities.

## Your laptop and your server are two deployments

The most common misreading is that one running Tangen holds development,
staging and production and you switch between them. It does not, and the
distinction decides how you deploy.

**An API process has exactly one database**, the one in its `DATABASE_URL`,
and one role, from `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE`. Nothing on a request selects a
database. So:

```text
your laptop                          your server
├── tangen dev                       ├── tangen start
├── DATABASE_URL=…/site_dev          ├── DATABASE_URL=…/site_prod
├── role: development (unset)        ├── TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
└── its own admin account            └── its own admin account
```

Two consequences worth knowing before your first deploy:

**You create an admin account once per database.** `members` is an ordinary
table, so the login you use locally does not exist on the server. The first
visit to a freshly provisioned deployment runs `/setup` and creates its owner.
That is intended: a production database that contains your laptop's password is
worse, not better.

**Content does not travel by itself.** Porter moves it: **export** a bundle
and **import** it, or an **instance-to-instance transfer**, where the sending
server streams the bundle to the receiving server's API over HTTP, because
nothing can open the other database for you. A Release publishes reviewed
drafts on the deployment where they live; it never crosses a database.

Schema is different from content and always travels the same way: `tangen
push`, run from a machine that can reach that deployment's database, with
that deployment's `.env`.

> A deployed process with no `DATABASE_URL` refuses to start rather than
> opening the local default, and a production role refuses destructive
> pushes, purges and seeds whatever is approved. See
> [Deployments](/reference/deployments).

## What runs

| piece | required | notes |
|---|---|---|
| the API process | **yes** | `tangen start`. Serves the REST API. **Not the Admin** - see below |
| PostgreSQL | **yes** | one database per deployment |
| media storage | **yes** | a persistent volume, or an S3-compatible bucket |
| Redis | no | queue, cache, realtime fan-out, and **preview tokens** |

Without Redis the queue, cache and fan-out fall back to PostgreSQL. Preview
still works: a token minted and spent against a server reporting
`capability redis: unavailable` returns the draft, so Redis is a performance and
fan-out dependency, not a correctness one for preview.

Several processes without Redis must set `REALTIME_FANOUT=postgres`, and
tell the platform how many there are (`TANGEN_REPLICAS`).

## Admin URLs and sessions across deployments

The Admin's URL path is `/{workspace}/…`; the session is a member token that
carries the workspace, the member and their role, and nothing else:

```json
{ "workspaceId": "wsp_acme", "role": "owner", "email": "…", "sub": "mem_…" }
```

One login covers the server it logged into. It does not cross to a different
server, because the account lives in that server's database.

The refresh token is an `HttpOnly` cookie with **no `Domain` attribute**, so it
is host-only: it is never shared with a sibling subdomain.

| arrangement | sessions | why |
|---|---|---|
| `admin.example.com` and `staging-admin.example.com` | **separate** | different hosts are different cookie jars, and the cookie has no `Domain`, so it never leaks to a sibling subdomain |
| localhost, several development instances | **separate** | on a development deployment the cookie is named `refresh_token_<PORT>` |
| **staging and production behind one host name**, on two ports | need `TANGEN_COOKIE_NAME` | browsers key cookies by host and ignore the port, so two deployed processes on one host would share `refresh_token`; set a name per deployment |

`Secure` is applied on staging and production roles; `TANGEN_COOKIE_SECURE`
overrides it in both directions, which is what a plain HTTP internal load
balancer that terminates TLS upstream needs.

### Pointing the Admin at its API

In development the Admin's Vite server proxies `/api` to the API process, so
the browser sees one origin and cookies simply work. Hosting the Admin
separately makes them two origins, and two things follow: the served
`index.html` names the API in its `tangen:config` meta tag, and the
deployment sets `ADMIN_URL` so the Admin's origin is allow-listed for CORS -
nothing is built in, nothing is repeated.

## Building and serving the Admin

`tangen start` runs the **API only**. `tangen dev` is what also runs the Admin,
by starting Vite inside the installed `@tangen/admin` against your project. For
a deployment you build the Admin once and serve the output as static files:

```bash
bun run tangen build          # writes dist/admin
```

Serve `dist/admin` from any static host - a CDN, an object store, nginx, or the
same reverse proxy that fronts the API. `--out <dir>` puts it somewhere else,
inside the project.

### One build, any host

The Admin reads its configuration at **runtime** from one public object,
`tangen:config`, so the same `dist/` works for staging and production and
behind any domain - and production needs no Admin server and no port of
its own. It looks in this order:

1. `window.__TANGEN_CONFIG__`, if a hosting page sets it before the bundle loads
2. the `tangen:config` meta tag in `index.html` (JSON)
3. **the Admin's own origin** - the default

Nothing is baked in at build time. Most requests already go to a relative
`/api/v1`, so if your proxy routes `/api` to the API from the same origin as
the Admin, **you configure nothing**. That is the arrangement to prefer.

To point a built Admin somewhere else, rewrite one line of the served
`index.html` - no rebuild:

```html
<meta name="tangen:config" content='{"apiUrl":"https://api.acme.com"}' />
```

The object never carries a secret or a server-only value: every field is
public by construction (`apiUrl` today). Both arrangements - same origin
behind one proxy, and split domains with one build - are proven in a real
browser against a real API by `test/browser/deployment.browser.ts`.

### CORS, when they are separate origins

An Admin on its own domain is a second origin, so the deployment must name
it. It is one variable, and its origin is allow-listed automatically:

```bash .env
ADMIN_URL=https://admin.example.com
```

You do **not** repeat it under `server.cors.origins`.

## What gets built

```bash
bun install
bun run tangen push       # schema, from a machine that can reach the database, with this deployment's .env
bun run tangen start      # the server
```

The generated artifacts in `app/generated/` are committed, so a build does not
need to reach the database to type-check.

**Which content tables a process serves.** A process builds its table
objects at boot from the schema registry of its database and refreshes them
when a push notifies it. The generated `content-tables.ts` is codegen and
type support; nothing at runtime depends on it.

## Required configuration

The minimum for a production process:

```bash
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://…
JWT_SECRET=…                      # required: the server refuses to boot without it
SERVER_URL=https://cms.example.com
FRONTEND_URL=https://example.com
ADMIN_URL=https://admin.example.com
MEDIA_DIR=/var/lib/tangen/media   # or STORAGE_ADAPTER=s3 with the bucket variables
```

The production role also keeps exception text out of 500 responses, makes the
refresh cookie `Secure`, and refuses destructive pushes, purges and seeds;
`NODE_ENV=production` derives the role when it is unset and switches to JSON
logs.

Every variable, with defaults and which are secret, is in
[Reference → Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables).

## Order

1. **Database reachable**, and empty or already migrated.
2. **Schema applied** - `tangen push` with this deployment's `.env`, the plan read.
3. **Secrets in place** - `JWT_SECRET` above all.
4. **Storage mounted** or the bucket configured and credentialed.
5. **Start the process.**
6. **Check health.**

Boot runs the platform's own system migrations unless `TANGEN_SKIP_MIGRATE=1`,
which is for operators who run `db:migrate` themselves.

## Health

```http
GET /api/health
```

Unauthenticated, and suitable as a liveness and readiness probe.

## Media

`MEDIA_DIR` must be a **persistent volume**. A container's filesystem is not
one, and every uploaded asset disappears on the next deploy. For anything with
more than one process, use an S3-compatible adapter instead - local disk is not
shared, and a production role on local media refuses to boot above one
replica.

## Secrets

From your platform's secret store, not a `.env` in the image. `JWT_SECRET`
signs member sessions and derives the site-session and SSO-token keys, so
rotating it invalidates sessions and stored SSO tokens.

## Schema changes on deploy

Applying schema is a **deliberate step with a plan you read**, not something a
container does on boot. Run `tangen push` from a job or a machine with database
access, before the new process starts.

### When the database is not reachable from your laptop

The usual arrangement: you develop locally, production's Postgres is inside a
private network, and port 5432 is not open to you. There is **no HTTP path** for
this - the Admin's schema endpoints are gated to the development role and a
writable source, because they are the Schema Builder, not a deploy channel.

So the push has to run somewhere the database is reachable. Two halves:

**Review the plan where you are.** `--plan` needs no database it can write to,
and `--json` makes it an artifact you can attach to a change request. Run it
against a copy of production, or against staging:

```bash
bun --env-file=.env.staging run tangen push --plan --json > plan.json
```

**Apply it where the database is.** A release job, a one-shot container, or a
shell on the box - anything inside the network, running the same commit with
production's variables:

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run tangen push       # prints the plan again, then applies
bun run tangen start      # only after the schema is in place
```

Order matters: the new process should not start against a database the new code
expects and the old schema does not provide.

> Platform migrations are different. The API runs those at boot, so the system
> tables appear when the process starts. **Content tables do not** - they come
> only from `tangen push`.

If you cannot reach the database from anywhere you control, you cannot migrate
it, and no Tangen command changes that. A bastion, a temporary tunnel, or a job
inside the network is the answer, and it is an infrastructure decision rather
than a Tangen one.

Production refuses destructive operations regardless of approval - see
[the schema workflow](/build/getting-started/schema-workflow).

## Related

- [Deployment scenarios on one machine](/operate/deployment/scenarios): three
  developer mindsets rehearsed locally with hosts-file domains and a sample
  reverse proxy
- [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables) ·
  [Deployments](/reference/deployments) ·
  [Configuration](/reference/configuration) ·
  [Deployments in practice](/build/deployments)

---

# Deployment scenarios on one machine

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/operate/deployment/scenarios
Section: Develop & Operate / Deployment
Verification: executable

> Three ways developers run development, staging and production, and a hosts-file simulation that makes one laptop feel like a laptop plus one or two servers.

# Deployment scenarios on one machine

Tangen has three deployment roles (development, staging, production) and each
is a deployment of its own: one process, one database, one `.env`. This
guide sets up every common arrangement on ONE machine, with hostnames from
your hosts file standing in for servers, so you can rehearse a deployment
before you rent one.

The whole simulation is: three hostnames, one small reverse proxy, one folder
per "server", and the same Tangen commands you would run on a real host.

## The building blocks

Four facts decide everything below. They are the platform's rules, not the
simulation's.

- **One process holds one database.** `DATABASE_URL` is the database; there
  is no second one, and no request can name another. Two deployments are two
  processes with two URLs and nothing in common but the code.
- **The role is the process's.** `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE` decides the safety
  policy (a production role refuses destructive pushes, purges and seeds,
  requires `JWT_SECRET`, sends secure cookies). It never selects data.
- **`tangen dev` is the laptop, `tangen start` is the server.** `tangen dev`
  runs the API plus the Vite Admin dev server. `tangen start` runs the API
  only; the Admin is the static `dist/admin` folder that `tangen build`
  produced, served by any web server or reverse proxy. A static Admin needs
  no port of its own.
- **The Admin shows the role, not a switcher.** Each deployment has its own
  Admin URL and its own accounts; the top bar names the role the process
  runs under.

Variables read by every deployment (in its `.env`, or exported in the shell;
the shell wins):

| variable | meaning |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | the one database this process holds |
| `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE` | `development`, `staging` or `production` (derived from `NODE_ENV` when unset) |
| `PORT` | the API port (bind it to loopback behind a proxy) |
| `ADMIN_URL`, `SERVER_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL` | the public URLs of this deployment; CORS and the generated links read them |
| `JWT_SECRET` | signs member sessions; one per process |

## Step 0: the machine

### Hostnames

Add one line to `/etc/hosts` (`sudo nano /etc/hosts` on macOS or Linux;
`C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows). `.test` is reserved for
exactly this and never resolves on the public internet.

```text
127.0.0.1 dev.tangen.test staging.tangen.test tangen.test
```

Check it:

```bash
ping -c 1 staging.tangen.test    # answers from 127.0.0.1
```

### Databases

Create one database per deployment:

```bash
createdb tangen_dev
createdb tangen_staging
createdb tangen_prod
```

### The reverse proxy

A real server puts nginx or Caddy in front of Tangen; here a 50-line Bun
script does the same job: it reads the `Host` header, sends `/api/*` and
`/media/*` to that deployment's API port, and serves that deployment's Admin
(Vite for development, the static build for the others). Save it as
`proxy.ts` in your project and run `bun proxy.ts`.

```ts
import { existsSync, statSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
import { join, extname } from 'node:path'

const PORT = Number(process.env.PROXY_PORT ?? 8080)
// Each "server" serves its own dist/admin; point these at the right folders.
const ROUTES: Record<string, { api: number; admin: number | string }> = {
  'dev.tangen.test': { api: 3000, admin: 3001 },                                   // tangen dev: Vite
  'staging.tangen.test': { api: 3002, admin: join(import.meta.dir, 'dist', 'admin') }, // static build
  'tangen.test': { api: 3004, admin: join(import.meta.dir, 'dist', 'admin') },         // static build
}
const MIME: Record<string, string> = { '.html': 'text/html; charset=utf-8', '.js': 'text/javascript', '.css': 'text/css', '.svg': 'image/svg+xml', '.json': 'application/json', '.woff2': 'font/woff2', '.png': 'image/png' }

async function forward(req: Request, port: number): Promise<Response> {
  const u = new URL(req.url)
  const headers = new Headers(req.headers)
  headers.delete('host')
  const body = req.method === 'GET' || req.method === 'HEAD' ? undefined : await req.arrayBuffer()
  let res: Response | undefined
  let lastError: unknown
  for (const host of ['127.0.0.1', '[::1]']) { // the API binds IPv4 loopback, Vite binds localhost (often IPv6)
    try { res = await fetch(`http://${host}:${port}${u.pathname}${u.search}`, { method: req.method, headers, body, redirect: 'manual' }); break } catch (e) { lastError = e }
  }
  if (!res) throw new Error(`nothing answers on :${port} (${lastError instanceof Error ? lastError.message : String(lastError)})`)
  const out = new Headers(res.headers); out.delete('content-encoding'); out.delete('content-length')
  return new Response(res.body, { status: res.status, headers: out })
}

Bun.serve({
  port: PORT,
  async fetch(req) {
    const host = (req.headers.get('host') ?? '').split(':')[0]
    const route = ROUTES[host]
    if (!route) return new Response(`no deployment for host "${host}"`, { status: 404 })
    const u = new URL(req.url)
    if (u.pathname === '/api' || u.pathname.startsWith('/api/') || u.pathname.startsWith('/media/') || u.pathname.startsWith('/embed/')) {
      return forward(req, route.api).catch((e) => new Response(`api down: ${e.message}`, { status: 502 }))
    }
    if (typeof route.admin === 'number') return forward(req, route.admin).catch((e) => new Response(`admin down: ${e.message}`, { status: 502 }))
    const file = join(route.admin, u.pathname)
    if (u.pathname !== '/' && existsSync(file) && statSync(file).isFile()) return new Response(Bun.file(file), { headers: { 'content-type': MIME[extname(file)] ?? 'application/octet-stream' } })
    if (!existsSync(join(route.admin, 'index.html'))) return new Response('run `tangen build` first', { status: 503 })
    return new Response(readFileSync(join(route.admin, 'index.html')), { headers: { 'content-type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' } })
  },
})
console.log(`proxy on :${PORT} for ${Object.keys(ROUTES).join(', ')}`)
```

The Admin behind this proxy is same-origin with its API, so the static build
needs no configuration at all: an Admin with an empty `tangen:config` calls
`/api` on its own origin. Only a split-domain deployment (Admin on one host,
API on another) rewrites the `tangen:config` meta tag in `dist/admin/index.html`,
as `tangen build` prints.

One limit of the sample proxy: it does not forward WebSockets, so Vite's hot
reload does not work through `dev.tangen.test`. Develop at
`http://localhost:3001` as usual and use the hostname to check the
deployment's Admin and its role badge.

## Mindset 1: laptop, then a staging server, then a production server

You develop locally and push the codebase to two other machines. In the
simulation each machine is a folder with its own `.env`.

```text
~/sim/laptop/       tangen dev            dev.tangen.test      → :3000 + Vite :3001
~/sim/staging/      tangen start          staging.tangen.test  → :3002 + dist/admin
~/sim/production/   tangen start          tangen.test          → :3004 + dist/admin
```

Set up:

```bash
git clone <your project> ~/sim/laptop
git clone <your project> ~/sim/staging       # on a real server: git pull + bun install
git clone <your project> ~/sim/production
```

Each folder gets a `.env` that holds ONLY what that machine needs:

```bash
# ~/sim/laptop/.env
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_dev
PORT=3000
ADMIN_PORT=3001
JWT_SECRET=<laptop secret>

# ~/sim/staging/.env
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=staging
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_staging
PORT=3002
JWT_SECRET=<staging secret>
ADMIN_URL=http://staging.tangen.test:8080
SERVER_URL=http://staging.tangen.test:8080
FRONTEND_URL=http://staging.tangen.test:8080

# ~/sim/production/.env
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_prod
PORT=3004
JWT_SECRET=<production secret>
ADMIN_URL=http://tangen.test:8080
SERVER_URL=http://tangen.test:8080
FRONTEND_URL=http://tangen.test:8080
```

A server's `.env` names its own database and nothing else. A deployed
process with no `DATABASE_URL` refuses to start.

Run (four terminals, or a process manager):

```bash
cd ~/sim/laptop      && tangen dev
cd ~/sim/staging     && tangen bootstrap && tangen push && tangen build && tangen start
cd ~/sim/production  && tangen bootstrap && tangen push && tangen build && tangen start
cd ~/sim/laptop      && bun proxy.ts      # with ROUTES pointing at ~/sim/staging/dist/admin and ~/sim/production/dist/admin
```

Then open `http://dev.tangen.test:8080`, `http://staging.tangen.test:8080` and
`http://tangen.test:8080`. Sign in to each: they are separate deployments
with separate sessions and separate accounts, as three servers would be. The
top bar of each names its role.

## Mindset 2: laptop with a local staging, then a production server

You keep staging on your own machine to review work before it goes out, and
only production is remote.

```text
~/sim/laptop/       tangen dev                                   dev.tangen.test
~/sim/laptop/       bun --env-file=.env.staging tangen start     staging.tangen.test   (same folder, second process)
~/sim/production/   tangen start                                 tangen.test
```

Because a process reads the `.env` you hand it, one folder serves two
deployments:

```bash
# ~/sim/laptop/.env          the development deployment, as in Mindset 1
# ~/sim/laptop/.env.staging  TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=staging, DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_staging, PORT=3002, its own JWT_SECRET and URLs
cd ~/sim/laptop && tangen dev                                          # holds tangen_dev
cd ~/sim/laptop && bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen push           # staging's schema
cd ~/sim/laptop && bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen start          # holds tangen_staging
```

Build the static Admin once (`tangen build`) and let the proxy serve
`~/sim/laptop/dist/admin` for `staging.tangen.test`. Production is exactly
the Mindset 1 production folder.

## Mindset 3: laptop, then one server that hosts staging and production

One rented machine runs both remote deployments. On a real server they are
two processes behind one nginx; here they are two processes in one folder
behind the sample proxy.

```text
~/sim/laptop/       tangen dev                                          dev.tangen.test
~/sim/server/       bun --env-file=.env.staging    tangen start         staging.tangen.test
~/sim/server/       bun --env-file=.env.production tangen start        tangen.test
```

One checkout, two `.env` files, and the process manager (systemd unit, pm2
ecosystem, Docker environment) picks which one each process gets:

```bash
# ~/sim/server/.env.staging
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=staging
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_staging
PORT=3002
ADMIN_URL=http://staging.tangen.test:8080
SERVER_URL=http://staging.tangen.test:8080
# JWT_SECRET from the process manager, not from this file

# ~/sim/server/.env.production
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tangen_prod
PORT=3004
ADMIN_URL=http://tangen.test:8080
SERVER_URL=http://tangen.test:8080
```

```bash
cd ~/sim/server && bun --env-file=.env.staging    x tangen push && bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen push && tangen build
cd ~/sim/server && JWT_SECRET=<staging secret>    bun --env-file=.env.staging    x tangen start
cd ~/sim/server && JWT_SECRET=<production secret> bun --env-file=.env.production x tangen start
```

Both hostnames serve the same `dist/admin` (one build, any deployment) and
each forwards `/api` to its own process. A member signed in to staging is not
signed in to production: different process, different secret, different
database. Were the two behind ONE host name on two ports, set
`TANGEN_COOKIE_NAME` per process, because browsers key cookies by host and
ignore the port.

## Proving it

Every arrangement above can be checked without a browser.

```bash
# The deployment as boot sees it: role, database, URLs, every key with its
# provenance, secrets as references. Run in the folder that deploys it.
bun --env-file=.env.staging x tangen doctor --deployment

# Each hostname answers from its own process
for h in dev.tangen.test staging.tangen.test tangen.test; do
  curl -s http://$h:8080/api/health; echo "  $h"
done

# Isolation: a staging API key does not exist on production, and production
# holds no staging content. The answer is 401, never staging data.
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <staging API key>" \
  "http://tangen.test:8080/api/v1/objects/page"
```

And in the browser: sign in at one hostname and read the role badge in the
top bar; the other two hostnames are other deployments with their own
sign-in.

## Choosing

| you want | mindset |
|---|---|
| the shape you will actually ship | 1 or 3 |
| to review work before it leaves your machine | 2 |
| the least to run while learning | 2, without the production folder |

Whatever you pick, the code, the schema and `app/config` are identical on
every machine. Only `.env` differs, and Porter moves the content.

---

# Running in production

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/operate/production
Section: Develop & Operate / Running Tangen
Verification: executable

> What changes between a development server and a production one, and what has to be set before it starts.

# Running in production

## There is no build step

A Tangen server runs its TypeScript directly under Bun. There is no bundle, no
`dist/`, no compile step to schedule. `tangen start` is the production entry
point:

```sh
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=production tangen start
```
The banner reports what it resolved:

```text
◆ tangen  workspace: wsp_northwind_systems  env: production
  mode          production
  api           http://localhost:3000
```
`mode production` is how you know you are not accidentally serving a
development configuration.

## Before it starts

Production is one of the three deployment roles, and it needs its own
database:

```sh
DATABASE_URL_PRODUCTION=postgres://…
JWT_SECRET=…
```
`JWT_SECRET` is the one that bites. Unset, the server generates a development
secret and says so - which is fine locally and means every restart invalidates
every session in production.

Then, once per database:

```sh
tangen bootstrap                 # creates the schema (with production's .env)
tangen push                      # applies your content model
```
`bootstrap` before `push`. A push against a database nobody bootstrapped now
tells you so by name, but the order is still the order.

## What differs from development

| | development | production |
|---|---|---|
| schema changes | `tangen push` as you work | a deliberate, reviewed step |
| `JWT_SECRET` | generated if absent, with a warning | set it |
| database | its own | its own, never shared |
| content | whatever you seeded | moved with Porter, not copied by hand |

Deployments share the code and never share data. Pushing on production applies
the same content model to a different database; it moves no content.

## Related

- [Deployments](/build/deployments)
- [Deployment](/operate/deployment)
- [CLI reference](/reference/cli)

# Public contract

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/public-contract
Section: Reference / Contracts
Verification: source

> Which Tangen packages and imports are supported, what stable and experimental mean, and what is internal.

# Public contract

What Tangen supports, and what may change without warning.

**A package existing is not evidence that it is public.** Tangen is developed in
a monorepo; most of what is in it is the platform's own. Only the imports listed
here are supported.

## What a project installs

```jsonc
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@tangen/cms":   "^0.1",
    "@tangen/api":   "^0.1",
    "@tangen/admin": "^0.1"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@tangen/cli":   "^0.1"
  }
}
```

`tangen create` writes exactly this, pinned to a range and never to `latest`.

## Supported imports

| import | status | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `@tangen/cms` | **stable** | the surface you write config and schema against: `defineWorkspace`, `defineObjectType`, `field.*`, `defineExtensions`, `defineGlobals`, `defineAuthConfig`, the route helpers, and the shared content types |
| `@tangen/sdk` | **stable** | the read/write client: `createClient`, the query builder, the Link guards, `TangenError` |
| `@tangen/sdk/node` | **stable** | Node and Bun SSR helpers. The root entry is browser-safe and imports no `node:` module |
| `@tangen/api` | **stable** | `createServer`, which your server entry calls |
| `@tangen/api/lean` | **experimental** | `createServerLean`, which resolves only the capabilities you give it |
| `@tangen/db/migrate`, `/content-tables`, `/custom-tables`, `/schema-kit`, `/reconcile` | **stable** | five subpaths. **The package root is not public** |
| `@tangen/graphql`, `@tangen/mcp`, `@tangen/knowledge`, `@tangen/realtime`, `@tangen/realtime-react`, `@tangen/porter`, `@tangen/nextjs`, `@tangen/astro`, `@tangen/toolbar` | **experimental** | opt-in capability and framework packages. Supported, still settling |
| `@tangen/types`, `@tangen/schema`, `@tangen/helpers` | **stable via the facade** | importable directly, but `@tangen/cms` re-exports them and is the documented path |

## Bundled with the platform

Two first-party extensions ship with the distribution and are declared in a
scaffolded project already: **`@tangen/ext-seo`** and **`@tangen/ext-flows`**.
You configure and enable them; you never install them. There is no supported
add command for either, and both move on the platform's version line rather
than their own.

Declaring an extension makes it available. Installing and enabling it stays per
workspace and per deployment, in the database, exactly as for any other
extension. Bundled does not mean always on.

## Present in the registry, but not an import surface

Some packages must be published because something public depends on them at
run time. **`@tangen/admin`, `@tangen/ui`, `@tangen/icons`, `@tangen/logging`,
`@tangen/studio-schema`, `@tangen/studio-compiler` and
`@tangen/realtime-admin`** are in that set: a scaffolded project installs
`@tangen/admin`, and `@tangen/api` depends on the rest.

Being installable is not a promise. Their exports are unsupported, they carry
no semver commitment, and no document names them as something to import. Seeing
one in `node_modules` is not permission to import it.

## Not public

- **The internals of every package above.** The platform's own. No semver
  commitment.
- **`@tangen/studio`, `@tangen/studio-react`, `@tangen/studio-runtime`,
  `@tangen/ext-porter`, `@tangen/ext-studio`, `@tangen/ext-review`,
  `@tangen/ext-variants` and `@tangen/ext-kitchen-sink`** are not published at
  all. `@tangen/studio` is in addition a deprecated shim over `studio-schema`,
  `studio-compiler` and `studio-runtime`.
- **Any `/src/` path.** `@tangen/sdk/src/client` and its kind do not resolve at
  all: each package declares its entry points, and a path that is not one of
  them is not reachable.
- **Relative paths into the monorepo.** `../../packages/...` is not an import,
  it is a copy of the platform.
- **First-party extensions other than the two bundled ones.** See
  [Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest).

Anything not listed above is internal.

## What the statuses mean

| status | promise |
|---|---|
| **stable** | breaking changes get a major version and a deprecation path |
| **experimental** | the shape can change in a minor version. Supported, and you will be told |
| **deprecated** | still works, has a replacement, will be removed in a major |
| **internal** | no promise at all, including that it still exists next week |

## The kernel contract

Every surface that reaches content resolves one execution with one actor and
converges on the same content operations. What is stable about that:

- the types `ActorContext`, `ExecutionContext`, `LocaleContext`, `JobRunRef`,
  `LifecycleActions` and `Identity` from `@tangen/cms`
- `ctx.exec` on every custom-route, job and extension context, and `ctx.tangen`
  bound to it; `ctx.clientFor` and `ctx.resolveActor` on extension contexts
- the refusal contract: `FORBIDDEN` with a reason, `VALIDATION`,
  `AUTHORITY_LOST` on a run, `object.publish_refused`
- `GET /api/v1/objects/:type/actions` and `/:type/:id/actions`, the one answer
  to "what may this actor do with this object next"
- the event envelope (`actor`, `initiator`, `execution`, `correlationId`,
  `causationId`, `resource`, `locale`) and the `audit_log` record behind it
- the attribution columns `created_by_kind`, `updated_by_kind`,
  `published_by_kind`, `scheduled_by`
- a task's `runAs`; a flow's `owner`, `runAs` and `identity`
- manifest `contract: 1`, capability `gates`, route `access` and `authority`
- the `X-Tangen-Correlation` and `X-Tangen-On-Behalf-Of` headers

Internal, and refused to extensions by a guard test: the storage layer that
acts with Tangen's own authority, the in-process event bus, the queue backends,
the guard functions behind the policy and the resolvers that build actors from
credentials.

## Versions

`@tangen/cms`, `@tangen/api`, `@tangen/admin` and `@tangen/cli` move in
**lockstep**: one `major.minor` line, and a test fails if they drift.
`@tangen/types`, `@tangen/schema`, `@tangen/helpers` and `@tangen/db` are
versioned independently and reached through the four above. `@tangen/sdk` is
**independent** - a client may be older or newer than its server, because it
speaks the REST contract, which is versioned by its `/api/v1` path.

## Related

- [Configuration](/reference/configuration)
- [SDK](/reference/sdk)
- [Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest)

# Configuration

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/configuration
Section: Reference / Contracts
Verification: source

> Every public configuration file, the define* helper it uses, and what belongs in each.

# Configuration

A Tangen project's configuration is TypeScript. Every file exports through a
`define*` helper from `@tangen/cms`, which gives you type checking on the shape
before anything runs.

**`app/config/` is for how the server runs.** Content types are not
configuration - they live in `app/content-objects/` and are applied with
`tangen push`.

## The files

| file | helper | holds |
|---|---|---|
| `app/tangen.config.ts` | - | the CLI anchor: project name and schema path. Keep it thin |
| `app/workspaces/index.ts` | `defineWorkspaces` | the workspace registry |
| `app/workspaces/<slug>/workspace.config.ts` | `defineWorkspace` | one workspace, composing the barrels below |
| `app/config/extensions.ts` | `defineExtensions` | which extensions this project declares |
| `app/config/auth.ts` | `defineAuthConfig` | site-user authentication |
| `app/config/storage.ts` | `defineStorageConfig` | where media lives |
| `app/config/mail.ts` | `defineMailConfig` | the mailer and form notifications |
| `app/config/localization.ts` | `defineLocalizationConfig` | locales and fallbacks |
| `app/globals/index.ts` | `defineGlobals` | workspace-level singletons |
| `app/config/ai.ts` | - | Content AI providers and models |
| `app/config/graphql.ts` `knowledge.ts` `mcp.ts` `dashboard.ts` `forms.ts` | - | per-capability options |

## The database

A deployment has one database, and it is never in a config file:

```bash .env
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host:5432/my_site
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=development
```

Every command and the API read `DATABASE_URL` through one resolver; a
deployed process with no URL refuses to start. See
[Deployments](/reference/deployments).

## Server and frontend

```ts tangen.config.ts (the workspace)
server: { url: 'https://cms.example.com', cors: { origins: ['https://example.com'], credentials: true } },
frontend: { url: 'https://example.com', previewUrl: 'https://example.com/preview?id={id}' },
```

| key | type | required | means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `server.url` | `string` | no | the API's public URL, used for self-referencing links |
| `server.cors.origins` | `string[]` | no | allowed origins. `['*']` is not recommended in production |
| `server.cors.credentials` | `boolean` | no | allow credentialed requests |
| `frontend.url` | `string` | no | your site, used for CORS and redirect links |
| `frontend.previewUrl` | `string` | no | preview template with `{id}`, `{type}`, `{slug}` |
| `frontend.previewUrls` | `Record<string, string>` | no | per-type preview overrides, falling back to `previewUrl` |
| `gateway` | `GatewayConfig` | no | CORS, rate limits and request limits for this workspace. A workspace may only **narrow** what the operator's ceiling (the `gateway` key of the root `tangen.config.ts`, which also holds `trustedProxy`) allows |

The URLs are the deployment's: `SERVER_URL`, `ADMIN_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL` and
`FRONTEND_PREVIEW_URL` in its variables win over the config, and a
development deployment defaults to localhost. There are exactly three
deployment roles. See [Deployments](/reference/deployments).

## Extensions

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@acme/tangen-analytics', options: { siteId: 'abc' } },
  { resolve: '../../extensions/my-extension' },   // a path, for one you are writing
])
```

`resolve` takes a package specifier or a path relative to `app/`. Use the
package specifier for anything installed; the path form is for an extension
living inside your own repository while you develop it. `options` is handed to
that extension as [`ctx.options`](/extend/configuration).

`resolve` is an npm package name or a path in your project. Declaring an
extension makes it **available**; installing and enabling it is per deployment
and lives in its database (`tangen extension install <id>`).

A new project starts with `defineExtensions([])`.

## Storage

```ts app/config/storage.ts
import { defineStorageConfig } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineStorageConfig({
  adapter: 's3',
  bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET!,
  region: process.env.S3_REGION!,
})
```

Changing the adapter does not move existing files, and delivery always goes
through the *current* adapter.

## Secrets

Configuration files are code and are committed. **Secrets are not.** A
credential is a **reference**: the config names the variable, the deployment
supplies the value, and `DATABASE_URL` itself is never in a file:

```ts
ai: { apiKey: { anthropic: 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY' } },   // the NAME of the variable
clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET!,
```

Which variables exist is [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables).
Extension secrets are declared in the manifest and are covered in
[Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest).

## Related

- [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables) ·
  [Deployments](/reference/deployments) ·
  [Authentication](/reference/authentication) ·
  [Public contract](/reference/public-contract)

---

# Environment variables

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/environment-variables
Section: Reference / Contracts
Verification: source

> Every environment variable Tangen reads, whether it is required, its default, and whether it is a secret.

# Environment variables

Configuration files are committed; secrets are not. Everything below is read
from the process environment.

**A test fails if the platform starts reading a variable this page does not
name**, so the list cannot drift from the code.

Columns: **when** is `boot` (read once at startup, changing it needs a restart)
or `live` (read per request).

## Required

| variable | default | secret | when | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | - | **yes** | boot | PostgreSQL connection string: the one database this deployment holds |
| `JWT_SECRET` | a generated dev secret in `.tangen/dev-jwt-secret` | **yes** | boot | Signs member JWTs, and derives the site-session key and the at-rest key for stored SSO tokens. **Required when `NODE_ENV` is `production` or `staging`** - the server refuses to boot without it. Rotating it invalidates sessions and stored SSO tokens |

## Core

| variable | default | secret | when | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `NODE_ENV` | unset, treated as development | no | boot | `production` or `staging` requires `JWT_SECRET`, keeps exception text out of 500 responses, makes the refresh cookie `Secure`, and switches to JSON logs |
| `PORT` | `3000` | no | boot | HTTP port |
| `REDIS_URL` | unset: reported as missing; Postgres queue, cache and fan-out | **yes** | boot | Redis for the queue, cache and realtime fan-out. `rediss://` for TLS |
| `REDIS_ENABLED` | `true` | no | boot | `false` switches Redis off on purpose; `redis.enabled: false` in the workspace config does the same |
| `TANGEN_REPLICAS` | `1` | no | boot | how many API processes serve this deployment, as the operator knows it. Production on local media refuses above 1 |
| `REALTIME_FANOUT` | `auto` | no | boot | `redis`, `postgres` or `local`. Several processes without Redis **must** set `postgres` |
| `TANGEN_WORKSPACE_ID` | `wsp_default` | no | boot | the workspace this deployment serves |
| `TANGEN_WORKSPACE_DIR` | `process.cwd()` | no | boot | the project root holding `app/` and the generated files |
| `SERVER_URL`, `ADMIN_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL`, `FRONTEND_PREVIEW_URL` | localhost from `PORT` / `ADMIN_PORT` / `FRONTEND_PORT` | no | boot | the **development** API, Admin, frontend and preview URLs, read by the resolver (`server.url`, `admin.url`, `frontend.url`, `frontend.previewUrl`) |
| `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE` | derived from `NODE_ENV`: `production`, `staging`, else `development` | no | boot | `development`, `staging` or `production`: the safety policy of this process (secure cookies, `JWT_SECRET` strictness, CORS strictness, error redaction, schema writes from the Admin, destructive push, purge, seed, developer tooling). Any other value refuses the boot |
| `MAIL_FROM`, `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT` | config `fromEmail`; `localhost`; `587` | no | boot | the sender and the SMTP transport of this deployment |
| `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASS`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `SENDGRID_API_KEY` | - | **yes** | use | mail credentials, by reference (`mail.apiKey` names the provider variable) |
| `AWS_S3_BUCKET`, `AWS_S3_REGION`, `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `MEDIA_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | - | no | boot | the s3 adapter's bucket and public base |
| `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | - | **yes** | use | the s3 credentials; `storage.accessKeyId` / `storage.secretAccessKey` may name other variables |
| provider keys (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, ...), `GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY`, `EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY` | - | **yes** | use | AI, translation and embedding keys, by reference; `ai.apiKey.<provider>` and `knowledge.embeddings.apiKey` may rename them per environment |
| `MEDIA_DIR` | `<project-root>/public/media` | no | boot | local media directory. **A persistent volume in production** |
| `TANGEN_SITE_JWT_SECRET` | derived from `JWT_SECRET` | **yes** | boot | a separate key for site-auth sessions |
| `TANGEN_SKIP_MIGRATE` | unset | no | boot | `1` skips boot-time system migrations and the SSO re-encryption, for operators who run `db:migrate` themselves |

## Database tuning

| variable | default | when | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TANGEN_DB_PREPARE` | `true` | boot | prepared statements. Set `false` for poolers that cannot carry them |
| `TANGEN_DB_POOL_MAX` | `10` | boot | pool size **per process** |
| `TANGEN_DB_IDLE_TIMEOUT` | never | boot | seconds before an idle connection closes |
| `TANGEN_DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | driver default | boot | seconds to wait for a connection |

## Search

| variable | default | when | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_FUZZY` | `false` | boot | typo tolerance via `pg_trgm`. Only the exact string `true` enables it |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_CONCURRENT` | `4` | boot | concurrent searches per process |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_PER_WORKSPACE` | `2` | boot | concurrent searches per workspace |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | boot | `statement_timeout` for one search |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS` | `100` | boot | ceiling on rows one search returns |
| `TANGEN_SEARCH_MAX_OFFSET` | `1000` | boot | deepest page a caller may request |

## Per-deployment values

Every deployment sets its own `DATABASE_URL`, `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE`, `JWT_SECRET` and URLs in its own `.env`; a laptop's file never names a server's database. There are no per-environment variable suffixes: `SERVER_URL_<ENV>`, `DATABASE_URL_<ENV>`, `TANGEN_ACTIVE_ENV` and `TANGEN_ENV_ID` went with the Environment model (September 2026, migration 0051), together with `TANGEN_KEEP_ENVIRONMENT` which only that migration reads. See [Deployments](/reference/deployments).

## Services

| variable | required when | secret | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SMTP_HOST` `SMTP_PORT` `SMTP_USER` `SMTP_PASS` `SMTP_FROM` | the mail service is `smtp` | `SMTP_PASS` **yes** | the SMTP transport |
| `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | the `s3` storage adapter omits explicit credentials | **yes** | picked up by the S3 adapter (AWS, R2, Spaces, MinIO) |
| `GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY` `GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_REFERER` | machine translation is on | key **yes** | machine translation |
| `EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY` | knowledge uses an OpenAI-compatible endpoint without `apiKey` in config | **yes** | bearer key for the embeddings endpoint |

## Behaviour switches

| variable | default | when | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TANGEN_CORS_MODE` | `enforce` | live | `enforce` (the default) refuses origins no workspace declared; `observe` restores the old process-wide union and only logs the divergences, as a migration window. An unrecognised value enforces |
| `TANGEN_ACCESS_LOG` | errors only | live | `1` logs every request, `0` none |
| `TANGEN_LOG_LEVEL` | `debug` in development, `info` in production | boot | the lowest level written: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. `warn` quiets a development boot |
| `TANGEN_QUERY_MONITOR` | on in development | live | forces the **Performance Monitor** on (`1`) or off (`0`). The Admin toggle wins. The variable keeps the older name; the product is Performance Monitor |
| `TANGEN_TELEMETRY` | follows `TANGEN_QUERY_MONITOR`'s default | live | collects recent operational events in memory (`1`) or not (`0`). Off keeps nothing subscribed - no ring, no metrics, no timer. **Nothing is ever sent anywhere** |
| `TANGEN_JOBS_INLINE` | unset | live | `1` runs queued tasks inline in the request process, for single-process deployments and tests |
| `TANGEN_COOKIE_SECURE` | `Secure` when `NODE_ENV` is production or staging | live | overrides the refresh cookie's `Secure` flag in either direction |
| `TANGEN_COOKIE_NAME` | `refresh_token_<PORT>` on a development deployment; `refresh_token` otherwise | live | the refresh cookie's name. Browsers key cookies by host and ignore the port, so two deployed processes behind one host name need a name each |
| `NO_COLOR` | unset | boot | disables ANSI colour |

## Development and tooling

| variable | read by | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `TANGEN_DEV_SECRET_FILE` | api | where the generated development JWT secret is kept |
| `TANGEN_SKIP_DB_CHECK` | cli | `1` skips `tangen dev`'s database reachability check |
| `ADMIN_PORT`, `TANGEN_DEV_API_URL` | admin dev server | the Vite dev server's port and API proxy target |
| `TANGEN_APP_ROOT` | admin dev server | the project root the Vite dev server loads `.env` from. Defaults to two levels above `@tangen/admin`; set it when the Admin runs outside a standard project layout |
| `TANGEN_API_URL`, `TANGEN_API_KEY` | cli (`tangen mcp`) | the MCP stdio bridge's target and key |
| `API_UPSTREAM` | admin (Docker) | where the Admin container's nginx proxies `/api`, `/media` and `/embed`. The Admin needs no API variable of its own - it resolves one at runtime from `window.__TANGEN_CONFIG__`, a `tangen:config` meta tag, or its own origin |
| `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` | Docker Compose | the bundled Postgres password |

## Production checklist

- `JWT_SECRET` set, and not the development file.
- `NODE_ENV=production`.
- `MEDIA_DIR` on a persistent volume, or an S3-compatible adapter configured.
- `REALTIME_FANOUT=postgres` if you run several processes without Redis.
- Every secret above supplied by your platform's secret store, not a `.env`
  file in the image.

## Related

- [Configuration](/reference/configuration) · [Deployments](/reference/deployments)

---

# Deployments

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/deployments
Section: Reference / Contracts
Verification: source

> One build, one database, one role - what a deployment is, the three roles, and the production safety rules.

# Deployments

A **deployment** is one build of the project, one PostgreSQL database, the
secrets that process needs, and a **role**. Development, staging and
production are three deployments: three processes, three databases, three
`.env` files. There is no environment inside a database, no `?env=` on a
request, no `--env` on a command.

```text
Project (code: schema, extensions, routes, config)
  └─ Workspace (a site: its content, members, roles, media, extensions)
       └─ Deployment (build + one database + secrets + role)
            └─ Runtime (the process that serves it)
```

## The three roles

```bash
TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE=development | staging | production
```

| role | for |
|---|---|
| `development` | building. Schema changes originate here; the Admin may write schema code |
| `staging` | review, and the rehearsal of a production change |
| `production` | live traffic |

**These are roles of the process, not names of databases.** You do not
invent a fourth; a value outside the three refuses the boot. When the
variable is unset, `NODE_ENV=production` means `production`,
`NODE_ENV=staging` means `staging`, and anything else is `development`. The
role is safety policy; it never selects content or a database.

## What is isolated

Each deployment has its own:

- **database** - `DATABASE_URL`, the one database the process opens. Every
  row of every workspace lives there; a request cannot reach another
- **content**, including drafts, versions, schedules and Releases
- **schema** - a type exists on a deployment once `tangen push` ran there
- **API keys, sessions and members** - issued and reconciled per deployment
- **media**, when the storage adapter or bucket differs
- **cache**, **Redis**, **search index**, **knowledge index**
- **extension installation state** - installed and enabled are per deployment
- **configuration and secrets** - the deployment's variables

Nothing is shared implicitly. There is no request parameter that crosses a
deployment boundary.

## Moving between them

| what | how |
|---|---|
| **schema** | `tangen push`, run on each deployment (from a laptop, a CI job, or a host inside the network). The plan is printed before anything is applied |
| **content, media, extension data, design assets** | Porter: **export** a bundle and **import** it, or an **instance-to-instance transfer** (the sending server streams the bundle to the receiver's API over a one-time code) |
| **a reviewed set of drafts, published together** | a **Release** - on the deployment where the drafts live. A Release never crosses a database |

Content does not flow automatically. Moving it is an explicit act.

## Production safety

Production is treated differently by the platform, not by convention. The
whole matrix is one function, `deploymentPolicy(role)`:

| protection | development | staging | production |
|---|---|---|---|
| secure refresh cookie | off | on | on |
| `JWT_SECRET` required (a generated secret is refused) | no | yes | yes |
| empty CORS allow-list fails closed | no | yes | yes |
| unmapped errors redacted from responses | no | yes | yes |
| the Admin schema builder writes code | yes | no | no |
| destructive schema push | with `--approve` per operation | with `--approve` per operation | refused |
| `tangen purge` (guarded drops, extension purge) | with approval | with approval | refused |
| seed and demo content | allowed | allowed | refused |
| developer tooling in the Admin | yes | no | no |
| config keys marked `required: 'production'` enforced | no | no | yes |

A drop on development or staging becomes a **guarded table** rather than a
deletion, kept aside until something explicitly purges it. On production a
destructive schema change is a reviewed migration outside `tangen push`.

## What the deployment supplies

A config file quotes no `process.env`. The URLs, Redis, storage, mail and
every key are the deployment's, read by one resolver at boot:

| the deployment sets | the resolver answers |
|---|---|
| `SERVER_URL`, `ADMIN_URL`, `FRONTEND_URL`, `FRONTEND_PREVIEW_URL` | `server.url`, `admin.url`, `frontend.url`, `frontend.previewUrl`; a development deployment defaults to localhost from `PORT` / `ADMIN_PORT` / `FRONTEND_PORT` |
| `REDIS_URL`, or `REDIS_ENABLED=false` | `redis.url` (missing is reported), `redis.enabled` (off on purpose is not) |
| `STORAGE_ADAPTER`, `AWS_S3_BUCKET`, `AWS_S3_REGION`, `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `MEDIA_DIR`, `MEDIA_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | `storage.*` |
| `MAIL_FROM`, `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT` | `mail.*` |
| `JWT_SECRET`, `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASS`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, the provider keys | secret **references** the deployment's provider resolves; a config file only ever names one |

The order is fixed for every key: defaults, then the workspace config, then
the deployment's variables, then secrets. A site declares its own keys in
`app/config/site.ts` (`defineSiteConfig`) and reads them as
`ctx.config.site` / `ctx.secrets` in routes and jobs; the Admin receives only
the keys marked `clientSafe`. `tangen doctor --deployment` explains every
key: value or reference, the layer that set it, and whether a reference
resolved. See [Configuration](/reference/configuration).

## One process, one database

**An API process has exactly one database**, resolved at boot from
`DATABASE_URL`. A deployed process with no URL refuses to start rather than
opening the local default. Every workspace of the project lives in that
database, isolated by `workspace_id`; a workspace that must live elsewhere
is its own deployment.

The CLI resolves the same variable: `tangen push` reaches the database of
the `.env` it runs with, and nothing on the command line points it
elsewhere (`--env` and `--prod` are refused with the reason).

## Admin accounts follow the database

`members` is an ordinary table, so it lives in the deployment's database.
Each deployment reconciles `app/config/members.ts` into its own members
table at boot (never a password), and runs its own `/setup` once to create
its first owner. A production database that does not contain your laptop's
login is the point.

## Coming from environments

Databases created before September 2026 held several environments side by
side. Migration `0051_remove_environments` keeps one environment's rows per
workspace and drops the rest; when a workspace holds data in more than one
it refuses and changes nothing until `TANGEN_KEEP_ENVIRONMENT=<slug>` names
the survivor. Export the others with Porter first; after the migration they
are deployments of their own.

## Related

- [Configuration](/reference/configuration) ·
  [Environment variables](/reference/environment-variables) ·
  [CLI](/reference/cli) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions)

# Fields

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/fields
Section: Reference / Content
Verification: source

> All 28 built-in field types, their configuration, storage, localization and query behaviour.

# Fields

A content type declares its fields as an **object map**: the key is the field
name, the value is a `field.*` builder.

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
import { defineObjectType, field } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineObjectType({
  name: 'article',
  label: 'Article',
  fields: {
    subtitle: field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', validation: { required: true }, localized: true }),
    body: field.richtext({ label: 'Body', localized: true }),
    heroImage: field.media({ label: 'Hero image', config: { mimeTypes: ['image/jpeg', 'image/webp'] } }),
    publishedAt: field.date({ label: 'Publish date' }),
  },
})
```

`title`, `slug`, `status`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` and `publishedAt` are
system fields - you do not declare them.

## Every builder takes one object

```ts
field.text({ label: 'Subtitle', validation: { required: true } })
```

The field's **name is the key**, never an argument.

A field may also be written as a **plain object**, which is what the Admin's
schema builder emits and the only form available for an extension-contributed
custom type, since `field.*` covers the built-ins only:

```ts
fields: {
  bio: { label: 'Short bio', fieldType: 'text', config: {}, required: false },
},
```

Options common to every builder:

| option | type | means |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | `string` | **required.** What the editor shows |
| `localized` | `boolean` | this field's value may differ per locale |
| `index` | `boolean` | give this field's column a database index. See below |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | soft-disable: keep the column and the data, hide the field from the Admin, REST, TangenQL and GraphQL. Reversible; `push` keeps the column |
| `previousName` | `string[]` | former names, so a rename moves data instead of dropping it |
| `validation` | rules | per-type validation |
| `admin` | object | editor presentation: `helpText`, `width`, and so on |
| `config` | object | the type's own options (`default`, `options`, `accept`, `targetType`, `min`, `max`, `fields`, `components`, `ai`, …). They live here and only here; writing one at the top level is a compile error, and `tangen check` names the place |
| `hooks`, `validate` | functions | per-field lifecycle and custom validation |

## The 28 types

### Text

| type | stores | notable options |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | a single line | `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern` |
| `textarea` | multiple lines | `maxLength` |
| `richtext` | structured rich text | - |
| `slug` | a URL-safe identifier, **unique per type** | `source` names the sibling field the Generate button derives from |
| `email` | an address, format-validated | - |
| `url` | a URL | - |
| `phone` | a phone number | - |
| `code` | source code | `language` |

### Numeric

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `number` | an integer or decimal |
| `range` | **two** numbers, `min` ≤ `max`, in one `numrange` column |
| `currency` | an amount with a currency |
| `rating` | a bounded score |

### Choice

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `boolean` | true or false |
| `select` | one of a fixed option list |
| `multiselect` | several of a fixed option list, as an array |
| `tags` | free-form strings |

### Time

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `date` | a date, or a date and time |
| `time` | a time of day |

### Structure

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `group` | named sub-fields, **flattened into columns** on the same row |
| `component` | one or more instances of a reusable component definition |
| `repeater` | an ordered list of rows, each with the same sub-fields |
| `object` | a reference to another content object, selectable across types |
| `json` | arbitrary JSON |

### References

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `relation` | a reference to one or many objects of a target type |
| `link` | a destination: content identity, or an external URL. See [Link](/reference/link) |
| `media` | one media asset |

### Other

| type | stores |
|---|---|
| `color` | a colour value |
| `geopoint` | a latitude and longitude |

## Content AI

A field can say whether Content AI may write it, and what good output looks
like. It goes under `config.ai`, not at the top level:

```ts
excerpt: field.textarea({
  label: 'Excerpt',
  config: { ai: { hint: 'One sentence, under 160 characters, no headline repetition.' } },
}),
sku: field.text({ label: 'SKU', config: { ai: { enabled: false } } }),
```

| key | default | does |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | whether AI may fill or suggest this field |
| `hint` | - | what the field holds and how to write it |

Turn `enabled` off for identifiers, codes and anything another system owns: a
generated SKU is worse than an empty one.

## Localization

`localized: true` puts the field's values in a per-locale side table. It is
per-field and opt-in: a type can have localized and non-localized fields side by
side.

**Media localizes at the asset level** - per-locale variants - so a media field
needs no flag.

## `index`

A field you filter or sort on repeatedly should carry `index: true`:

```ts
section: field.text({ label: 'Section', index: true }),
topics: field.tags({ label: 'Topics', index: true }),
```

`tangen push` creates `<type>_<field>_idx` for it - a B-tree, or a GIN index for
an array-backed type such as `tags` or `multiselect` so containment queries use
it. `push --plan` names the index before it creates it, and `tangen doctor`
reports a declared index the database does not have.

Not every type can carry one: `richtext`, `group` and the other container types
have no single column to index, and `index: true` on one is ignored rather than
refused. `slug` already has a unique index of its own, per workspace.

Setting `index: false` later drops the index; the column and its data stay.

## Query behaviour

Not every type participates in every operation.

| | |
|---|---|
| **filterable** | most scalar types. `link` is **not** filterable in v1 |
| **unique** | `slug` is unique per type. `link` cannot be unique |
| **listable** | most types appear as list columns; `link` does not |
| **expanded by depth** | `relation` only. `media` resolves at every depth including `0`; `object` fields are values on the row; `link` consumes no depth |
| **backlinks** | `_referencedBy` works through **many relations** only, and refuses `link` |

See [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql).

## Custom field types

An extension can contribute a field type by **inheriting a built-in
primitive** - it gets that primitive's storage and baseline validation, and adds
its own validation and editor. See the Extend section.

## Related

- [Link](/reference/link) · [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) ·
  [Configuration](/reference/configuration) · [CLI](/reference/cli)

# Link

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/link
Section: Reference / Content
Verification: source

> The link field: stored shape, resolved shape, routing boundary, and what it deliberately does not do.

# Link

A `link` field holds a destination that is either **Tangen content**, held by
identity, or an **external URL**.

An internal link stores `{ type, id }` and nothing derived from it. Tangen does
not store a canonical href for internal content, because it does not know your
routes. **A slug is not identity**: rename a slug and every link to it still
points at the same object.

## Declaring one

```ts app/content-objects/page/schema.ts
import { defineObjectType, field } from '@tangen/cms'

export default defineObjectType({
  name: 'page',
  label: 'Page',
  fields: {
    cta: field.link({
      label: 'Call to action',
      config: {
        allowedKinds: ['internal', 'external'],
        allowedTargets: ['page', 'article'],
        anchor: true,
        query: true,
      },
    }),
  },
})
```

| option | type | default | means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allowedKinds` | `('internal' \| 'external')[]` | both | which destinations the editor offers, and validation accepts |
| `allowedTargets` | `string[]` | any readable type | content types an internal link may point at |
| `anchor` | `boolean` | `true` | offer an anchor |
| `query` | `boolean` | `true` | offer query parameters |
| `validation` | rules | - | the ordinary common, domain, URL and link rules |

`localized: true` works like any field: the *authored destination* may differ
per locale. That is different from an internal link naming a locale of its own
target, which is `locale` below.

## Stored shape

Internal:

```json
{
  "type": "internal",
  "target": { "type": "page", "id": "obj_01H..." },
  "locale": "fr",
  "anchor": "team",
  "query": { "source": "footer" }
}
```

External:

```json
{
  "type": "external",
  "url": "https://example.com/pricing",
  "anchor": "plans",
  "query": { "ref": "docs" }
}
```

`anchor` is stored without the `#`; `#team`, ` team ` and `team` all store as
`team`. `query` is structured, never a raw string, and its keys are stored
sorted so two links that mean the same thing compare equal.

## Resolved shape

A read returns a different shape from the one you store.

Internal - **identity plus current facts**:

```json
{
  "type": "internal",
  "targetRef": { "type": "page", "id": "obj_01H..." },
  "target": {
    "type": "page", "id": "obj_01H...",
    "slug": "about", "title": "About us", "status": "published"
  },
  "locale": "fr",
  "anchor": "team",
  "query": { "source": "footer" }
}
```

`targetRef` is **always present**, so a broken link stays repairable in the
editor. `target` is `null` when the target cannot be resolved for this read -
missing, deleted, or not published in this status. It carries exactly five
keys: `type`, `id`, `slug`, `title`, `status`. No relations, no media, and no
links of its own, so a link can never start an expansion chain.

External - **one derived href**:

```json
{ "type": "external", "href": "https://example.com/pricing?ref=docs#plans" }
```

`href` is `url` with the query merged and the anchor appended. Deterministic,
and the only field.

## The routing boundary

**Tangen owns the destination. Your application owns the URL.**

There is deliberately no `hrefOf(link)` that covers both branches: for an
internal target it would have to invent a path, which is the thing v1 does not
do. Use the guards, and build the path with your own router:

```ts app/lib/link.ts
import { isInternalLink, isExternalLink, isLinkResolved, linkSuffix } from '@tangen/sdk'
import type { ResolvedLink } from '@tangen/sdk'

export function hrefFor(link: ResolvedLink): string | null {
  if (!isLinkResolved(link)) return null            // render as plain text
  if (isExternalLink(link)) return link.href
  if (isInternalLink(link) && link.target) {
    return `/${link.target.type}/${link.target.slug}${linkSuffix(link)}`
  }
  return null
}
```

`linkSuffix()` returns the `?query#anchor` part, or `''`.

An unresolved link is not an error. It means the target is not available for
this read, and the right rendering is plain text rather than a link to nowhere.

## What Link does not do

| | |
|---|---|
| **consume relation depth** | a link resolves the same at any `depth`, including `0` |
| **filter** | `link` is not a filterable type in v1. No operators over the destination |
| **enforce uniqueness** | not a unique type |
| **appear as a list column** | not listable |
| **have a default value** | a destination has no scalar default |
| **support backlinks** | `_referencedBy` **refuses** a link field loudly rather than returning nothing. Backlink discovery is relations only in v1 |

## Errors

An invalid link answers in the ordinary validation envelope: **422
`VALIDATION_ERROR`**, reported under the field's name. The rejected URL is
never echoed back.

External schemes default to `https`, `http`, `mailto` and `tel` unless the
field narrows them.

## Related

- [Fields](/reference/fields) · [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) ·
  [SDK](/reference/sdk) · [Errors](/reference/errors)

# Preview

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/preview
Section: Reference / Content
Verification: source

> Preview tokens, the draft-read endpoint, TTLs, scoping and the live-preview stream.

# Preview

Preview lets a frontend read **draft** content that no API key may read, using
a short-lived token instead of a key.

There are four endpoints. Three are control; only one serves content.

| method | path | auth | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/preview/token` | member session | mint a token |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/preview/validate` | member session | check a token is live |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/preview/stream` | member session | SSE: draft changes as they happen |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/preview/object/:id` | **the token itself** | read one draft object |

## The token

```text
prev_<32 hex characters>
```

| property | value |
|---|---|
| **default TTL** | 3600 seconds (1 hour) |
| **maximum TTL** | 86400 seconds (24 hours) |
| **minimum TTL** | 60 seconds |
| **storage** | Redis, with the TTL as its expiry |
| **scope** | one workspace, and **optionally one `objectId`** |

A token scoped to an object reads that object and nothing else. An unscoped
token reads any draft in its workspace.

**Preview requires Redis.** Without it there is nowhere to hold a token with an
expiry, and the endpoints refuse.

### Minting

```http
POST /api/v1/preview/token
Content-Type: application/json

{ "objectId": "obj_01H...", "expiresInSeconds": 900 }
```

Minting needs a **member session** - it is an Admin action. Your frontend never
mints its own token; it receives one, in the preview URL the Admin builds from
`frontend.previewUrl`.

## Reading a draft

```http
GET /api/v1/preview/object/obj_01H...?type=article&locale=fr
X-Tangen-Preview-Token: prev_a1b2...
```

The header **is** the credential. There is no `Authorization` on this request,
and an API key is not accepted.

The response is the draft object with media expanded at every depth (blocks
included) and links resolved, localized to `locale` when given.

Responses are **`no-store`**. Draft content is never cached by the platform, by
a CDN, or by a browser.

## Failure

| condition | answer |
|---|---|
| header absent | `401 UNAUTHORIZED` - "Missing X-Tangen-Preview-Token header" |
| token unknown or expired | `401 UNAUTHORIZED` |
| token scoped to a different object | refused |
| object in another workspace | refused |
| Redis unavailable | refused |

A failed preview read never falls back to published content. It fails, and your
frontend renders the published page or a not-found.

## Security

- **A token is a draft-read credential.** Anyone holding it reads unpublished
  content for its lifetime. Treat it like a password.
- **Prefer object-scoped tokens with short TTLs.** An editor previewing one
  article needs one object for a few minutes.
- **Never put a token in a page a search engine can reach**, and never render it
  into HTML your published site serves.
- Preview responses are `no-store`; do not cache them yourself, and do not
  reuse a preview response to warm a published cache.
- The token grants **read** only. It cannot write, publish, or reach any other
  endpoint.

## The live-preview stream

`GET /api/v1/preview/stream` is Server-Sent Events over a member session: the
Admin editor pushes a draft's changes as they are typed. The SDK wraps the
browser side of it (`onLivePreview`, `isLivePreview`, and the message-type
constants) so an iframe can re-render without a fetch.

## SDK

```ts
import { fetchPreviewObject } from '@tangen/sdk'

const draft = await fetchPreviewObject({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  id, type: 'article', token, locale: 'fr',
})
```

Returns the object, or `null` on any failure.

## Related

- [Configuration](/reference/configuration) - `frontend.previewUrl` and the
  per-type overrides · [SDK](/reference/sdk) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Preview in practice](/build/content/preview)
