# Knowledge

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/knowledge
Section: Reference / Content
Verification: executable

> Semantic search and ask-with-citations over your own content: the two endpoints, the grants they need, and the three things that must be in place first.

# Knowledge

Knowledge indexes your content as vectors and answers two questions over it:
*what is relevant to this* (`/knowledge/search`) and *answer this, citing my
content* (`/knowledge/ask`).

> **Status: public, constrained.** The endpoints, grants and error codes below are
> real and enforced. But Knowledge cannot run on a stock installation: it needs
> the **pgvector** extension in your database and an **embedding model**, and
> Tangen provides neither. Outside those prerequisites every endpoint is a
> documented `404` or `409`, not a broken feature. Treat the retrieval *quality*
> as untuned; the contract is what is documented here.

## The three prerequisites

| | why | what happens without it |
|---|---|---|
| `knowledge.enabled` in your config | nothing indexes and no endpoint answers while it is off | `POST /api/v1/knowledge/search` → `404` |
| **pgvector** in the database | the vectors have nowhere to live | `tangen knowledge index` refuses and tells you to run `CREATE EXTENSION vector;` |
| an **embedding model** | there is no default provider - enabling must never quietly bill an API key | `embeddings` is required when `enabled` is true |

There is no `tangen enable knowledge`. It is configuration:

```ts app/config/knowledge.ts
import type { KnowledgeConfig } from '@tangen/cms'

export const knowledgeConfig: KnowledgeConfig = {
  enabled: true,
  embeddings: { provider: 'openai', model: 'text-embedding-3-small' },
}
```

then `knowledge: knowledgeConfig` in your workspace config. `tangen knowledge
status` tells you which of the three is missing.

### Bringing your own embedder

`embeddings.adapter` replaces the provider entirely, which is how you run
Knowledge with a local model - or with no external service at all:

```ts
const local = {
  name: 'my-embedder',
  dimensions: 384,
  async embed(texts: string[]): Promise<number[][]> { /* … */ },
}

export const knowledgeConfig: KnowledgeConfig = {
  enabled: true,
  embeddings: { adapter: local },
}
```

The index records which model built it. Change the model or its dimensions and
every query answers `409 KNOWLEDGE_MODEL_MISMATCH` until you
`tangen knowledge index --rebuild` - a deliberate refusal, because querying one
vector space with another model's vectors returns confident nonsense.

## Opting content in

Nothing is indexed unless it says so, per type and per field:

```ts app/content-objects/article/schema.ts
export default defineObjectType({
  name: 'article',
  knowledge: { enabled: true },
  fields: {
    body: field.richtext({ label: 'Body', knowledge: true }),
  },
})
```

A field without `knowledge: true` never reaches the index, so the title is often
all that gets indexed if you forget.

## Building the index

```bash
tangen knowledge index
tangen knowledge status
```

```text
  Enabled: yes
  Embeddings: openai/text-embedding-3-small (1536 dims)
  Types opted in: article
  Index model: openai/text-embedding-3-small (1536 dims)
  Chunks: 2 (object: 2)
  Audiences: public: 2
```

Indexing is not automatic on write - it is a command you run, or schedule.

## Search

```http
POST /api/v1/knowledge/search
Authorization: Bearer <api key>

{ "query": "how do refunds work", "limit": 5 }
```

```json
{ "data": [ { "sourceKind": "object", "sourceId": "…", "sourceGroup": "article",
              "field": "body", "content": "…", "title": "…", "score": 0.82 } ] }
```

`sources`, `types`, `tables`, `locale` and `audience` narrow the search.

## Ask

`POST /api/v1/knowledge/ask` retrieves, then generates an answer with citations
using the workspace's configured AI provider. It needs Content AI configured as
well as Knowledge; without a provider key it fails rather than answering from
the model's own memory.

Send `Accept: text/event-stream` (or `?stream=1`) for token streaming; the
default is a single JSON response.

> The retrieval half of `/ask` is the same one `/search` uses and was verified
> with it. The **generation** half was not exercised in that run - it needs a
> provider credential - so treat the answer envelope as stated from the source
> rather than observed.

## Grants

**Two are needed**, and this is the one that surprises people:

| grant | without it |
|---|---|
| `search: read` | `403` - *"This API key has no 'search' read grant"* |
| `objects: read` for the retrieved type | the request succeeds and returns **`{ "data": [] }`** |

A search key with `search: read` alone retrieves nothing from content, because
every hit is filtered against the key's own read grants before it is returned.
That is deliberate - Knowledge is not a way around the permission model - but it
looks like an empty index. Grant both.

Knowledge has its own `public` / `internal` audiences, granted per key under
`search.audiences`. A key's grant is the ceiling; a request's `audience` may
only narrow within it, and omitting it means `public` only.

## Errors

| code | status | means |
|---|---|---|
| - | `404` | Knowledge is disabled for this workspace |
| `FORBIDDEN` | `403` | the key lacks `search: read`, or the audience it asked for |
| `KNOWLEDGE_NOT_INDEXED` | `409` | nothing has been indexed yet |
| `KNOWLEDGE_MODEL_MISMATCH` | `409` | the index was built by a different model or dimension count |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR` | `422` | no `query` |

## Related

- [Permissions](/reference/permissions) - the grants above
- [Search](/build/search) - keyword search, which needs none of this

---

# TangenQL

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/tangenql
Section: Reference / Querying
Verification: source

> The query language: filters, operators, boolean groups, relations, sorting, pagination, depth and what it refuses.

# TangenQL

TangenQL is a **JSON query object**, not a string language. There is no parser
and no grammar to escape: you build an object, and the compiler turns it into
SQL. The same object works through the SDK, `POST /api/v1/objects/:type/query`,
and the local client inside a custom route.

```ts
const { data, meta } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .where({ featured: true, views: { gt: 100 } })
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```

## Filters

A filter is a map of field names to conditions. **Every condition ANDs.**

```ts
.where({ featured: true, views: { gt: 100 } })   // featured AND views > 100
```

A bare value means `eq`:

```ts
.where({ views: 100 })            // same as { views: { eq: 100 } }
.where({ title: 'Launch day' })
```

`null` means absence:

```ts
.where({ note: null })            // same as { note: { exists: false } }
```

## Operators

| operator | on | means |
|---|---|---|
| `eq` | any | equal. The bare-value shorthand |
| `ne` | any | not equal |
| `gt` `gte` `lt` `lte` | numbers, dates | ordered comparison |
| `in` | any | one of. On a **multiselect** it overlaps rather than compares |
| `nin` | any | none of. On a multiselect, the absence of all of them |
| `contains` | strings | case-insensitive substring |
| `ncontains` | strings | case-insensitive substring, negated |
| `startsWith` | strings | case-insensitive prefix |
| `exists` | any | `true` for present, `false` for absent |

```ts
.where({ views: { in: [0, 100] } })
.where({ title: { contains: 'LAUNCH' } })     // case-insensitive
.where({ title: { startsWith: 'la' } })
.where({ tags: { in: ['blue'] } })            // multiselect: overlaps
.where({ note: { exists: false } })
```

A string operator on a non-string value is refused, not coerced.

## Boolean groups

`_or` and `_and` take arrays of conditions. **Conditions inside one branch AND
together**, and a top-level condition ANDs with the group.

```ts
.where({ _or: [{ views: { gt: 90 } }, { title: { contains: 'draft' } }] })

// (featured AND views < 10) OR (views = 50)
.where({ _or: [{ featured: true, views: { lt: 10 } }, { views: { eq: 50 } }] })

// (views > 90 OR views = 0) AND featured
.where({ _or: [{ views: { gt: 90 } }, { views: { eq: 0 } }], featured: true })
```

Groups nest **4 levels deep**. Nesting past that is refused before anything
runs.

## Relations

A **dotted path** filters by a field on the related record, one level deep:

```ts
.where({ 'author.title': { contains: 'jane' } })
.where({ 'cats.title': { contains: 'Rex' } })    // through a many relation
```

An unknown prefix, a prefix that is not a relation, and a path deeper than one
level are all refused.

`_referencedBy` selects objects that a **many** relation points at:

```ts
await tangen.objects('author')
  .where({ _referencedBy: { type: 'article', field: 'contributors' } })
  .get()

// only referrers in a given status count
.where({ _referencedBy: { type: 'article', field: 'contributors', status: 'draft' } })
```

It refuses a field that is not a many relation. **It refuses `link` fields
loudly** - links do not participate in backlink discovery in v1.

## Sorting

```ts
.sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
```

**camelCase is canonical.** System fields sort under their content-model names:
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `publishedAt`, `title`, `slug`, `id`, `status`.
Custom fields sort under the name you gave them.

The storage spelling (`created_at`, `updated_at`, `published_at`) is still
accepted for compatibility and compiles to an identical query.

**Default: `createdAt` descending** - newest first.

## Pagination

```ts
.limit(20).offset(40)                    // offset paging
.limit(20).after(meta.cursor)            // keyset paging
.total(false)                            // skip the count
```

`meta` always carries the page facts: `total`, `limit`, `offset`, `cursor` and
`hasMore`.

`total: false` skips the count query and **still answers `hasMore` exactly** -
it is not an estimate. A cursor walks the same order as the sort, and mixing a
cursor with `offset` is refused.

## Publication state

```ts
.status('published')    // default for an API key
.status('draft')
.status('any')
```

A draft is not in a published read. Reading drafts through an API key needs the
`objects: read_draft` action.

## Relation depth

```ts
.depth(1)
```

| depth | a relation field is |
|---|---|
| `0` | the target's id, and nothing is fetched for it |
| `1` | the target object |
| `2` | the target object, with **its** relations expanded |

**The ceiling is 5.** Depth `6` is refused with a `422 VALIDATION_ERROR` naming
the field, before any query is planned. A non-integer, a negative, `NaN`,
`Infinity` and a string are all refused the same way.

On a REST read the gateway **clamps** an over-depth integer to the ceiling and
reports it in `meta.clamped` rather than refusing. The refusal above applies
where no clamp runs: the local client, an extension, the compiler used directly.

A cycle stops at the object already on the path, however deep the request.

**Media expands at every depth, including 0** - it is an always-resolved field
type, not a depth leak. It resolves on the object you asked for, not on an
expanded relation target. **Object fields** are values on the row at every
depth. **Links** consume no depth at all.

## Projection

```ts
.props(['id', 'title', 'slug'])          // exactly these keys come back
.populate('author', ['id', 'title'])     // project ONE relation's expanded record
```

`props` is also the opt-out for media: a projection that omits a media field
returns no media.

## Labels

Labels are **REST-body options**. The SDK builder has no method for them.

```jsonc
// POST /api/v1/objects/article/query
{
  "query": { "labels": { "any": ["launch", "evergreen"] } },
  "includeLabels": true
}
```

`all`, `any` and `none` narrow by attached labels; `includeLabels: true`
attaches them to each row as `_labels`.

## Locale

`locale` is a **top-level key of the request body**, beside `limit` and
`depth` - it is not part of `query`, and on this route it is **not** a
query-string parameter:

```json
// POST /api/v1/objects/page/query
{ "query": { "path": { "eq": "/company/about" } }, "limit": 1, "locale": "fr" }
```

A `?locale=fr` on the query route is **ignored, not refused**: you get a `200`
carrying default-locale content, which looks like a missing translation rather
than a mis-addressed request. The SDK's `.locale('fr')` puts it in the right
place for you.

## What it refuses

- an unknown field name
- an unknown operator (`{ views: { between: [1, 2] } }`)
- a bare array as a condition (`{ views: [1, 2] }`)
- a string operator on a non-string value
- an unknown content type
- a relation path deeper than one level
- `_referencedBy` through a non-many relation, or through a link
- a depth outside `0..5` (where no clamp runs - see Relation depth)
- a cursor combined with `offset`

Every refusal is a `422 VALIDATION_ERROR` with the offending field named.

## Performance

- `total: false` removes a count query on large tables and keeps `hasMore`
  exact.
- Keyset paging (`after`) does not degrade as `offset` grows.
- `props` narrows what is selected and serialized.
- Depth is a budget: each level is another expansion pass.

## Related

- [SDK](/reference/sdk) · [Fields](/reference/fields) · [Link](/reference/link)
  · [Errors](/reference/errors) · [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api)

---

# SDK

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/sdk
Section: Reference / Querying
Verification: source

> @tangen/sdk: creating a client, reading and writing content, media, errors, cancellation and what has no SDK surface.

# SDK

```bash
bun add @tangen/sdk
```

The root entry is **browser-safe**: it imports no `node:` module. Node and Bun
server helpers live in `@tangen/sdk/node`.

## Creating a client

```ts app/lib/tangen.ts
import { createClient } from '@tangen/sdk'

export const tangen = createClient({
  apiUrl: process.env.TANGEN_API_URL!,
  apiKey: process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY!,
})
```

| option | type | default | means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `apiUrl` | `string` | required | the API origin, e.g. `https://cms.example.com`. The SDK adds the API path; a base already ending in `/api/v1` also works |
| `apiKey` | `string` | required | the key. Keep it server-side |
| `fetch` | `FetchFn` | global `fetch` | your own fetch, for instrumentation or a proxy |
| `timeoutMs` | `number` | `30000` | per-request timeout |
| `retries` | `number` | `0` | extra attempts for 429, 502, 503, 504 and network failures |
| `onResponse` | `RequestObserver` | - | called once per response with timings. Throwing here is swallowed |
| `toolbarDetail` | `boolean` | `false` | opt this key in as the Toolbar's drill-down fetcher. Requires `permissions.toolbar.enabled` on the key |

## Reading content

```ts
const { data, meta } = await tangen
  .objects('article')
  .where({ featured: true })
  .sort('publishedAt', 'desc')
  .depth(1)
  .limit(20)
  .get()
```

The builder is typed by your generated registry: `objects('article')` is a
literal union, so a typo is a compile error and the row comes back fully typed.

| method | does |
|---|---|
| `.where(query)` | the [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) filter |
| `.sort(field, direction)` | ordering, e.g. `.sort('publishedAt', 'desc')`. camelCase field names are canonical |
| `.limit(n)` `.offset(n)` `.after(cursor)` | paging |
| `.total(false)` | skip the count, keep an exact `hasMore` |
| `.depth(n)` | relation expansion, `0`–`5` |
| `.props([...])` `.populate(field, [...])` | project the row, and one relation's expanded record |
| `.status('published' \| 'draft' \| 'any')` | publication state |
| `.locale(code)` | which locale to read |
| `.serialize(...)` `.cacheStrategy(...)` | response options |
| `.get()` | run it, returning `{ data, meta }` |
| `.find(id)` `.findBySlug(slug)` | one object |

## Writing content

Available when the key grants the action.

| method | needs |
|---|---|
| `.create(values)` | `objects: write` |
| `.update(id, values)` | `objects: write` |
| `.delete(id)` | `objects: delete` |
| `.publish(id)` `.unpublish(id)` | `objects: publish` |
| `.publishPreflight(id)` | `objects: publish` - the cascade plan, no write |
| `.schedule(id, at)` `.unschedule(id)` | `objects: publish` |

## Globals, media, search

```ts
const settings = (await tangen.globals('site_settings').get()).data.values
const assets   = await tangen.media.list({ limit: 20 })
const hits     = await tangen.search('pricing')
const locales  = await tangen.locales()
```

`tangen.media` is **read-only by design**: list, read, and build public asset
URLs. Uploading is a REST call, not an SDK method.

`tangen.knowledge` (`search`, `ask`, `askStream`) requires the `knowledge`
capability to be on server-side. `askStream` accepts an `AbortSignal`.

## Cancellation

Every method accepts `{ signal }`, a native `AbortSignal`. Aborting cancels the
request **and stops the retry loop**, so a cancelled read does not quietly
retry three more times.

```ts
const controller = new AbortController()
const p = tangen.objects('article').limit(50).get({ signal: controller.signal })
controller.abort()
```

## Errors

Every failure throws `TangenError`, carrying the server's code and status. See
[Errors](/reference/errors).

```ts
import { TangenError } from '@tangen/sdk'

try {
  await tangen.objects('article').create({ title: '' })
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof TangenError && e.code === 'VALIDATION_ERROR') {
    // e.fieldErrors names the offending fields
  }
}
```

## Links

```ts
import { isInternalLink, isExternalLink, isLinkResolved, linkSuffix } from '@tangen/sdk'
```

See [Link](/reference/link) for what these are for and why there is no
`hrefOf()`.

## Also exported

`pickVariant` and `getOrCreateVisitorId` for A/B experiments · the preview
helpers (`fetchPreviewObject`, `onLivePreview`, `isLivePreview`, and the
message-type constants) · the request observers (`observeRequests`,
`observeInFlight`, `parseServerTiming`) · the SSR timing collector
(`createSsrRequestCollector`, `renderSsrTimingsTag`).

## Not in the SDK

**Site authentication has no SDK surface.** Registering, logging in, refreshing
and reading the current site user are REST calls your application makes
directly. This is a known limitation, not an oversight, and the endpoints are
in [Authentication](/reference/authentication). Do not expect
`tangen.auth.login()` - it does not exist.

Media **uploads**, form **submissions** and schema operations are likewise REST
or CLI, not SDK.

## Related

- [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Authentication](/reference/authentication) ·
  [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) · [Link](/reference/link)

---

# Delivery API

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/delivery-api
Section: Reference / Querying
Verification: source

> The REST endpoints an API key can call, grouped by the scope that grants them.

# Delivery API

Everything below is `https://<your-api>/api/v1/…` with an API key:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <key>
```

The [SDK](/reference/sdk) wraps most of this and is the recommended path. Use
REST directly when you need something the SDK does not cover - uploads, form
submissions, and site authentication.

**A key is scoped to one workspace on one deployment.** Endpoints are grouped
below by the [scope and action](/reference/permissions) that grants them; a key
without the action gets `403 FORBIDDEN`.

## Content — `objects`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/objects/:type/query` | `read` — the [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) endpoint. The one you will use most |
| `GET` | `/objects/:type` | `read` — list |
| `GET` | `/objects/:type/:id` | `read` — one object |
| `GET` | `/objects/:type/by-slug/:slug` | `read` |
| `GET` | `/objects/:type/versions` · `/versions/:versionId` | `read` |
| `GET` | `/objects/:type/slug-check` | `read` — is a slug free |
| `POST` | `/objects/:type` | `write` — create |
| `PATCH` | `/objects/:type/:id` | `write` — update. Send `If-Match` |
| `DELETE` | `/objects/:type/:id` | `delete` |
| `POST` | `/objects/:type/:id/publish` · `/unpublish` · `/stage` | `publish` |
| `POST` | `/objects/:type/:id/publish/preflight` | `publish` — the cascade plan, no write |
| `POST` | `/objects/:type/schedule` · `DELETE` same path | `publish` |
| `GET` `POST` `PUT` `DELETE` | `/objects/:type/:id/labels` | `read` / `write` |

Reading returns **published** content. Drafts need the separate `read_draft`
action **and** an explicit `status`.

```bash
curl -X POST https://cms.example.com/api/v1/objects/article/query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANGEN_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "query": { "featured": true },
        "sort": { "field": "publishedAt", "direction": "desc" },
        "limit": 10,
        "depth": 1
      }'
```

```jsonc
{
  "data": [ /* rows */ ],
  "meta": { "total": 42, "limit": 10, "offset": 0, "cursor": "…", "hasMore": true }
}
```

## Globals — `globals`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/globals` | `read` |
| `GET` | `/globals/:name` | `read` |
| `PUT` `PATCH` | `/globals/:name` | `write` |

## Media — `media`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/media` · `/media/folders` | `read` |
| `GET` | `/media/asset/:id` · `/asset/:id/usage` | `read` |
| `GET` | `/media/file/:id` · `/media/transform` | `read` |
| `POST` | `/media/upload` | `write` |
| `PATCH` | `/media/asset/:id` | `write` |
| `DELETE` | `/media/asset/:id` | `delete` |

`GET /media/file` and `/media/transform` serve bytes and are reachable without
a key, so a browser can load an image.

## Search — `search`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/search` | `read` |

## Forms — `forms`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/forms` · `/forms/:formId` · `/forms/:formId/schema` | `read` |
| `POST` | `/forms/:formId/submit` | `submit` |
| `GET` | `/forms/:formId/submissions` | `read` |

## Custom tables — `tables`

| method | path | action |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/tables/:name/query` | `read` |

## Localization

| method | path |
|---|---|
| `GET` | `/i18n/locales` — which languages this workspace serves |

## Site authentication

Fourteen endpoints under `/auth/…`, for your site's **end users** rather than
for your application's key. They are in
[Authentication](/reference/authentication).

## Unauthenticated

A small set answers without a credential: `GET /api/health`,
`GET /api/v1/media/file`, `GET /api/v1/media/transform`, `GET /media/*`,
`GET /llms.txt`, the form embed asset, and the GraphiQL shell.

## Not public

The **Admin API** is not part of this contract. Endpoints under `/admin/…`,
`/auth-users/…`, the extension data routes, schema writes, releases, Porter,
workspace and member management, and the playground exist for the Admin panel
and change without notice. Being able to reach one with a member session is not
a promise that it will still be there.

`POST /objects/bulk-update`, `/objects/migrate` and `/objects/export` are Admin
operations, not Delivery.

## Headers

| header | on | means |
|---|---|---|
| `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | request | the API key |
| `ETag` | read response | the version token for this object |
| `If-Match` | write request | apply only if the object is still at this version. See [`STALE_OBJECT`](/reference/errors) |
| `Retry-After` | `429` | when to retry |

## Errors

Every failure is the envelope in [Errors](/reference/errors).

## OpenAPI

There is no OpenAPI specification for v1. This page is the contract.

## Related

- [SDK](/reference/sdk) · [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Authentication](/reference/authentication)

---

# GraphQL

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/graphql
Section: Reference / Querying
Verification: executable

> The generated GraphQL API: how to turn it on, what the schema looks like, and what it will not do.

# GraphQL

Tangen can serve your content model as GraphQL as well as REST. The schema is
**generated from your content types**, so it changes when you push.

> **Status: experimental.** The endpoint, the authentication and the permission
> model are the same ones REST uses and are stable. The *shape of the generated
> schema* - field names, argument names, the connection wrapper - has not been
> frozen, and no external project has been built on it. Use it where a breaking
> change between releases is acceptable. [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) through
> the [SDK](/reference/sdk) is the supported path for a site you have to keep
> running.

## Turning it on

```bash
tangen enable graphql
```

That writes `app/config/graphql.ts` and wires it into your workspace config:

```ts app/config/graphql.ts
import { defineGraphqlConfig } from '@tangen/cms'

export const graphqlConfig = defineGraphqlConfig({
  enabled: true,
  // mutations: true,          // opt-in create/update/publish/delete
  // introspection: true,      // schema introspection for tooling
})
```

Restart, and `POST /api/v1/graphql` answers. Nothing to install: `@tangen/graphql`
is a dependency of `@tangen/api`, so it is already in your project.

**While GraphQL is off, `POST /api/v1/graphql` is a `404`** - the route is
indistinguishable from absent.

## Authentication

Exactly the same credential REST takes:

```http
POST /api/v1/graphql
Authorization: Bearer <api key>
Content-Type: application/json

{"query": "{ articles { data { title } } }"}
```

No credential is a `401`. See [Authentication](/reference/authentication).

## Permissions

Grants are enforced **in the resolvers**, per type, and a refusal is a refusal -
never an empty list.

| situation | answer |
|---|---|
| key has no `objects: read` for the type | `errors[0].extensions.code = "FORBIDDEN"`, `data: null` |
| `status: "draft"` without `objects: read_draft` | `FORBIDDEN`, naming the grant |
| no credential | `401` before the query is parsed |

A read returns **published content only**, exactly as REST does.

## The generated schema

For a content type named `article` you get:

| field | arguments | returns |
|---|---|---|
| `articles` | `where`, `orderBy`, `limit`, `offset`, `after`, `locale`, `status` | `ArticleConnection` |
| `article` | `id`, `slug`, `locale`, `status` | `Article` |
| `global` | `name` | the global's values |

A connection is `{ data, meta }`, not the Relay `edges`/`node` shape:

```graphql
{
  articles(limit: 5, where: { section: { eq: "world" } }) {
    data { id title slug section }
    meta { total }
  }
}
```

```json
{ "data": { "articles": { "data": [ { "id": "…", "title": "Hello Tangen", "slug": "hello-tangen", "section": "world" } ], "meta": { "total": 1 } } } }
```

`where` mirrors [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql)'s operators. `status` is a
string: `status: "draft"` is a request for drafts and needs the grant above.

## Mutations

**Off by default.** With `mutations: false` (the default) any mutation is
rejected by the schema itself:

```text
The mutation operation is not supported by the schema.
```

Set `mutations: true` and the schema gains five per type:

```text
createArticle · updateArticle · publishArticle · unpublishArticle · deleteArticle
```

They run through the same handlers, validation and permission checks the REST
endpoints use - a mutation is not a way around a grant. A key with `read` but
not `write` gets `FORBIDDEN`:

```json
{ "errors": [ { "message": "You do not have permission to write 'article'",
                "path": ["createArticle"], "extensions": { "code": "FORBIDDEN" } } ],
  "data": { "createArticle": null } }
```

`input` takes `title`, `slug` and the type's own fields. As with REST, a create
without a `slug` leaves it null rather than deriving one.

## Introspection and the GraphiQL page

`GET /api/v1/graphql` serves a GraphiQL console. It is a static page and needs
no credential; every query it sends does.

> The console is served whether or not GraphQL is enabled, so seeing it is not
> evidence that the API is on. `POST` is the test: `404` means off.

Introspection is on in a development configuration. Turn it off with
`introspection: false` where you do not want the schema published.

## What it does not do

- **No SDL endpoint.** `GET /api/v1/graphql/schema` is a `404`; use
  introspection.
- **No subscriptions over `POST`.** A `Subscription` type is generated only
  while a realtime hub is running in the process, and it is served over the
  realtime socket rather than this route.
- **No file uploads.** Media goes through the REST media endpoints.
- **No typed client.** `tangen types` generates types for the SDK, not for
  GraphQL.

## Related

- [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) - the query vocabulary `where` mirrors
- [Permissions](/reference/permissions) - the grants the resolvers check
- [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) - the REST surface this parallels

# Authentication

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/authentication
Section: Reference / Access
Verification: source

> The four authentication systems, the Site users extension's options, its REST endpoints, and why there is no SDK auth surface.

# Authentication

Tangen has **four** independent things called authentication. Confusing them is
the most common mistake in this area.

| system | who | credential | for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Admin members** | your team | email + password, member JWT | the Admin panel |
| **API keys** | your application's server | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | reading and writing content |
| **Site users** | your site's end users | site JWT + refresh token | accounts on the site you build |
| **Preview tokens** | an editor previewing | a short-lived token | reading drafts |

This page is about **site users**. API keys are in
[Permissions](/reference/permissions).

Site users is the `@tangen/ext-auth` extension (bundled with `@tangen/cms`,
`tangen extension install auth`). It is the first **site identity provider**
on the platform's seam: a workspace may run a different provider instead,
and everything below that reads "the site user" keeps working.

## `defineAuthOptions`

The extension's options, on its entry in `app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts app/config/extensions.ts
import { defineExtensions } from '@tangen/cms'
import { defineAuthOptions } from '@tangen/ext-auth'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-auth', options: defineAuthOptions({
    allowRegistration: true,
    allowAnonymous: false,
    roles: ['user', 'moderator', 'admin'],
    otp: { channels: ['email'] },
    providers: [
      { name: 'google', clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID!, clientSecret: 'GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET' },
    ],
    profileFields: [
      { name: 'bio', label: 'Bio', fieldType: 'textarea', config: { validation: { maxLength: 500 } } },
      { name: 'company', label: 'Company', fieldType: 'text' },
    ],
    token: { accessTtl: '15m', refreshTtl: '30d' },
    ssoRedirectUrl: 'https://example.com/auth/callback',
  }) },
])
```

| option | type | default | means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `providers` | `SsoProviderConfig[]` | none | SSO providers: `google`, `github`, or `oidc` with an `issuer` (any OpenID Connect provider). `clientSecret` is the NAME of the deployment variable, read through `ctx.secrets` only; the built-in hosts are manifest grants and an issuer's host is granted through `network:option(providers.*.issuer)` |
| `profileFields` | `ProfileFieldDef[]` | none | extra columns on the user record. Each becomes a **real column**, added by `tangen push` |
| `roles` | `string[]` | `['user', 'moderator', 'admin']` | the roles this site hands out |
| `allowRegistration` | `boolean` | `true` | may new users sign up with a password |
| `allowAnonymous` | `boolean` | `false` | enable guest sessions |
| `otp.channels` | `('email' \| 'sms')[]` | `['email']` | where a one-time code may go |
| `otp.ttlSeconds` | `number` | `600` | how long a code lives |
| `otp.allowSignup` | `boolean` | `true` | may a code create the account it is for |
| `sms.send` | `(to, message) => Promise<void>` | - | the SMS sender the `sms` channel needs (or an `onOtpSend` hook) |
| `mail` | `{ fromEmail?, fromName?, otpSubject?, resetSubject? }` | - | the mailer's sender and subjects for codes and reset messages |
| `token.accessTtl` | `string` | `'15m'` | access JWT lifetime |
| `token.refreshTtl` | `string` | `'30d'` | refresh token lifetime; refresh tokens always rotate |
| `ssoRedirectUrl` | `string` | - | where to send the browser after SSO, with `?accessToken=…&refreshToken=…` appended |
| `hooks` | `SiteAuthHooks` | - | lifecycle hooks: `onBeforeRegister`, `onAfterRegister`, `onBeforeLogin`, `onAfterLogin`, `onOtpSend`, `onPasswordResetRequest`, `hashPassword`, `verifyPassword`, `buildTokenPayload` |

### Profile fields

A profile field uses the **same shape as a content field** - the same
`fieldType` names and the same `config`. Sections and `component` are the only
exclusions. `adminEditable: false` keeps a field to what the user writes.

Names must be **snake_case**, and this is checked at compile time:
`profileFields: [{ name: 'firstName', … }]` is a type error that names the
offending field, before `tangen push` ever runs.

Each field becomes a real column on the user table, so adding one is a schema
change and needs a push.

## Endpoints

Site authentication is **REST**, under `/api/v1/ext/auth`. Every route wants
the site key (an API key granted **Site users → sessions**), except the SSO
callback the provider's redirect lands on.

| method | path | does |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/register` | create an account (201) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/login` | exchange credentials for tokens |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/logout` | revoke the session (`refreshToken` in the body), or every session |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/refresh` | exchange a refresh token for a new pair |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/me` | the current user, with profile fields and sign-in methods |
| `PATCH` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/me` | update the current user's name and profile |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/otp/send` | send a one-time code to `{ email }` or `{ phone }` |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/otp/verify` | exchange a code for tokens (creates the account on first use) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/password-reset/request` | start a reset |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/password-reset/confirm` | complete a reset (ends every session) |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/anonymous` | start a guest session |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/anonymous/convert` | turn a guest into a real account |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/sso/:provider` | begin the provider's flow (`?mode=json` answers the URL) |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/ext/auth/sso/:provider/callback` | finish it (public; register it with the provider, `?workspace=` included) |

`/api/v1/admin/ext/auth/*` is the **Admin's** user-management surface, not
part of the site-user API.

## There is no SDK auth surface

`@tangen/sdk` has no `auth` namespace, no `login()`, no `getSession()`. Site
authentication is REST-only in v1: you call the endpoints above with `fetch`,
store the tokens, and send the access token yourself.

This is a real limitation, and it is recorded rather than hidden. Do not expect
an SDK method to appear - if an example shows one, the example is wrong.

```ts app/lib/site-auth.ts
export async function login(email: string, password: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.TANGEN_API_URL}/api/v1/ext/auth/login`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-Tangen-Key': process.env.TANGEN_API_KEY! },
    body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
  })
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('login failed')
  return (await res.json()).data   // { accessToken, refreshToken, expiresIn, user }
}
```

## Security notes

- Keep the **API key** on the server. It is not a site-user credential and must
  never reach a browser.
- A site-user access token is short-lived by default (15 minutes) and refresh
  tokens rotate. Store the refresh token where your framework stores sessions.
- The access token carries `aud: tangen:site` and is signed with
  `TANGEN_SITE_JWT_SECRET` (else a key derived from `JWT_SECRET`), so it never
  verifies as an Admin member. Set `TANGEN_SITE_JWT_SECRET` in production.
- `allowAnonymous` creates real user rows with `isAnonymous: true`. Treat them
  as untrusted until converted.
- Enabling a provider requires its client id and secret; put the secret in the
  deployment's variables and name it in the config, never paste it.
- Blocking a user, changing their password, or revoking a session ends the
  session at once: the access token stops verifying on the next request.

## Related

- [Permissions](/reference/permissions) · [Configuration](/reference/configuration)
  · [Errors](/reference/errors) · [SDK](/reference/sdk)

# Permissions

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/permissions
Section: Reference / Access
Verification: source

> Roles, API key scopes and actions, extension permissions, and why a capability is not a permission.

# Permissions

Four different questions, often confused:

| question | answered by |
|---|---|
| Who are you? | **authentication** |
| What kind of account is this? | **role** (members) or **scope + action** (API keys) |
| May you do this specific thing? | **permission** |
| Does this deployment even have that feature? | **capability** |

## Capability is not permission

A capability is `on`, `off` or `unavailable` for a whole deployment. A
permission is about *you*.

- `search` being **`off`** means nobody can search here, whatever their role.
- `search` being **`unavailable`** means it cannot run here at all - a
  dependency or credential is missing - and an operator fixes that, not an
  admin.
- Having no `search: read` action means **you** cannot search, while everyone
  else can.

They produce different errors, and code that treats them alike will tell a user
something false about their own account. An unavailable capability is not a
`403`.

## Member roles

Four, for people who use the Admin:

| role | can |
|---|---|
| `owner` | everything, including workspace deletion and billing-level settings |
| `admin` | everything operational: schema, members, keys, settings |
| `editor` | create, edit and publish content |
| `viewer` | read |

Field-level access rules can narrow what a role sees or edits per content type.

## API keys

A key grants **actions within scopes**. Anything not granted is refused.

| scope | actions |
|---|---|
| `objects` | `read`, `read_draft`, `write`, `publish`, `delete` |
| `media` | `read`, `write`, `delete` |
| `globals` | `read`, `write` |
| `search` | `read` |
| `tables` | `read` |
| `forms` | `read`, `submit` |
| `webhooks` | `read`, `write`, `delete` |
| `schema` | `push`, `pull` |

### The permission document

A key's permissions are an object keyed by scope. Each built-in scope takes
`{ actions: [...] }` - a bare array is refused with a `422` naming the field:

```json
{
  "label": "Website",
  "permissions": {
    "objects": { "actions": ["read"] },
    "media":   { "actions": ["read"] },
    "globals": { "actions": ["read"] }
  }
}
```

Per-type overrides go beside `actions` and win over it:

```json
{ "objects": { "actions": ["read"], "types": { "invoice": [] } } }
```

Two things worth stating plainly:

- **`read` does not include drafts.** A key with `objects: read` sees published
  content only. Reading drafts is the separate `read_draft` action, and it is
  the one that turns a public key into a preview key.
- **A key can be narrowed to specific types.** A per-type override wins over
  the global action list.

Knowledge retrieval has its own audiences, `public` and `internal`, granted per
key under `search.audiences`. **`search: read` on its own retrieves nothing from
content**: every hit is filtered against the same read grants a direct query
would need, so a Knowledge key wants `objects: read` too. See
[Knowledge](/reference/knowledge).

A key that lacks an action gets **`403 FORBIDDEN`**, never a silent empty
result.

## Extension permissions

An extension declares the capabilities it requires in its manifest. Missing one
makes the extension `unavailable` with a safe reason - it never starts, and it
contributes nothing.

Extensions do not get a private authorisation system: an extension route that
touches content goes through the same object permissions as any other caller.

## Identities: agents and services

A key can also be the **credential of an identity**. An identity is a record of
its own (`kind: 'agent'` for an AI agent, `kind: 'service'` for a deployment's
own automation) that holds both a permission document in the key model
(`permissions`) **and** capabilities in the member model (`capabilities`, from
the same catalogue a role uses). A key minted with `identityId` carries no
grants of its own: a request with it runs as the identity, every row, event and
revision it touches names the identity's id with the `agent` or `service` kind,
and suspending or deleting the identity invalidates every credential of it at
once. A plain key never satisfies a capability; an identity does.

Identities are managed by members holding `manage:apiKeys`, in the Admin under
**AI → Agents (MCP)** or over `GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/admin/identities`.
An agent may name the member it acts for with `X-Tangen-On-Behalf-Of: <memberId>`;
that records the member as the initiator and changes nothing about authority.

## Scope

Every credential is scoped to **one workspace on one deployment**. A key
issued on development does not exist on production, and there is no request
parameter that changes that. Crossing workspaces is a super-admin capability,
not something a key or a role can do.

## Related

- [Authentication](/reference/authentication) · [Errors](/reference/errors) ·
  [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api) ·
  [Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest)

# CLI

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/cli
Section: Reference / Operations
Verification: source

> Every tangen command, its flags, and the rules that govern destructive operations and production.

# CLI

`tangen` is a dev dependency of every Tangen project.

```bash
bun run tangen <command> [--workspace <id>]
```

Every command acts on **the deployment it runs on**: the database in
`DATABASE_URL`, under the role in `TANGEN_DEPLOYMENT_ROLE`. There is no flag
that selects an environment (`--env` and `--prod` are refused with the
reason); run the command with the right `.env`.

## Project

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `tangen create` | scaffold a new project. `--name`, `--with-demo`, `--with-hooks`, `--website`, `--ai` / `--no-ai`, `--skip-db-check` |
| `tangen dev` | run the API and the Admin together. Honours `PORT` and `ADMIN_PORT` |
| `tangen start` | run the API for production |
| `tangen build` | build the static Admin a deployment serves. `--out <dir>`, default `dist/admin`. One artifact for every host - the Admin resolves its API at runtime |
| `tangen bootstrap` | prepare a workspace from configuration |

## Schema

The loop you live in: edit `app/content-objects/`, check, push, get types.

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `tangen check` | validate the schema. Touches no database |
| `tangen diff` | what a push would change |
| `tangen push` | apply the schema, after printing the plan |
| `tangen pull` | write the database's schema back into code |
| `tangen add` | scaffold a content object, field or component |
| `tangen schema regenerate` | rewrite `content-tables.ts` from the registry. No DDL - recovery after a push that stopped after its apply |
| `tangen types` | regenerate types |

### `tangen push`

| flag | does |
|---|---|
| `--plan` | print the plan and stop. `--json` for machine-readable |
| `--dry-run` | run the whole preflight without applying |
| `--approve <token>` | approve one destructive operation. Repeatable |
| `--all-workspaces` | apply to every workspace in the project |
| `--typecheck` | type-check the schema first |

**The plan is always printed before anything is applied.** It names every
statement, in order, and what each would cost.

## Destructive operations

A destructive operation is one that can lose data. The policy has four rules,
and none of them is a prompt you can hold enter through.

**1. Every destructive operation needs its own token.** An approval for one
never authorises another.

```text
drop-type:<type>
drop-field:<type>.<field>
purge-component-field:<component>.<key>
purge-guarded:<name>
purge-extension:<id>@<env>
```

```bash
tangen push --approve drop-field:article.subtitle
```

Push tells you the exact tokens it wants. An unrecognised token is reported
rather than ignored.

**2. Production refuses destructive operations, whatever you approve.** There
is no `--force` that changes this. To remove something from production you
change it on development, rehearse on staging, and take the removal to
production as a reviewed migration.

**3. A drop is guarded, not a deletion.** Dropping a column or a table renames
it aside; the data is recoverable until an explicitly approved purge. The plan
marks these `[guarded: recoverable until purged]`.

**4. Ambiguous operations never apply.** An operation the planner cannot
classify is refused, not guessed at. Safe operations in the same plan still
apply.

`tangen purge guarded` is the separate, approved removal of a guarded table.
`tangen purge extension <id> --approve purge-extension:<id>`
removes an extension's data from this deployment, and **refuses on
production**.

## Operations

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `tangen doctor` | drift, orphans, unapplied history, and what an uninstall retained |
| `tangen doctor --deployment` | the deployment as boot sees it: binding and sharing, live database identity, every key with provenance (references, never values), extension activation, integrations, findings; exit 1 on an error |
| `tangen extension bundle [<dir>] [--minify] [--json]` | Builds the extension's client module (`client`, else `src/index.tsx`) into the runtime Admin bundle its manifest `ui` names (default `dist/admin.js`): one ES module, with React, react-dom, react-router-dom, `@tangen/ui` and `@tangen/icons` read from the Admin's shared runtime rather than bundled. Exit 0 done, 2 could not. |
| `tangen connections rotate-key [--json]` | Re-seals every connection in this deployment's database under the current connections key (`TANGEN_CONNECTIONS_KEY` or `connections.encryptionKey`, else the session secret), opening each with the previous key from `TANGEN_CONNECTIONS_KEY_PREVIOUS` (never from the command line). Rows neither key opens are named and left alone; `tangen doctor --deployment` reports them as `CONNECTION_UNREADABLE`. Exit 0 done, 1 rows remain unreadable, 2 could not run. |
| `tangen migrate layout` | move a v1 `app/` layout to the v2 structure. Idempotent |
| `tangen reconcile` | reconcile extension installation state |
| `tangen release` | **read-only**: `list` and `status`. Creating, approving and applying a release happens in the Admin or over the API |
| `tangen purge` | approved deletion of extension data or guarded tables |
| `tangen workspace create` / `remove` | add or remove a workspace in a multi-workspace project |
| `tangen object` | manage content **types**: `enable`, `disable`, `delete` |
| `tangen db reconcile` | alias of `tangen reconcile` |
| `tangen reset-password` | reset a member's password |

## Extensions and capabilities

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `tangen extension` | `create`, `install`, `enable`, `disable`, `upgrade`, `uninstall`, `list`, `status`, `inspect` |
| `tangen extension install <id> [--yes] [--approve-optional <grant,...\|none>] [--approve-grants <grant,...>]` | reviews the grants the extension asks for before anything is written: each grant by tier with the publisher's reason and what it allows, optional grants with the feature they enable, and what the extension cannot do; in a terminal you are asked, in CI `--yes` approves and `--approve-optional` narrows the optional ones. The approval is recorded on the installation and is what the extension runs with. `--approve-grants` is the CI form: the approved set is exactly the list. A committed `tangen.policy.ts` (`export default { grants: { allow?: [...], deny?: [...] } }`, patterns such as `network:*.example.com`; deny wins) is honoured, and a successful install records `{ version, integrity, grantedGrants }` in `tangen.lock` so a new grant shows in a pull request |
| `tangen extension upgrade <id> [--yes]` | re-reviews against what was approved: a new required grant refuses the upgrade until approved, a grant the new version no longer asks for is revoked |
| `tangen extension inspect <id>` | the manifest overview and the grant review against what this workspace approved (`granted` / `denied` per grant) |
| `tangen enable` / `tangen disable` | switch a capability on or off in the project config |

Declaring an extension in `app/config/extensions.ts` makes it **available**.
Installing and enabling it are separate, per-deployment acts, and an
operator's choice is not overwritten by re-declaring it in code.

## AI and agents

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `tangen ai init` | write the agent guardrails and the Tangen Agent Skill into an existing project. `--force`, `--tools claude,codex,gemini,cursor,windsurf`. `tangen create` already does this |
| `tangen ai status` | which Content AI provider keys this process can see |
| `tangen skills update` | refresh this project's `tangen-*` skills from the installed CLI. Leaves your own skills alone |
| `tangen mcp` | the MCP stdio bridge. Reads `TANGEN_API_URL` and `TANGEN_API_KEY` |
| `tangen mcp expose` | read-only report of what an agent can see over MCP. `--json` |
| `tangen knowledge index` | build or refresh the knowledge index. `--rebuild`, `--yes` |
| `tangen knowledge status` | what the index holds, and which prerequisite is missing. See [Knowledge](/reference/knowledge) |

## Machine-readable output

`--json` is supported where a plan or a list is the output - notably
`tangen push --plan --json`. Exit codes are non-zero on refusal, so a CI step
that ignores stdout still fails correctly.

`--yes` skips interactive confirmation where a command has one. It does **not**
approve a destructive operation; only `--approve <token>` does.

## Related

- [Fields](/reference/fields) - what `tangen push` applies ·
  [Deployments](/reference/deployments) ·
  [Configuration](/reference/configuration) ·
  [Extension lifecycle](/reference/extension-lifecycle)

# Errors

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/errors
Section: Reference / Operations
Verification: source

> The public error codes, their HTTP statuses, and the ones your application is expected to handle.

# Errors

Every failure carries a **stable code** you can switch on. The message is for a
human and may change; the code will not.

```jsonc
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "title is required",
    "fieldErrors": { "title": "required" }
  }
}
```

Through the SDK this arrives as a `TangenError` with `code`, `message`,
`statusCode`, and `fieldErrors` when the code carries them.

## Codes your application should handle

| code | status | when |
|---|---|---|
| `VALIDATION_ERROR` | **422** | the request is well-formed and wrong: a missing required field, a bad operator, a depth outside `0..5`, an invalid link. `fieldErrors` names each offending field. Some argument-level refusals use **400** |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 | no credential, or one that is not valid |
| `FORBIDDEN` | 403 | a valid credential without the action for this request |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | the object does not exist, or is not visible in this status |
| `TYPE_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | the content type is not in this deployment's schema. Usually a missing `tangen push` |
| `FIELD_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | the field is not on that type |
| `CONFLICT` | 409 | a uniqueness collision, most often a slug |
| `STALE_OBJECT` | **409** | you are overwriting a version you did not read. See below |
| `NEEDS_CASCADE` | 409 | publishing would leave a required relation pointing at a draft. Retry with the cascade, or publish the dependency first |
| `CASCADE_BLOCKED` | 409 | the cascade itself cannot proceed |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | too many requests. Honour `Retry-After` |
| `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | 413 | the body exceeds the request limit |
| `BAD_REQUEST` | 400 | malformed at the protocol level |

## Optimistic concurrency: `STALE_OBJECT`

Every content read returns an **`ETag`**. Send it back as **`If-Match`** on a
write, and the write only applies if nobody changed the row in between.

```ts
const res = await fetch(`${api}/api/v1/objects/article/${id}`, {
  method: 'PATCH',
  headers: {
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${key}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'If-Match': etag,                 // the ETag from the read
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'New title' }),
})
```

If the row moved, you get **409 `STALE_OBJECT`**:

```jsonc
{
  "error": {
    "code": "STALE_OBJECT",
    "message": "article \"obj_01H...\" changed since you read it: reread it and apply your edit to the current version.",
    "details": { "objectId": "obj_01H...", "type": "article", "currentEtag": "W/\"...\"" }
  }
}
```

The refusal carries the **current** ETag so you can reread and retry. It never
carries the competing content.

The token is the row's own `updated_at` at full database precision, base64url
in a weak ETag, and the check is added to the UPDATE's `WHERE` - so it is the
database's check, not the application's, and two writers racing cannot both
win. Omitting `If-Match`, or sending `*`, means "any version" and skips the
condition.

## Capability and configuration codes

These say a feature is not available here rather than that you did something
wrong.

| code | means |
|---|---|
| `UNAVAILABLE` | a capability this request needs cannot run in this deployment |
| `AI_NOT_CONFIGURED` | no AI provider key is configured |
| `KNOWLEDGE_DISABLED` / `KNOWLEDGE_NOT_INDEXED` / `KNOWLEDGE_PACKAGE_MISSING` | the knowledge capability is off, unindexed, or its optional package is not installed |
| `FORM_DISABLED` / `FORM_CLOSED` / `FORM_NOT_OPEN` | the form exists and is not accepting submissions |
| `ENTRY_LIMIT` | the form reached its configured submission limit |

A capability being unavailable is **not** a permission error. See
[Permissions](/reference/permissions).

## Upstream and realtime

`UPSTREAM_ERROR` and `UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT` mean a third-party service Tangen
called failed or was slow; the provider's own message is not passed through.
The `REALTIME_*` codes belong to the realtime transport and are documented with
it.

## What errors never contain

Stack traces, SQL, driver text, secrets, or the value that was rejected. In
production an unexpected internal failure is a generic message with a request
id - the detail is in the server's log, not in the response.

## Related

- [SDK](/reference/sdk) · [Permissions](/reference/permissions) ·
  [TangenQL](/reference/tangenql) · [Delivery API](/reference/delivery-api)

# Extension manifest

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/extension-manifest
Section: Reference / Extensions
Verification: source

> Manifest v1: every field, what it declares, and how config, secrets, migrations and dependencies work.

# Extension manifest

An extension is a package with a `tangen.extension.ts` at its root. The
manifest **declares** what the extension contributes; nothing in it runs at
import.

```ts tangen.extension.ts
import type { TangenExtensionManifest } from '@tangen/cms'

export default {
  id: 'acme.reviews',
  name: 'Reviews',
  version: '1.0.0',
  description: 'Customer reviews on any content type.',

  requires: {
    capabilities: ['media'],
    extensions: [{ id: 'acme.core', version: '^1' }],
  },
  optional: {
    extensions: ['acme.analytics'],
    services: ['acme.analytics.events@^1'],
  },
  provides: {
    services: ['acme.reviews.moderation@1'],
  },
  grants: {
    required: ['content:read', 'content:update:types(review)', 'db:own'],
    optional: ['ai:generate'],
  },

  config: {
    moderation: { type: 'boolean', label: 'Hold reviews for moderation', default: true },
    webhookUrl: { type: 'string', label: 'Notify URL', required: false },
    apiToken:   { type: 'string', label: 'API token', secret: true },
  },
  secrets: ['ACME_REVIEWS_KEY'],
  migrations: './src/migrations.ts',

  server: './src/server.ts',
} satisfies TangenExtensionManifest
```

## Identity

| field | type | required | means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `string` | **yes** | globally unique, `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*`. Namespace it: `acme.reviews` |
| `name` | `string` | **yes** | what an operator sees |
| `version` | `string` | **yes** | the extension's own version |
| `description` | `string` | no | one line |
| `contract` | `1` | no | the framework contract the extension is written against. `1` means every server surface it uses receives an execution and a client bound to it (`ctx.exec`, `ctx.tangen`), its capabilities may declare `gates`, its routes may declare `access` and `authority`, and it imports nothing from the internal set ([Public contract](/reference/public-contract)) |

## Dependencies

```ts
requires: {
  capabilities: ['media', 'search'],
  extensions: [{ id: 'acme.core', version: '^1' }],
},
optional: { extensions: ['acme.analytics'] },
```

| field | means |
|---|---|
| `requires.capabilities` | runtime capability ids that must be **available** in the process - `media`, `search`, `mail`, `knowledge`, `redis`, `realtime`, `scheduler`, `webhooks`, and the rest. **One missing makes the extension `unavailable` with a safe reason, and it never starts** |
| `requires.extensions` | extensions that must be installed **and enabled in the same workspace**. A dependency is `'id'` or `{ id, version }` |
| `optional.extensions` | used when present, and the extension works without them |
| `requires.services` | typed services another extension must provide here, as `<ns>.<name>@<range>` (`seo.service@^1`). No active provider whose declared major satisfies the range → your extension is `blocked`, with the reason naming the service |
| `optional.services` | typed services used when present; `ctx.services.get` answers `undefined` otherwise, and the missing ones are reported as `service:<ref>` |
| `provides.services` | the typed services you offer, in your own namespace with a bare major (`acme.reviews.moderation@1`); fulfil each from `onStart` with `ctx.services.provide(ref, impl)`. Providing one you did not declare is refused |

A required capability that is `off` or `unavailable` is not an error you can
catch - the extension simply does not become active there, and the reason says
which one.

## Grants

```ts
grants: {
  required: [
    { grant: 'content:read', reason: 'Reads reviews to moderate them' },
    { grant: 'content:update:types(review)', reason: 'Flags and hides reviews' },
    'db:own',
  ],
  optional: [
    { grant: 'ai:generate', reason: 'Drafts replies with your AI provider', enables: 'AI replies' },
  ],
},
```

Say **why** for every grant that reads or changes platform data (MEDIUM and
HIGH tiers): the reason is shown to the person installing your extension,
in `inspect`, and in the Admin, exactly as you wrote it; a missing one is a
validation warning. An optional grant's `enables` names the feature so a
denial reads "AI replies disabled" rather than a grant id.

`grants` is the authority your extension **runs with** off a route - in event
handlers, in tasks that say `runAs: 'extension'`, in lifecycle hooks. It is
not `requires` (what must exist for the extension to start) and not
`permissions` (the capabilities you define for the roles editor).

| field | means |
|---|---|
| `grants.required` | REQUIRED with a `server` entry (the validator refuses a server entry without a `grants` block; an empty list means it needs none, and holds none): what the extension cannot work without. Declaring it binds those surfaces to an actor that holds exactly these grants and never an administrator's authority: reads see the published web unless the query asks for drafts and `content:read:draft` is held; writes need `content:create` / `content:update` / `content:publish` / `content:delete`, optionally scoped `:types(a,b)` |
| `grants.optional` | grants that unlock more when approved; the extension must work without them |

The grant language is `<family>:<verb>[:<scope>(a,b)]`: `content:*` (with
`types(...)` for a type list and `fields(...)` for a field allow-list -
`content:update:fields(seo.*)` may write every field of the `seo` group and
nothing else; a write naming another field, `title` included, is refused
with a 403 that names it), `media:read|write|delete`, `globals:read|write[:names(...)]`,
`search:read[:audiences(internal)]`, `webhooks:*`, `tables:read`,
`schema:pull`, `locales:all` or `locales:en,fr`, `capability:<id>` for a role
capability, and facility grants such as `db:own`, `ai:generate`,
`jobs:enqueue`, `network:<host>` and `connections:<id>` that gate what `ctx`
hands you. `network:api.example.com` opens `ctx.http` to that host
(`network:*.example.com` for its subdomains, `network:localhost:8080` with a
port); a host that resolves to a private address stays refused unless
`network:private` is held. `secrets:<name>` opens a platform-wide secret to
`ctx.secrets` - your own declared `secrets` need no grant. The other
facilities follow the same rule: `db:own` opens `ctx.db`, `ai:generate`
opens `ctx.ai`, `jobs:enqueue` opens `ctx.enqueue` and `ctx.tangen.enqueue`,
`events:emit` opens `emit`, `delegation:act-as` opens `ctx.resolveActor`.
Without the grant the facility is absent from `ctx`, or refuses with a 403
that names the grant. `ctx.store` (your own storage) needs no grant. A grant the platform does not know fails validation; a privileged
one (`db:platform`, `network:any`, `secrets:any`, `schema:push`) validates
with a warning and can only be approved by a trusted install, never from a
marketplace.

Omit `grants` and the extension keeps the authority it has today.

## Configuration

```ts
config: {
  moderation: { type: 'boolean', label: 'Hold for moderation', default: true },
  apiToken:   { type: 'string',  label: 'API token', secret: true },
},
```

| key | type | means |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | `'string' \| 'number' \| 'boolean' \| 'string[]' \| 'json'` | **required** |
| `label`, `description` | `string` | what the Admin shows |
| `required` | `boolean` | install and upgrade fail without it |
| `default` | `unknown` | used when the value is absent |
| `secret` | `boolean` | **the value is a credential: redacted in logs and diagnostics, and never echoed back** |

Declaring config is what lets the platform validate the options at install and
upgrade, show them in the Admin, and know which ones never to print.

Values are supplied per workspace, in `app/config/extensions.ts`:

```ts
export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@acme/tangen-reviews', options: { moderation: false } },
])
```

## Secrets

Two different things, and the distinction matters:

| | where it lives | for |
|---|---|---|
| `config` with `secret: true` | the workspace's extension options, in the database | a per-workspace credential an operator enters in the Admin |
| `secrets: ['ACME_REVIEWS_KEY']` | **the process environment** | a deployment-wide credential |

## Deployment roles

```ts
deploymentRoles: ['development'],            // a developer tool
deploymentRoles: ['development', 'staging'], // never in production
```

The deployment **roles** the extension may be active on; omit it to allow
every deployment. `tangen extension install` and `enable` refuse a
deployment of another role, boot never adopts the extension there, and the
activation gate answers `not-permitted` for any row that slips through - so
the extension contributes nothing observable on that deployment, whatever
the rows say. Its config keys stay declared; nothing it declares is required
where it is not active.

`secrets` is a list of deployment variable **names** the server entry reads.
Declaring them means the platform knows they are credentials; it never reads
their values into anything it might log. Nothing in the manifest ever contains
a secret's value.

## Migrations

```ts src/migrations.ts
import type { ExtensionMigration } from '@tangen/cms'

export default [
  { id: '0001_create_reviews', sql: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS acme_reviews (...)` },
] satisfies ExtensionMigration[]
```

| field | means |
|---|---|
| `id` | stable, ordered by position, **never renamed after it has run** |
| `sql` | SQL only, so its checksum is the truth of what ran |

They run **in declared order at INSTALL and UPGRADE**, each in its own
transaction, recorded in the platform's ledger with a checksum. They never run
at import, REGISTER, ENABLE or START.

Rules: never edit or reorder one that has run · write them idempotently
(`IF NOT EXISTS`) · prefix your tables · scope every row by `workspace_id`.
**No runtime DDL, ever** - an extension does not create a table
outside this mechanism.

An extension whose migrations are pending is **not active**, and the
reason says so.

## Contributions

| field | contributes |
|---|---|
| `capabilities` | capability definitions the extension provides. A definition may name the platform `gates` it opens (`gates: ['content.rawCss']` lets a holder write raw CSS on a block), so the platform never names an extension's capability itself |
| `fieldTypes` | custom field types, inheriting a built-in primitive |
| `contentTypes` | content types the extension owns |
| `customTables` | tables planned and created by `tangen push` |
| `sidebarPanels` | panels beside the content editor |
| `pages` | Admin pages |
| `routes` | HTTP routes under the extension's mount. A route may declare `access` (the same `{ roles?, capability? }` rule a page uses, decided on the server) and, for a `public` route, `authority` (the grants its `ctx.tangen` holds; default: read published content) |
| `commands` | CLI commands |
| `dashboardWidgets` | dashboard widgets |
| `contentHooks` | `beforeChange`, `afterChange`, `beforeDelete`, `afterDelete` |
| `realtime.channels` | realtime channels |
| `versionedData` | whether the extension's per-object data is versioned with the object |
| `server` | path to the server entry |
| `onInstall`, `onUninstall` | non-schema setup and advisory cleanup. **They receive the workspace only - no database handle** |

## Distribution

An extension reaches a project by `resolve` in `app/config/extensions.ts`:
either an **npm package name** or a **path inside the project**.

Some first-party Tangen extensions are not currently published as packages, so
they cannot be installed by name from an external project. Do not assume a
first-party extension is installable because it exists.

## Related

- [Extension lifecycle](/reference/extension-lifecycle) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions) ·
  [Configuration](/reference/configuration) ·
  [Public contract](/reference/public-contract)

# Extension lifecycle

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/extension-lifecycle
Section: Reference / Extensions
Verification: source

> The eleven stages an extension moves through, what each may do, and what disable, uninstall and purge mean.

# Extension lifecycle

```text
REGISTER → INSTALL → ENABLE → MOUNT → START → STOP → DISABLE → UPGRADE → UNINSTALL → PURGE → DISPOSE
```

Eleven stages. They mean different things, and a stage that "sort of" happened
is the source of most extension bugs.

| stage | scope | what happens | what may **not** happen |
|---|---|---|---|
| **REGISTER** | process | the manifest is read and recorded: id, version, dependencies, contributions | **nothing runs.** No worker, no timer, no connection, no query, no migration |
| **INSTALL** | workspace, per deployment | the extension is added to this deployment's database. **Migrations run**, in order, each in a transaction, recorded with a checksum. `onInstall` runs | - |
| **ENABLE** | workspace, per deployment | an operator switches it on here | migrations do not run again |
| **MOUNT** | process | its routes and Admin contributions are attached | - |
| **START** | process | its workers, subscribers and timers begin - **only** if it is available and required | - |
| **STOP** | process | no new background work; loops end | - |
| **DISABLE** | workspace, per deployment | an operator switches it off here. It contributes **nothing**: no routes, no hooks, no panels, no jobs | its data is not touched |
| **UPGRADE** | workspace, per deployment | a newer version is applied. **New migrations run** | - |
| **UNINSTALL** | workspace, per deployment | it is removed from this deployment | **its data is not dropped** |
| **PURGE** | workspace, per deployment | the separate, approved deletion of that deployment's data | - |
| **DISPOSE** | process | every handle it holds is released | - |

Every stage is per **workspace**, in the deployment's database, except REGISTER and DISPOSE,
which are per process.

## Nothing starts at import

This is the rule the platform enforces most strictly. Importing an extension's
module, registering it, installing it, or running `onInstall` must not create a
network client, a timer, a worker, a subscriber or a connection.

Background work belongs in START, which only runs when the extension is
actually available and wanted here.

## Availability

An extension is `on`, `off` or `unavailable`, like any capability:

| state | means |
|---|---|
| `on` | installed here, enabled here, its code is loaded, and everything it requires is available |
| `off` | not installed here, or installed and switched off. **An operator's choice** |
| `unavailable` | it cannot run here: a required capability is missing, a dependency is not active, its migrations are pending, or this process has not loaded its code |

**Enabled in the database with the code not loaded in this process is
`unavailable`, never `on`.** Restarting the server picks it up.

An operator's disable or uninstall is **state**, and re-declaring the extension
in code does not overwrite it. Declaring makes it available; installing and
enabling are separate, deliberate acts.

## Uninstall does not delete data

`extension_data`, the extension's own tables' rows, its migration ledger and
its content types all survive an uninstall, and a reinstall adopts them.

**PURGE** is the separate deletion, and it is guarded:

```bash
tangen purge extension acme.reviews \
  --approve purge-extension:acme.reviews
```

It **refuses in production**. An owned table is not dropped but kept aside as a
guarded table once no installation remains anywhere, and only
`tangen purge guarded` drops it.

`tangen doctor` reports what an uninstall retained.

## Published and draft extension data

When an extension stores per-object data keyed by a content object's id, the
platform maintains a **published snapshot** beside the draft: publishing the
object copies the data into it, and unpublishing clears it. A Delivery read of
the object serves the published snapshot, never the draft.

## Related

- [Extension manifest](/reference/extension-manifest) ·
  [Permissions](/reference/permissions) · [CLI](/reference/cli) ·
  [Deployments](/reference/deployments)

# Flow reference

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/flow
Section: Reference / Extensions
Verification: source

> Node kinds, condition operators, built-in actions, trigger types and the limits, as the implementation declares them.

# Flow reference

Every table here is validated against the implementation by `docs:check`.

## Node kinds

```text
trigger · condition · switch · transform · wait · loop · action
```

## Condition operators

| operator | true when |
|---|---|
| `eq` | equal |
| `neq` | not equal |
| `gt` | greater than |
| `lt` | less than |
| `contains` | contains the operand |
| `not_contains` | does not contain it |
| `exists` | the path resolves |

## Built-in actions

```text
http · content · query · email · label · run_flow · log
```

plus `code`, which is dispatched before the action map and so is not one of its
entries.

## Platform trigger types

```text
object.created · object.updated · object.published · object.unpublished
object.deleted · object.scheduled · media.uploaded · member.invited
member.created · member.updated · form.submitted · site_user.registered
site_user.login
```

Plus `manual`, `schedule`, `webhook`, and any `ext:<id>:<name>` or `custom:<name>`
an active extension or site helper declares.

## Node configuration

| node | key fields | outlets |
|---|---|---|
| `condition` | `conditions: [{ path, op, value }]` | `yes`, `no` |
| `switch` | `path`, `cases: string[]` | `case:<value>`, `default` |
| `transform` | `output` - an object of expressions | one |
| `loop` | `path`, optional `limit` | **`body`** |
| `wait` | `minutes`, `hours`, `days` | one |
| `action` | `action`, `config` | one, plus `on error` when connected |

## Retry policy

Declared per node as `data.retry`. Nothing retries by default.

| field | default | bounds |
|---|---|---|
| `maxAttempts` | `1` | 1 to `5` |
| `backoff` | `exponential` | `exponential`, `fixed` |
| `baseDelaySeconds` | `30` | 1 to `3600` |

Only a `retryable` failure is retried; `unknown` is not.

## Limits

| limit | value |
|---|---|
| loop iterations | **20** - a longer collection is truncated and records `truncatedFrom` |
| subflow depth | **5** |
| wait minimum | **60 seconds** |
| code CPU | ~1 second |
| code output | **64KB** |
| run retention | **30 days** by default (`runRetentionDays`) |

## Contribution types

From `@tangen/ext-flows/contract`:

| type | shape |
|---|---|
| `FlowOutputField` | `{ key: string; label?: string; type?: 'string' \| 'number' \| 'boolean' \| 'json' \| 'array' }` |
| `FlowActionContribution` | `{ name, label, description?, capability?, configFields?, output?, handler }` |
| `FlowTriggerContribution` | `{ type, label, description?, capability?, payloadFields? }` |
| `FlowActionMeta` | the handler's third argument: `flowId`, `flowName`, `trigger`, `idempotencyKey`, `attempt` |
| `FlowHelpers` | `{ actions?, triggers? }` - the site-helper shape |

`key` is a **dot-path into the returned object** - `lead.id`, `response.status`.

## Options

```ts
{ resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: {
    // Allow private networks is a manifest setting now (Settings, Extensions, Flows), permission-aware under network:private
    failureThreshold: 5,           // consecutive failures before a flow is disabled
    runRetentionDays: 30,
} }
```

## Admin API

| route | does |
|---|---|
| `GET  /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/catalog` | triggers and actions available here |
| `GET  /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows` | list |
| `POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows` | create |
| `PATCH /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/:id` | update |
| `POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/:id/run` | queue a run |
| `POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/:id/test` | dry run, log returned inline |
| `GET  /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/runs` | run history |
| `POST /api/v1/admin/ext/flows/flows/:id/runs/:runId/cancel` | cancel |

Member-authenticated. `/api/v1/ext/*` mounts only `key` and `public` routes,
which is why these live under `/admin/ext/`.

## Related

- [Flow](/extensions/flow) · [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions)

# Flow contract import

Source: https://docs.tangen.app/reference/flow-contract
Section: Reference / Extensions
Verification: source

> The public import surface for Flow contributions and site helpers, and which entry point is not one.

# Flow contract import

## Two supported paths

| you are | import from | how |
|---|---|---|
| an extension contributing actions or triggers | `@tangen/cms` | write them **inline** in `defineExtensionServer`, which types them for you |
| a **site** adding helpers | `@tangen/ext-flows/contract` | `defineFlowHelpers`, with the named contribution types |

The two now agree field for field, so a `FlowActionContribution` is assignable
to what `defineExtensionServer` accepts. They disagreed until Stage G5: the
contract said `{ key, label?, type? }`, which everything consumes, and
`@tangen/types` said `{ path, … }`, which nothing ever read. `key` won, because
every built-in and every shipped contribution already used it.

Either style compiles. Writing inline is usually simpler; annotating is useful
when you build contributions in a separate module.

## `@tangen/ext-flows/contract`

```ts
import {
  defineFlowHelpers,
  type FlowActionContribution,
  type FlowTriggerContribution,
  type FlowActionMeta,
  type FlowOutputField,
  type FlowHelpers,
} from '@tangen/ext-flows/contract'
```
The entry is isomorphic - types plus one identity function, importing nothing
but `@tangen/types`. It resolves on a server, in a bundler, and in a test.

`defineFlowHelpers` is an identity function. It exists for inference and costs
nothing at run time:

```ts
// app/flows/index.ts
export default defineFlowHelpers({
  actions: [{
    name: 'site_notify_sales',
    label: 'Notify sales',
    configFields: [{ key: 'channel', label: 'Channel', kind: 'text' }],
    handler: async (config) => ({ notified: String(config.channel ?? '') }),
  }],
  triggers: [{ type: 'custom:sales.escalated', label: 'Sales escalated' }],
})
```
Site helpers reach Flow through the extension's own options:

```ts
// app/config/extensions.ts
import siteFlowHelpers from '../flows'

export default defineExtensions([
  { resolve: '@tangen/ext-flows', options: { ...siteFlowHelpers } },
])
```
## The package root is not a server import

```ts
import '@tangen/ext-flows'          // ✗ fails outside the Admin bundler
```
The root entry is Flow's Admin barrel: it pulls the canvas pages, which import
the Admin's own `@/kit` alias. On a server that fails with
`Cannot find module '@/kit'`.

This is deliberate, not a defect awaiting repair. Every extension's Admin UI
uses that alias, and it resolves only in the Admin's build. **Use
`@tangen/ext-flows/contract`.**

## Related

- [Flow contributions](/extend/flow-contributions)
- [Public contract](/reference/public-contract)
